title: NIT Rourkela scientists develop lead-free light-emitting materials for safer lighting and security applications
content: Researchers from the National Institute of Technology Rourkela (NIT Rourkela), in collaboration with researchers from IIT Guwahati, IIT Bombay, and NISER Bhubaneswar, have developed new materials that can emit different colours of light under ultraviolet (UV) light exposure. These materials respond to changes in heat and moisture and can have applications in security systems, sensors, and lighting technologies. The research investigated bismuth-based compounds as safer alternatives to lead-based photoluminescent materials, which are widely studied for their light-emission properties but raise significant environmental and health concerns because of lead toxicity. Many materials used for producing light contain lead, which is harmful to human health and the environment. To find a safer alternative, the researchers have investigated bismuth-based compounds, a class of compounds containing both organic and inorganic components, which can offer useful light-emitting properties without relying on lead. Prof. Saroj L Samal, Associate Professor, said, “The most interesting aspect of this material is its ability to undergo reversible structural transformation in response to heat and moisture, accompanied by change in its light emission properties.” This discovery has the potential for protecting important documents and products from counterfeiting. For example, special inks containing the developed material can be used on certificates, signatures, and security labels. Their light-emitting properties could be checked under UV light after controlled heating, which could help verify whether an item is genuine. It could also be useful in humidity sensors. Since its light emission changes with moisture, it may help monitor humidity in food packaging, storage facilities and other places where moisture levels need to be controlled. Further studies will focus on developing efficient and stimuli-responsive luminescent materials for anti-counterfeiting, improving the sensitivity and reliability of sensors, and optimising the performance of white-light-emitting diodes. These efforts could help translate the findings into practical technologies for optical security, environmental monitoring and cost-effective, energy-efficient lighting.

title: Why better data could be the key to AI-driven food R&D
content: Picture a product developer creating a plant-based protein drink for three different markets. The product concept is clear; the information needed to build it is not. Supplier specifications are locked inside PDFs. Trial results sit in spreadsheets. Regulatory requirements arrive by email. Even a single ingredient can carry a different name in each document: “haldi” in one file, “turmeric” in another and “Curcuma longa” in a regulatory note. None of these files is wrong. The problem is that the information is scattered. As a result, the developer spends more time searching, matching, and verifying data than working on the product itself. This has become common across food, beverage, and wellness R&D. Creating a product is no longer only about getting the taste and texture right. It is also about managing and connecting an ever-growing volume of data. Why the data load keeps growing Food product development is becoming more complex, and food safety sits at the centre of that complexity. The World Health Organization’s 2026 estimates, which cover 42 foodborne hazards, found that unsafe food caused an estimated 866 million illnesses and 1.5 million deaths worldwide in 2021. Chemical hazards accounted for 73% of these deaths, with inorganic arsenic and lead alone responsible for 42% and 31% of chemical-related deaths, respectively. The economic toll is just as stark: WHO puts the productivity lost to foodborne disease at $310 billion in 2021. The challenge multiplies when companies develop products for several markets at once. Each market brings its own allergen rules, contaminant limits, permitted claims and labelling norms, and the ingredients themselves vary. In wellness products, for instance, the composition of a botanical can shift with its source, harvest season and processing. With every new ingredient, supplier and market, the volume of information that must be checked and connected keeps growing. Giving data a common language The answer is not another database. It is a shared vocabulary with the relationships built in, which is exactly what an ontology provides. FoodOn, an open food ontology described in npj Science of Food in 2018, was created to tackle a familiar problem: food data siloed across disparate languages and data dictionaries. Still actively maintained, it now contains tens of thousands of classes covering food products, their plant and animal sources, and the processes used to make them. Inside a company, the principle is simple. Turmeric is turmeric, whatever name appears in a spreadsheet, supplier document or regulatory file. An ontology can link that one ingredient to its specification, supplier lot, test results, claims and market requirements. Instead of merely matching keywords across thousands of documents, AI can recognise that different names refer to the same ingredient and connect it to the details that matter. A question such as “Which approved ingredients could breach the lead limit in Market B?” then shifts from a slow, manual exercise to a rapid, data-driven check. Where GenAI fits Generative AI can read supplier documents, scan scientific literature, suggest alternative ingredients and help draft R&D reports. But when information is fragmented, AI can miss important connections or produce answers that are hard to verify. In some cases, it may generate details that sound plausible but are simply not true. An ontology can help address this by grounding GenAI in structured, connected facts. Rather than guessing from loose text, the model can draw on linked information about an ingredient, its supplier, its test history, the rules it must satisfy and the claims made for it, and show where each answer came from. This makes AI outputs easier to check and, ultimately, easier to trust. The ontology provides the map; GenAI makes that map usable. Safety built in, not bolted on In most organisations, even when quality checks run throughout development, some risks only become visible late, once a finished batch reaches the lab. Connected data can bring those risks into view at the design stage. If a developer selects a rice-based protein, the system can flag a potential inorganic arsenic risk well before a pilot batch is made, since rice absorbs arsenic from soil and water more readily than most other cereals. If a recipe changes, implications for allergens and cross-contact can surface immediately. This matters because many foodborne illnesses are preventable, and catching risks upstream reduces rework, delays and costly product recalls. The scientist stays in the loop AI can produce a formulation that is confident and wrong. It cannot taste bitterness, feel grittiness or predict how a blend will behave after months in a humid warehouse. Consider one high-protein beverage project. The AI recommended a pea protein isolate with added calcium and a stabiliser system, a combination that met every target for protein, nutrition and ingredient constraints on paper. In the lab, however, the proteins aggregated after heat processing, leading to visible settling and a chalky mouthfeel. The team had to rework the mineral load and the stabiliser system before the formulation could move forward. The working rule is simple: AI proposes; scientists decide. Every suggestion should trace back to a source, be tested at the bench and be signed off by a qualified person. This matters most in safety and regulatory decisions, where accountability cannot be delegated to software. What comes next The future of food R&D is not about robot chefs. It is about shorter development cycles, because no one has to waste time hunting for information. It is about keeping institutional knowledge within the organisation, even after a scientist moves on. And it is about building safety and compliance into a product from day one, rather than adding them at the end. The messy, unglamorous work of cleaning, naming and connecting data will decide who gets real value from AI. The advantage may not go to the company with the most powerful model, but to the one whose data both people and machines can understand. (Vicky Dodani is the Co-founder of Agrizy) (Disclaimer: The views and opinions expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the views of YourStory.)

title: How to get corporate gifting right across multiple cities
content: Sending Diwali gifts to a handful of employees or clients is relatively simple. Sending hundreds of gifts to recipients spread across different cities is another matter. Addresses need to be verified, budgets finalized, packaging standardized and deliveries timed to arrive before the festival. A missed shipment, incorrect address or last-minute change can quickly complicate the exercise. For businesses managing large-scale Diwali gifting, the key is to plan early, coordinate the details and ensure that every recipient has a consistent experience, regardless of location. Start with a detailed recipient list The first step is to organize all recipient information in one place. This should include names, delivery addresses, contact numbers, and any other information required to complete the delivery. For employee gifting, it may also be useful to group recipients according to city or office location. Client and partner lists can be organized separately so that different gifting requirements are easier to manage. Checking the information before placing the order is important. Incorrect or incomplete addresses can create delivery problems, particularly when gifts are being sent to several cities. Personalize where it matters Large-scale gifting does not have to feel completely impersonal. Businesses can add small details that make gifts feel more thoughtful. A personalized greeting card, recipient name or company message can add a sense of occasion without making the process significantly more complicated. For key clients or long-term partners, businesses may choose a more customized gift, based on the relationship. The goal is to find the right level of personalization for each recipient group while keeping the overall process manageable. Use bulk ordering to simplify the process When a business is managing a large number of recipients, placing individual orders can quickly become time-consuming. Bulk ordering can make the process more organized, particularly when the same or similar gifts are being sent to multiple locations. A single gifting plan can cover product selection, quantities, packaging, and delivery requirements. This also makes it easier for the internal team to monitor the overall budget and track the progress of the campaign. Businesses planning corporate Diwali gifts can also establish recipient categories in advance, making it easier to decide which gift goes to which group. Keep packaging consistent Packaging plays an important role in professional Diwali gifting. When gifts are being sent to different cities, consistent packaging can create a unified brand experience. The same box style, colour scheme, greeting card or branding element can be used across the entire order. This helps ensure that recipients receive gifts that feel like part of the same Diwali campaign, even if they are in different locations. Packaging should also be practical enough to protect the contents during transportation. Fragile products or items sensitive to heat may need additional consideration. Set a clear budget Diwali gifting costs can increase quickly when the recipient list is large. Setting a budget before selecting products helps businesses narrow down suitable options. The budget can be divided by recipient category. For example, employee gifts may have one price range, while client or business-partner gifts may have another. It is also useful to account for packaging, delivery, and personalization costs rather than looking only at the product price. Track every shipment Once the Diwali gifts are ordered, tracking becomes one of the most important parts of the process. A simple tracking sheet can include the recipient, city, order status, and delivery status. This allows the business team to quickly identify delayed or unsuccessful deliveries and take action where required. For larger gifting programmes, having one person or team responsible for monitoring the campaign can make communication much easier. It also prevents different departments from working with separate or outdated recipient lists. Decide what the gift should include The next step is deciding what will go into the Diwali gift. Businesses have several options, from traditional sweets and dry fruits to chocolates, snacks, candles and curated hampers. The choice can depend on the recipient group. Employee gifts may follow one format, while important client or partner gifts may have a different product mix. A consistent selection across cities can make large-scale gifting easier to coordinate. At the same time, businesses can create different categories of gifts based on the relationship with each recipient. This balance can help maintain consistency without making every gift identical. Plan for different delivery locations Sending gifts across multiple cities requires attention to delivery coverage and timelines. Businesses should confirm whether the selected gifting provider can deliver to all the required locations and understand how long each delivery may take. This becomes especially important during Diwali because demand for gifting and delivery services can increase significantly around the festival. Businesses can group orders by city and create a delivery schedule before placing them. This makes it easier to track which gifts have been dispatched, which are in transit, and which have already reached the recipients. Start planning before the festive rush One of the easiest ways to make multi-city Diwali gifting smoother is to start early. Early planning gives businesses more time to finalize recipient details, compare gifting options, approve designs, and schedule deliveries. It also leaves room to handle unexpected issues, such as an incorrect address or a product becoming unavailable. Waiting until the last few days can limit the available options and put additional pressure on both the business team and the delivery network. Making multi-city Diwali gifting easier Diwali gifting across several cities requires more planning than a small personal gifting exercise, but the process becomes manageable when it is treated as a structured campaign. A clear recipient database, suitable gifts, consistent packaging, planned delivery schedules, and proper tracking can help businesses coordinate gifting across locations. The aim is not simply to send gifts to as many people as possible. It is to create a consistent and thoughtful festive experience, even when recipients are spread across different cities. title: Why women should build their front row; AI automation and its impact on jobs
content: Dear Reader, India’s ambition to achieve defence self-reliance gets a big boost. Sarvam has inked a five-year agreement with the defence ministry to develop AI tech for the armed forces. The Bengaluru-based AI company will design, develop and deploy AI applications for operations, training, and decision-support, and also provide follow-on technical assistance. The deal envisages shared foundation models, agentic infrastructure, and geospatial and perception systems. In other news, the high-stakes boardroom battle at the Tata Group continues. Tata Trusts Chairman Noel Tata has challenged the resolution to reappoint N Chandrasekaran as the chairman of Tata Sons. The resolution was passed at the board meeting of the Tata conglomerate’s holding company on September 17. According to sources, Noel has called the reappointment “void”, arguing that it was taken out of turn and was not on the meeting’s agenda. Meanwhile, as it reshapes its workforce amid heavy AI investments, Microsoft is offering employees an exit option. The American tech major has announced a voluntary exit programme for eligible employees in India, the US, the UK, and Canada. The package includes one month’s base salary for each completed year of service, besides health insurance and career transition services. Globally, around 60,000 employees are eligible for the programme. Microsoft has about 23,000 employees in India. However, it’s not clear how many would be eligible in the country. Lastly, Wall Street is closely watching the upcoming Big Tech earnings, which could serve as testimony to AI growth in an otherwise turbulent market. In today’s newsletter, we will talk about Why women should build their front row AI automation and its impact on jobs Here’s your trivia for today: At what temperature do Fahrenheit and Celsius match? (Scroll down for the answer) Women in Tech Kripa Venkatachalam of Cadence urges women to build their front row As part of our Women in Tech series, Kripa Venkatachalam, VP, India Technical Field Organisation & Global Customer Success at Cadence Design Systems, reflects on gender barriers, changing workplace policies, mentorship, and the importance of having people who egg you on. Her career spanning more than two decades has taken her through diverse roles across companies, including LSI Logic Corporation, Synopsys, GlobalFoundries, and Siemens EDA. Today, as VP, India Technical Field Organisation & Global Customer Success at Cadence Design Systems, she has what she calls a “front-row seat” to how the world’s chips are designed in India. Key takeaways: Kripa believes women need to seek support, leverage their network, and not always put the burden on themselves. “You have to make your family work for you, your workplace work for you, your society work for you. You have to lean in and take the help,” she says. At informal forums in Cadence, she often speaks about the need for people, especially women, to create their own front row—people cheering for them. “The front row has to assure you. Organisations and managers have to look closer, look harder, and encourage women forward,” she reiterates. As she looks ahead, Kripa resists the idea of tying her ambitions to a title. She describes her career as a jungle gym rather than a ladder, an image she credits to Sheryl Sandberg. <Funding Alert> Startup: Cent Amount: $15M Round: Series A Startup: Simplismart Amount: $14M Round: Series B Startup: Live2.ai Amount: Rs 130 Cr Round: Pre-Series B TechSparks Capital no longer creates jobs: Yatish Rajawat of Hundred Million Jobs At TechSparks 2026, K Yatish Rajawat, Co-founder of Hundred Million Jobs, a non-profit initiative to create 100 million net jobs in India over the next decade, said MSMEs, data laws, entrepreneurship and reskilling will shape the next wave of employment in the country. Key takeaways: Rajawat identified three trends reshaping the economy. One, the old formula, wherein Rs 100 crore of investment generates around 10,000 jobs, no longer holds, said Rajawat. Schemes such as the production-linked incentive are tied to capital rather than employment, he added. The second trend is the impact of AI and automation. AI is already affecting white-collar work across sectors. MSMEs, which he called the country’s largest job engine, are also losing jobs to automation. The third is platform consolidation. Rajawat argued that dominant ecommerce and social media platforms hold consumer data, which new entrepreneurs need, and this kind of monopoly prevents new businesses from succeeding. If entrepreneurship stalls, so does job creation, he said. Phone replacement: Apple has acknowledged that some of its iPhone Duo handsets have developed problems with their screens, just days after the highly anticipated smartphone went on sale. It has urged affected users to contact the company for a replacement. Fundraise: Troovy, a food and snacks brand, has raised Rs 100 crore in a Series B round of funding led by Fireside Ventures, with participation from Sharrp Ventures and other investors. The Gurugram-based brand will use the funding for R&D, expanding its manufacturing capacity, and scaling distribution across quick commerce and offline channels, as it looks to launch a wide range of products. title: ‘Cope harder’: Vaishnaw defends India's iPhone PLI scheme
content: Assembling iPhones makes great headlines for India. Owning the supply chain is where the real power lies. Apple assembled around 55 million iPhones in India in 2025, a 53% increase from 36 million units in 2024. The country now accounts for about a quarter of Apple's global iPhone output, according to a Bloomberg report. The growth has strengthened India's position as an alternative manufacturing base to China. While skeptics question whether snapping together foreign components delivers true high-tech independence, the government points to ₹3.25 lakh crore in tax collections and 12 lakh new jobs as proof that the PLI scheme is already paying off handsomely. Vaishnaw counters criticism with tax and employment figures The debate intensified after a Bloomberg Opinion video questioned whether India should replicate China's manufacturing model. It highlighted India's dependence on imported components and the cost of government subsidies supporting phone production. Union Electronics and IT Minister Ashwini Vaishnaw responded on X on October 27, defending the government's Production Linked Incentive (PLI) scheme for mobile manufacturing. According to the figures he shared, the government had paid Rs 19,000 crore in incentives, while direct tax collections reached Rs 25,000 crore. The sector had also generated Rs 3 lakh crore in Goods and Services Tax (GST) collections. Mobile PLI stats as follows: Government incentive paid: Rs 19,000 Cr. Direct tax collected: Rs 25,000 Cr. GST collected: Rs 3,00,000 Cr. Electronics manufacturing employs 25 Lakh people; mobile manufacturing alone employs 12 Lakh. Cope harder!! https://t.co/G3bDU6ldGg — Ashwini Vaishnaw (@AshwiniVaishnaw) October 27, 2026 Vaishnaw also cited employment figures, saying electronics manufacturing supported 25 lakh jobs, including 12 lakh in mobile phone manufacturing. He ended his post with the pointed remark, “Cope harder!!” The figures form the government's case for continuing to support domestic manufacturing. However, tax collections and job creation are only part of the discussion. India's iPhone growth comes with a supply chain challenge India's expanding role in Apple's manufacturing network is a significant development. In 2025, the country assembled around 55 million iPhones, up from 36 million in 2024. Apple also began assembling all variants of its iPhone 17 line-up in India, including the Pro and Pro Max models, according to The Times of India. Yet assembling a finished product is different from manufacturing all its components locally. India continues to depend on imports for several critical parts, including processors, memory chips, displays, camera lenses and batteries. This matters because the economic value generated by manufacturing depends partly on how much of the supply chain operates within the country. Greater domestic production of components could help Indian suppliers capture more value while reducing reliance on overseas manufacturers. The next test is building more of the iPhone in India The government's manufacturing push now faces a more demanding test: turning higher production volumes into a deeper domestic electronics ecosystem. That means expanding local component manufacturing, bringing more suppliers into the country and strengthening research and design capabilities. These steps could help India progress beyond final assembly and establish a more substantial presence in global electronics supply chains. India's iPhone production growth demonstrates that the country can attract large-scale manufacturing. Whether that translates into lasting economic gains will depend on its ability to build more of the technology and supply chain behind each device.

title: From Homemade Badi to GomatiRoots: Shital Kumari Secures Funding
content: Key Takeaways GomatiRoots is building a brand around Bihar's traditional badi. The startup received Rs 1 lakh in funding through YourStory's Shuru Kar initiative. Shital Kumari's startup is connecting rural women with markets. The company generated Rs 32 lakh in revenue in its first financial year. Last September, in 2025, the Bihar Idea Festival concluded at Bapu Sabhagar in Patna. YourStory launched the festival under its initiative, The Bharat Project , in collaboration with the Bihar Industries Department and the Chandragupt Institute of Management, Patna (CIMP). The objective was to take entrepreneurship beyond metropolitan cities and select groups of people, reaching young people in smaller towns and villages and helping them turn their business ideas into reality. Shital Kumari was among those present at the event. She wanted to start her own business but had several questions. What business should she start? How would she get started? Where would the money come from? And what would happen if her efforts failed? Life had already exposed her to numerous challenges. Taking the risk of starting a business was not easy, but she decided to take a step towards turning her idea into reality. Nearly a year later, Shital's efforts reached an important milestone. Through YourStory's Shuru Kar initiative, she received funding of Rs 1 lakh for her startup , GomatiRoots . The funding came from Shradha Sharma, Founder and CEO of YourStory and The Bharat Project. For Shital, the amount represented more than financial support; it was also a sign of confidence in her idea. Through GomatiRoots, Shital aims to give Bihar's traditional badi and other indigenous food products a distinct identity. She wants badi, a traditional lentil-based food product that has been part of Indian households for generations, to establish itself as a trusted brand in the market. Building a Business Amid Challenges To understand Shital's entrepreneurial journey, it is important to look back at her early life. She grew up in Bihar and completed her education at government institutions. She studied up to Class 10 at Shri Guru Gobind Singh Girls High School, completed her intermediate education at RPM College, and earned an honours degree in Physics from the College of Commerce. She wanted to pursue a BTech degree, but that dream did not materialise. Nevertheless, she continued her education and later completed an MA from Nalanda Open University. A friend helped her with Rs 4,500 to pursue her studies. In 2018, her life took a major turn when she lost her younger brother. Following his death, her family moved to Muzaffarpur. As the family struggled to cope with the loss, Shital lost her mother during the COVID-19 pandemic. After her mother's death, the responsibility of caring for her younger siblings fell on her shoulders. She moved to Patna to support her family and began looking for work. Over the next two to three years, she took up video editing, taught children, and even sold lychees whenever necessary. Throughout this period, she continued preparing for the Union Public Service Commission (UPSC) examination . During this time, she learned about the Bihar Laghu Udyami Yojana , a state government initiative designed to support small entrepreneurs. She applied for the scheme and received Rs 50,000 as the first instalment. She also received training to start her business. Later, she received a second instalment of Rs 1 lakh. In addition, she took a loan of Rs 2 lakh and laid the foundation for GomatiRoots in Patna. Speaking to YourStory, Shital says, "There were several phases in my life when taking care of my family was the most important responsibility. After my mother passed away, looking after my younger siblings became my priority. I worked in video editing, taught children, and even sold lychees. At the same time, I continued preparing for the UPSC examination. When I learned about the Bihar Laghu Udyami Yojana, I felt that perhaps I finally had an opportunity to start something of my own. I did not have much money, but I decided to begin with whatever resources I had." How Her Mother's Homemade Badi Inspired a Business GomatiRoots did not begin with a long-standing business ambition. Instead, the idea emerged from a deeply personal experience. After her mother's death, Shital often missed the badi her mother used to make. When she began looking for a similar product in the market, she could not find one that matched the taste and quality she remembered. Some products raised concerns about adulteration, while others did not offer the varieties she preferred. What began as a personal search soon revealed a potential business opportunity. Shital started researching the market, speaking to people, and learning more about badi. During her research, she observed that while India had several well-established pickle and papad brands, badi had not achieved the same level of recognition. Yet, in Bihar and many other parts of India, lentil-based badi is a regular part of everyday meals. It is eaten with lentils, vegetables, and other dishes, and the tradition of making it at home has continued for generations. Despite its popularity, badi often remains a locally produced food item rather than a recognised packaged brand. Shital believed that the product could establish a stronger market presence if it were made available throughout the year with consistent quality and better packaging. This insight gradually shaped the idea behind GomatiRoots. For her, badi was more than a food product. It represented memories of her mother, the taste of home, and an opportunity to bring Bihar's culinary traditions to a wider audience. Shital says, "The idea of building a brand around badi was not something I had thought about since childhood. After my mother passed away, I looked for a product in the market that tasted like the badi she used to make. That was when I realised there was a need for a reliable brand. I studied the market and spoke to people. There are several pickle and papad brands, but I did not see the same kind of identity for badi. I felt that if we could make it available throughout the year with consistent quality, people would embrace it." Turning Traditional Flavours Into a Brand GomatiRoots started with badi, but its product range has since expanded to include several traditional varieties. These include urad dal badi, moongori, chana dal badi, Bihari masala badi, and kohrauri. The company also offers traditional fryums such as tisiyori and tilauri. Through these products, Shital aims to bring greater recognition to flavours that have long been part of households and local communities. One of the biggest challenges in this business is the seasonal nature of badi production. Traditionally, making badi depends heavily on sunlight and weather conditions. Unfavourable weather can affect both production and product quality. Ensuring that customers receive a consistent product throughout the year is therefore not easy. Shital has tried to address this challenge through research and experimentation. Her goal is to ensure that customers receive the same quality every time they purchase a product, regardless of the season. According to Shital, the business has received encouraging customer feedback within its first year of operations. Repeat orders from retail shopkeepers, in particular, have strengthened her confidence. These orders indicate that customers are not simply trying the product once but are willing to buy it again. However, maintaining this trust requires continuous improvements in production, packaging, and storage. Shital says, "Making badi available throughout the year is one of our most important priorities. Traditionally, it has been prepared according to the weather and availability of sunlight. But if we want to build a brand, customers must receive consistent quality every time. We have conducted research at our level and improved our production methods. Over the past year, we have received repeat orders from shopkeepers. When customers tell us that our products taste like homemade food, that means a lot to us." Limited Capital, a Larger Market, and New Challenges GomatiRoots initially relied on government scheme assistance and a loan to get its operations started. With limited resources, Shital had to account for every expense carefully. Purchasing raw materials, developing packaging, delivering products to retail outlets, and building brand awareness all required money. Rather than expanding in multiple directions at once, she chose to grow the business gradually. The company currently generates revenue by supplying products to retail stores, restaurants, and cloud kitchens, as well as selling directly to customers. GomatiRoots products are available at more than 50 stores in Patna. The company is also working to expand its presence in other districts of Bihar through distributors. Its products are available on Amazon, Flipkart, and JioMart. Customers can also place orders through the company's website, gomatiroots.com. In addition, the business reaches customers directly through exhibitions, fairs, and canopy stalls. Funding Through YourStory's Shuru Kar Initiative During its first financial year of operations, GomatiRoots generated revenue of Rs 32 lakh. Shital is now looking to expand into larger retail networks and quick-commerce platforms. However, entering large retail stores and organised markets requires a reliable supply chain. The business must also address product shelf life, packaging, and storage requirements. Shital is working to overcome these challenges. She also plans to bring more people on board to strengthen e-commerce operations and direct-to-consumer sales. She says, "We started the business with very limited capital. In the beginning, we had to account for every rupee. We had production and packaging expenses on one side and the challenge of reaching retail stores on the other. Large retail companies also want to know whether a brand can maintain a consistent supply. We are gradually strengthening our sales record and distributor network. We intend to use the Rs 1 lakh funding received through YourStory's Shuru Kar initiative for working capital and marketing as well." Connecting Women's Work With Market Opportunities GomatiRoots' ambitions extend beyond increasing product sales. Shital wants women and small producers who make traditional food products in Bihar to benefit from access to larger markets. Some of the company's products are prepared in collaboration with rural women's self-help groups (SHGs). These include different varieties of tisiyori made with flaxseed, potatoes, and rice, along with rice-based tilauri and kohrauri. The women already have experience preparing these traditional foods. GomatiRoots aims to help them connect with buyers and access wider markets. Shital is also in discussions with JEEViKA , Bihar's rural livelihoods initiative. She was invited as a buyer to the Saras Mela and now hopes to establish long-term partnerships to source traditional products directly from JEEViKA Didis . Her objective is to ensure that the women receive fair prices for their products and gain access to regular income opportunities. In the future, she also wants to work with farmers in Bihar so that the lentils used to make badi can be cultivated locally, allowing farmers to benefit from the business. Over the next three to five years, Shital hopes to take GomatiRoots beyond Bihar and into major cities across India. Her plans include expanding into large retail stores, online marketplaces, and quick-commerce platforms. The company also hopes to open its own store and eventually export its products internationally. Alongside expansion, Shital wants to formalise business operations, obtain the necessary licences, increase production capacity, and make better use of available business support schemes. One of her long-term goals is to create year-round work opportunities for up to one lakh women associated with JEEViKA's self-help groups. For now, this remains an ambition that she hopes to pursue as the business grows. Shital says, "I want the growth of GomatiRoots to translate into higher incomes for women in Bihar. Many women here have excellent skills in preparing traditional food products, but they lack the means to reach larger markets. If they receive regular work and fair prices, their efforts can gain greater recognition. We also want to work with farmers so that the lentils used in badi can be grown in Bihar itself. My dream is to take these flavours across the country and around the world." The Road Ahead Shital Kumari's story is not about building a business with abundant capital, an established market, and plenty of resources from the outset. She found her way forward while managing family responsibilities, took up different jobs, and used support from a government scheme to establish her business. The Rs 1 lakh funding she subsequently received through YourStory's Shuru Kar initiative has further strengthened confidence in her idea. Her search for the badi her mother used to make helped her identify a gap in the market, one she is now working to address through her brand. GomatiRoots still faces several challenges. It must increase production while maintaining quality, strengthen customer trust, and build a more organised business to compete in larger markets. However, Shital has a clear goal: she wants badi to become more than a product associated with a particular household or region. She wants customers to recognise the brand by name and purchase it with confidence. Entrepreneurship in India is often associated with large investments and technology startups. But the story of GomatiRoots, which emerged from Bihar, offers a different perspective. Its foundation is not a new technology but a traditional food product that has been part of everyday meals for generations. The real challenge lies in adapting that product to market requirements, building a trusted identity, and creating income opportunities for the people involved in its production. For Shital, the journey is still in its early stages. She dreams of a day when someone in any part of India looking to buy lentil-based badi will think of GomatiRoots. The coming years will determine how far this ambition takes her. For now, her journey demonstrates that entrepreneurship does not always require an entirely new idea. Sometimes, the beginnings of a business can be found in the familiar flavours of home. Hokar Nidar Shuru Kar. title: Government working to utilise procurement process for promoting startups: DPIIT Secretary
content: The government is working to leverage the procurement process to promote startups, a top official of the Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade said on Tuesday. Speaking at the curtain-raiser event for National Startup Awards 6.0, Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade (DPIIT) Secretary Amardeep Singh Bhatia said that there is a need for more private initiatives to engage with startups and bring them into their supply chain network. "We are also working with other agencies to see how government procurement can also be better used for promoting startups by providing them with at least early access to demand," he said. Elaborating on the move to enhance participation of startups in government procurement, DPIIT Additional Secretary Ateesh Kumar Singh said that there are already certain facilities available in the form of relaxations to the GFR (General Financial Rules). "Also, here are certain circulars which have been put out by various agencies to make the pathway into the government procurement process easier. The partaking of those benefits still remains a challenge. It is there where we are trying to make sure that the offerings are available to them," he said. Singh said that a lot of problems also occur due to information asymmetry. "One part of the problem is to tell people what is available. The second part of the problem is partaking in those things. We are also trying to address challenges in our existing system. We are working with various ministries, including the Department of Finance, Public Enterprises and MSME. This is ongoing work and we will come up with a new framework," he said. He said that the number of startups in the country has grown to over 2.5 lakh, with more than half of them located in tier 3 and smaller towns. Under the 6th Edition of the National Startup Awards (NSA 6.0), winning startups across the 20 sectoral categories and the two startup-focused special categories will be eligible for a cash prize of Rs 25 lakh per category, subject to the applicable award guidelines. The student innovator and aspiring entrepreneur award will carry a total prize pool of Rs 25 lakh across four sub-categories. In addition to monetary recognition, the National Startup Awards seek to facilitate mentorship, investor engagement, market access, industry partnerships and enhanced visibility within India’s startup ecosystem. The 20 categories will also include three special categories comprising women-led startups, startups from the north-eastern region and student innovators or aspiring entrepreneurs.

title: When content becomes infinite, what makes people pay attention?
content: We are living in a world where content is no longer scarce. There is more news, more videos, more creators, and, AI that can generate almost anything we ask for. But this abundance brings a new challenge: when everyone is creating content, how do you get someone to stop scrolling, pay attention, and come back? On the sidelines of TechSparks 2026, Avinash Mudaliar, Co-founder and CEO of HT Media Labs and the creator of Saregama Carvaan; Deepit Purkayastha, Co-founder and CEO of Inshorts; and GSN Aditya, COO of Eloelo Group, came together for a discussion titled The Format Is the Product: When Content Becomes Infinite . The conversation explored how formats shape the way audiences consume content, what makes a format resonate in an increasingly crowded digital landscape, and why the format itself can be as important as the content it carries. What is the differentiator in all this: the format, distribution, personalisation or the relationship with the consumer? “Actually, the four items you mentioned aren't rivals. They are congruent; they co-exist. And all of them need to be married in a particular combination to get a person to come back. Right now, the problem is not content. Content has become infinite. Time has become finite,” said Mudaliar. He explained that when he was building Carvaan, he had a clear target audience: people who didn't want to open an app, create a playlist, log in, pay, go through the entire rigmarole just to listen, and then go to a search bar and search for a song. Carvaan put in 5,000 songs in a fully digitised, personalised product, without advertising itself as digital. Instead, it recreated the experience of listening to old-time radio, limiting the choices available and allowing listeners to immerse themselves in the music. With OTT Play, the focus was primarily on personalisation, helping users decide what to watch, where to watch it and how. Purkayastha said that when he started Inshorts 12 years ago, people were beginning to consume content on smartphones, but no app was truly innovating on how they consumed news and information on these devices. “Today, people come to us because they want a reliable, factual source of information. They want to stay updated on the world, but they don't want the noise and provocativeness of social media. We are a source reliable enough that they can use it during their digital detox,” he said. For Eloelo, the micro-drama format unlocked the ability to tell many more stories faster and reach a wider audience. “I think people's tastes continue to change, and while there is infinite content, the top 5% is often where most of the eyeballs go. So it comes down to your ability to keep reinventing the story arc, tell new stories, and deliver them through state-of-the-art data science to personalise content so people always see what they want to see,” said Aditya. The role of AI There's a general perception that AI can create everything, so what will audiences actually value? Purkayastha says that while AI platforms are increasingly meeting consumers’ on-demand information needs, people still want real-time updates. “AI can't imagine what's happening at TechSparks right now. Someone has to feed it into the system. That is live content generation, and that is news. Summaries and articles are the collateral that emerge from it. “When an event happens, the question is which sources and distributors will be trusted. Trust becomes the most interesting capital they build, and I think LLM agents will value it too.” Aditya believes AI will accelerate content creation but cannot replace human creativity. “It's a great enabler for people to tell stories, but I don't think it will substitute for human creativity,” he says, pointing out that despite the money and data invested in Hollywood and Bollywood, no deterministic system can predict whether a story will be a hit. “People's tastes continuously change, and their expectations change. That can only be solved by human creativity.” He added that AI would speed up storytelling workflows, while creativity and inspiration would remain human-driven. Trust and verification Mudaliar points to trust and verification as key differentiators in an AI-driven content ecosystem. “There's a very interesting concept we're trying out at HT Tech right now. HT is already a trusted source for most LLMs for India-oriented news and beyond, simply because we've been around for the last 100 years. We take pride in our journalism, and we put out verified stories. We are now building another ecosystem within HT called HT Verify,” he explained. “For example, our team member here is capturing this event, creating a video out of it that will also be made into social content, and writing maybe 3,000 words on it, written to the schema AI LLMs prefer and made citable by the AI. So you are literally training the AI that this content is not only trustworthy, it's also verified and ready for consumption. That results in your content being cited and picked up, and then transmogrified for the user,” he added. For Purkayastha, understanding audiences beyond urban India meant identifying a gap in trustworthy local content. When Inshorts began exploring consumption patterns in smaller cities in 2019, as mobile internet use surged following Jio's arrival, the team realised that local news from smaller towns often went unreported. “We realised that the biggest gap in those markets was that content generation wasn't happening in a trustworthy way,” he says. The company addressed this gap with Public, a platform featuring verified creators who report on their towns and cities. Launched in 2019, it has since reached about 80 million users. For Aditya, micro-drama economics have created opportunities to tell stories for more specific audiences rather than chase mass appeal. With lower production costs and shorter turnaround times, creators can experiment with stories rooted in particular regions and communities. “I no longer have to make storylines that only appeal to a large catchment of people. I can now talk about storylines relevant to, say, a district in Uttar Pradesh, and the P&L still works. So we're now able to tap into Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh, Karnataka, Kerala, each of these,” he said. Mudaliar believes the industry still has a long way to go in designing products for India's diverse linguistic audiences. Despite the emphasis on building for Bharat, he argues, many products continue to draw inspiration from platforms designed primarily for urban consumers. “98% of India consumes in a local language. He doesn't know how to search; he doesn't know how to write in English; he's trying. For him, voice search is the first point of contact because he doesn't know how to type. That's why even Google Maps, even your Uber drivers, use voice. So why aren't we building voice-first products for India?” he asked.

title: Jio Platforms gains 27% on day one of listing, becomes second most valued company in India
content: After making a strong debut on the National Stock Exchange today, the shares of Jio Platforms closed at Rs 1,419, at a gain of 26.81%. Jio Platforms achieved a market capitalisation of Rs 13,06,761.47 crore on its first day of trading, making it the second most valued company on the Indian stock markets, next only only to its parent firm Reliance Industries. The top five Indian companies in terms of market capitalisation now are: Reliance Industries (Rs 16 lakh crore), Jio Platforms (Rs 13 lakh crore), Bharti Airtel (Rs 12 lakh crore), HDFC Bank (Rs 10.57 lakh crore), and ICICI Bank (Rs 9.89 lakh crore). Tata Consultancy Services has moved to the sixth place (Rs 8.90 lakh crore). Jio Platforms' share opened at Rs 1,358 today, gaining 21.3% over the issue price of Rs 1,119 apiece. The company's Rs 30,213-crore IPO received an overwhelming response from investors last week. It was oversubscribed in less than two hours on opening day, and closed with a 22X oversubscription. As it positions itself as a technology firm, Jio Platforms is betting on digital services, artificial intelligence, and cloud computing to drive growth beyond telecom. "There is no either-or at Jio: the network is our technology," said Akash Ambani, Managing Director of Jio Platforms, highlighting the company's in-house 5G core, cloud-native radio access network, and software platform serving 533.3 million customers. “Connectivity was the first product we built on that platform. Digital services, AI and cloud are what we are layering on top of it now," he said. Meanwhile, brokerage houses are bullish on the prospects of Jio Platforms. Motilal Oswal, in its note, said scaling up digital platforms (cloud, enterprise communications, IoT, and managed services, along with international tie-ups for 5G/UBR technology) will offer Jio Platforms the next leg of growth beyond the connectivity business. The brokerage house has set a bull-case target price of Rs 1,690 crore and a bear-case target price of Rs 1,035. Image credit: NSE The copy was updated with additional information.

title: Info Edge’s Hitesh Oberoi to step down as MD and CEO; founder Sanjeev Bikhchandani to take over
content: Hitesh Oberoi, Managing Director and Chief Executive Officer of Info Edge, will step down from his full-time executive role on December 2, 2026, after nearly 27 years with the company, including more than 16 years as MD. The parent of Naukri.com announced the leadership change alongside its second-quarter FY27 results. Sanjeev Bikhchandani, the founder of Info Edge, will take over as Executive Vice Chairman, Managing Director and Group CEO from December 3, 2026, subject to shareholder approval. The move will see Bikhchandani return to an active management role after serving as Executive Vice Chairman. According to the company's regulatory filing, his term will run until April 26, 2031. Oberoi, however, will continue to be associated with the company. Subject to shareholder approval, he will remain on its board as a Non-Executive, Non-Independent Director. Info Edge said he had chosen to step back from his full-time executive role to devote more time to education, entrepreneurship, institution building, investing and philanthropy, while spending more time with his family. In a statement, Oberoi said that after nearly 27 years, he felt it was the right time to begin transitioning out of his full-time operating role. He added that he would miss the colleagues and teams who had made those years special. Bikhchandani said the two had built Info Edge together over more than 27 years. Oberoi's tenure spans much of Info Edge's growth. According to a report citing the company's filing, its market capitalisation increased from Rs 2,500 crore to Rs 80,000 crore during his tenure. Oberoi formally took over as CEO and MD in 2010, when Bikhchandani moved into the role of Executive Vice Chairman. The company said it has a strong institutional foundation, supported by senior leaders who have been with Info Edge for more than 20 years. Investors will be watching how the leadership change affects Info Edge’s core recruitment business and broader strategy. The move comes after CFO Chintan Thakkar stepped down in November 2025, with co-promoter Ambarish Raghuvanshi taking over as interim CFO.

title: PhysicsWallah partners with DPIIT to support early-stage ventures
content: PhysicsWallah’s School of Startups (PW SoS) has signed a two-year memorandum of understanding with the Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade (DPIIT) to support early-stage ventures, particularly in Tier-II and III cities and rural areas. The partnership combines training and mentoring with prototype development, incubation, investor access and seed capital. “Supporting entrepreneurs beyond Tier-I cities is key to building a stronger startup ecosystem in India. Our partnership with PhysicsWallah School of Startups will help grassroots innovators access the resources, mentorship and infrastructure they need to turn their ideas into scalable, job-creating businesses across Bharat,” said Ateesh Kumar Singh, Additional Secretary at DPIIT. PW SoS, an accredited incubator under Uttar Pradesh’s StartinUP initiative, has programmes for founders at different stages. PW UDYAMI combines 90 days of live online training with a year of mentorship. Aarambh Immersion is a five-day residential programme for prototype development, pitches and networking. The Growth Stage CEO Programme is designed for 200 DPIIT-recognised startups across four hybrid cohorts, while the six-month PW DeepTech Accelerator targets selected ventures. The annual National AI Startup Challenge and SeedX are intended to offer proof-of-concept opportunities, corporate pilots and seed investment. The release also cites incubation and seed grants through the StartinUP Business Incubation Centre in Uttar Pradesh. Rounaq Mustafa, Head of PW SoS, said the aim was to widen access to support. “True empowerment means making knowledge, mentorship and funding accessible to aspiring entrepreneurs across Bharat. Through our partnership with DPIIT and Startup India, PW School of Startups aims to support aspiring founders.” The tie-up comes as the ecosystem grows and public support expands. DPIIT recently shared that it had recognised 2,50,046 startups across more than 770 districts, with 52% based in non-metro cities. The Startup India Seed Fund Scheme had approved Rs 775.67 crore for 4,194 startups through 244 incubators, including 2,356 ventures in Tier-II and III cities. In April, the government notified a Rs 10,000 crore Startup India Fund of Funds 2.0, which channels capital through investment funds rather than directly giving grants to every startup. Policy is also addressing research-led businesses, which often need longer development periods and more capital. In February, the government extended the recognition window for deeptech startups to 20 years and raised their turnover limit to Rs 300 crore. Private programmes are specialising too. Google’s 2026 India accelerator selected 20 AI-focused startups from around 2,500 applications for technical and commercialisation support.

title: Startup news and updates: daily roundup (October 28, 2026)
content: From Jio Platforms making a strong debut on the National Stock Exchange on Wednesday with its shares gaining 21.3% over the issue price of Rs 1,119 apiece, to AI that can generate almost anything we ask for, here are the latest developments across sectors. Featured Stories When content becomes infinite, what makes people pay attention? We are living in a world where content is no longer scarce. There is more news, more videos, more creators, and, AI that can generate almost anything we ask for. But this abundance brings a new challenge: when everyone is creating content, how do you get someone to stop scrolling, pay attention, and come back? On the sidelines of TechSparks 2026, Avinash Mudaliar, Co-founder and CEO of HT Media Labs and the creator of Saregama Carvaan; Deepit Purkayastha, Co-founder and CEO of Inshorts; and GSN Aditya, COO of Eloelo Group, came together for a discussion titled The Format Is the Product: When Content Becomes Infinite. Read more Latest News Jio Platforms makes strong market debut, lists on NSE with a gain of 21.3% Jio Platforms made a strong debut on the National Stock Exchange on Wednesday with its shares gaining 21.3% over the issue price of Rs 1,119 apiece, resulting in a market capitalisation of Rs 12.5 lakh crore. The share opened at Rs 1,358 and reached an intraday high of Rs 1,374.50. It was trading at Rs 1,366.60 at 11:41 am with a market capitalisation of Rs 12,58,045.70 crore. Jio Platforms' Rs 30,213-crore IPO received an overwhelming response from investors. It was oversubscribed in less than two hours on opening day, and closed with a 22X oversubscription. Read more Funding News Healthy snack brand Troovy raises Rs 100 Cr in Series B round led by Fireside Ventures Troovy, a food and snacks brand, has raised Rs 100 crore in a Series B round of funding led by Fireside Ventures, with participation from Sharrp Ventures and other investors. The Gurugram-based brand will use the funding for R&D, expanding its manufacturing capacity, and scaling distribution across quick commerce and offline channels, as it looks to launch a wide range of products. Troovy was founded in 2023 by Mansi Baranwal and Aditya Mukherjee with the goal of providing nutritious food. Its portfolio spans categories such as snacks, sauces and spreads, and millet pasta. It says its vacuum-cooked potato chips have 10-12% oil and high protein, compared with 35-40% oil in mainstream chips. It also promises clean-label ketchups and seasonings without synthetic additives or preservatives. Read more Other News QwikBuild raises $2.3M in pre-seed funding, enters Japan through JV Bengaluru-based enterprise AI startup QwikBuild has raised $2.3 million in pre-seed funding from Globalway Inc, Blume Ventures, Marsshot, DeVC and angel investors, including Groww founder Lalit Keshre and Cure.fit founder Ankit Nagori. The company also announced a joint venture with publicly listed Japanese firm Globalway to enter Japan’s enterprise market. QwikBuild uses autonomous AI agents to build bespoke enterprise software in days, enabling businesses to automate workflows, modernise legacy systems and integrate applications with existing platforms such as SAP and Salesforce. The startup currently serves enterprises across India, the US and Singapore. PhonePe rebrands Indus Appstore, targets digital goods market with 200 million devices PhonePe has rebranded its homegrown app marketplace, Indus Appstore, as PhonePe Appstore, as it expands into digital goods and services. The platform is available on more than 200 million devices through original equipment manufacturer (OEM) partnerships, with Uttar Pradesh, Maharashtra, Bihar, Karnataka and Telangana among its top markets. Alongside apps and games, users can access gift cards and digital top-ups, with gaming top-ups scheduled to launch first. PhonePe has also introduced phonepeappstore.com, a webstore for discovering and purchasing digital products through browsers. The platform aims to offer developers alternative distribution and monetisation opportunities through payments, advertising and digital sales. ixigo co-founder Rajnish Kumar launches Rs 1 crore fund to back IIT Kanpur startups ixigo co-founder and Group Co-CEO Rajnish Kumar has launched the Rs 1 crore Made in Fire Fund to support technology-led startups founded by graduating IIT Kanpur students. Beginning with the Class of 2026, the initiative will select 10 startups per batch, offering each Rs 10 lakh in non-dilutive prototype funding. Beyond capital, founders will receive mentorship from Kumar, ixigo’s leadership team and its wider entrepreneur network, alongside product reviews, go-to-market guidance, hiring support and investor introductions. The fund will prioritise founder conviction, customer understanding and execution over pitch decks, backing ventures across AI, SaaS, deep tech, mobility, healthcare and other technology sectors. CHOSEN Extends Series A with Backing from Wellbeing Nutrition Founders CHOSEN, India's first exposome-based dermocosmetic brand, has extended its Series A round with investment from Wellbeing Nutrition founders Avnish Chhabria and Saurabh Kapoor, joining Fireside Ventures, L'Oréal's BOLD, and Alkemi Growth Capital. The fresh capital will strengthen R&D, expand the formulation pipeline across topicals and nutraceuticals, and fund a dermatologist-led Centre of Excellence. Founded in 2020 by Dr Renita Rajan, the Chennai-based brand formulates melanin-rich Indian skin, targeting pigmentation, texture, contour and hair ageing. It offers over 50 products prescribed by more than 2,000 doctors, and raised a $5 million Series A in May 2026. Bellatrix Aerospace appoints Kiran U as CFO to drive growth and international expansion Bengaluru-based in-space mobility company Bellatrix Aerospace has appointed Kiran U as its Chief Financial Officer (CFO) to lead its financial strategy and support business expansion. A Chartered Accountant and Company Secretary, Kiran brings over 17 years of experience across financial planning, treasury, capital raising, taxation, audit and investor relations. In his new role, he will focus on capital efficiency, funding diversification, financial discipline and operational scalability as the company pursues international opportunities and expands its commercial pipeline. Bellatrix Aerospace develops in-space propulsion technologies, including Arka Hall Effect Thrusters and Rudra Green Propulsion Systems, for satellite and space missions. PB Money secures SEBI licence to expand retail access to bonds PB Money, an investment platform strategically partnered with Paisabazaar, has received a Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) licence as an Online Bond Platform Provider (OBPP). The licence allows the platform to manage the entire bond investment journey, covering investor onboarding, KYC, bond discovery, order placement, payments and post-investment servicing. Through its partnership with Paisabazaar, PB Money aims to reach a wider consumer base and simplify access to fixed-income products. Investors can compare bonds based on parameters such as yield, credit rating and investment amount, helping them evaluate options and diversify their portfolios." PhysicsWallah’s School of Startups partners with DPIIT to support 25,000 startups PhysicsWallah’s School of Startups (PW SoS) has partnered with the Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade (DPIIT) under a two-year agreement to support 25,000 early-stage startups across India. The initiative will focus on entrepreneurs in Tier-II and Tier-III cities and rural areas, offering training, mentorship, incubation, seed funding and investor access. Programmes include PW UDYAMI, a 90-day online course with one year of mentorship, and a six-month DeepTech Accelerator. The partnership will also support prototype development, corporate pilot projects and growth-stage funding readiness, aiming to strengthen regional entrepreneurship and innovation. Read more Let’s Game Now raises Rs 30 Cr from Anand Mahindra and other investors Let’s Game Now, an Indian gaming and esports company, has closed a Rs 30 crore investment round backed by Anand Mahindra, Bestvantage Investments and a UAE-based family office. The company will use the funding to accelerate the development of the Indian Super Gaming League (ISGL), a franchise-based competition combining gaming, sports, entertainment and technology. The league has also received backing from actors Ranveer Singh and Abhishek Bachchan. Let’s Game Now claims a community of over 1.4 million members and has organised more than 2,000 events. Bestvantage Investments advised the company exclusively on the investment round. Oracle, Snowflake bring AI Data Cloud to Oracle Cloud Infrastructure Oracle and Snowflake have announced that Snowflake AI Data Cloud will be available as a native, first-party service on Oracle Cloud Infrastructure (OCI), expanding options for enterprises seeking to use their data for artificial intelligence and analytics. Customers will be able to purchase, provision and consume the service directly through Oracle, with unified pricing and billing. They can also use Oracle Universal Credits, simplifying procurement and enabling them to draw on existing cloud commitments. The integration is designed to bring Snowflake’s analytics and AI capabilities closer to enterprise data held across Oracle services, including Oracle Fusion Cloud Applications, NetSuite and Oracle databases. HCLTech launches AI-powered nano GCC offering with AWS HCLTech has launched an AI-powered nano Global Capability Centre (GCC) offering built on Amazon Web Services (AWS), aimed at helping enterprises transition from AI experimentation to business outcomes. Part of its GCC 360 solution suite, the model combines HCLTech’s advisory expertise and AI platforms, including AI Force, with AWS infrastructure and agentic AI services. The offering targets established GCCs seeking AI-led transformation and mid-market companies looking to enter new geographies with lower risk. It focuses on compact, product-centric teams, AI-enabled workflows, autonomous IT operations, engineering, data analytics and intelligent business operations. BonV Aero completes high-altitude logistics drone trials Bhubaneswar-based uncrewed aerial systems manufacturer BonV Aero has completed fleet testing of its logistics drones across remote, high-altitude locations, demonstrating payload transport at elevations ranging from 10,500 to 16,500 feet. The trials involved carrying a 32-kg payload and evaluated the performance of heavy-payload unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) in challenging operating conditions. The latest trials build on the company’s earlier achievement of lifting 30 kg to 19,024 feet at Umling La in Ladakh in 2023. It has also supplied 45 heavy-payload UAVs to the Indian Army’s Eastern Command. Vashi Integrated Solutions plans 22 solar marts across 10 states Vashi Integrated Solutions plans to establish 22 Vashi Mart outlets across 10 states by FY 2026-27 to improve access to solar equipment and installation essentials for rooftop solar installers. The initiative aims to address procurement challenges, particularly in Tier 2 and Tier 3 markets, by bringing inventory and technical support closer to project locations. The first phase will cover Maharashtra, Uttar Pradesh, Kerala, Gujarat, Rajasthan, Andhra Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh, Assam, Uttarakhand and Odisha. The outlets will primarily serve residential rooftop solar installations, while also supporting smaller commercial and industrial projects. Freshworks acquires Israeli company Robusta Dev Freshworks, the Nasdaq listed SaaS company has acquired Israeli firm Robusta Dev Ltd for an undisclosed value. Robusta is a developer of an open source project monitoring platform. A statement from Freshworks said this acquisition strengthens its capabilities in the segments of incident management and IT operations. It further added it bridges the gap between deep diagnostic intelligence, IT service management, and modern incident orchestration powered by platforms like FireHydrant. "Our technology lets AI Agents do that effectively in large enterprise environments, where there are so many raw events that investigating each one individually would be exorbitant from a token cost perspective. We're incredibly excited to join Freshworks, which gives us the scale and platform to bring that experience to engineering teams everywhere, while keeping humans firmly in control of decisions that touch production," said Natan Yellin, co-founder and CEO of Robusta. Freshworks said the combined entity will bring its AI-powered incident intelligence capabilities into Freshservice workflows while deepening interoperability with incident response platforms like FireHydrant. The statement said the technology platform of Robusta is optimised for large scale production environments where it covers diagnosis, treatment and prevention. (The copy will be updated with the latest news through the day)

title: ‘Keep learning, keep adapting’: Priyank Kharge tells IT professionals to stay ahead of AI
content: If there’s one rule for surviving the AI tech shift, it’s that your learning curve can never plateau. As artificial intelligence reshapes industries and job requirements, IT professionals must keep upgrading their skills and adapting to changing business needs, said Karnataka IT Minister Priyank Kharge on Tuesday. Speaking at the inauguration of RSM US Integrated Services India Private Limited’s new office at Manyata Tech Park in Bengaluru on October 28, Kharge said the pace of AI adoption was creating uncertainty around future roles, making continuous learning essential for professionals. “AI is one of the most disruptive technologies we have seen, and the speed and scale at which it is being adopted are unprecedented,” he said. While predicting exactly how jobs and skill requirements will evolve remains difficult, Kharge said professionals must focus on building capabilities that remain relevant to industry and global markets. “The opportunity lies in our ability to keep learning, adapt quickly and build capabilities that remain relevant to industry and global markets,” he added. Karnataka’s talent pool keeps global businesses interested Priyank Kharge also highlighted Karnataka’s talent pool as a key factor in attracting global businesses and Global Capability Centres (GCCs), which handle specialised business and technology operations for multinational companies. “We have not seen a talent pool as agile as Karnataka’s, one that is ready to unlearn, relearn and be deployed at scale,” he said. The minister credited the state’s workforce alongside its policies and infrastructure for helping attract investment. He pointed to Bengaluru’s Outer Ring Road (ORR), where approximately 800,000 people work along a 9-km stretch, describing it as one of the world’s most densely concentrated talent pools. He added that Karnataka would continue strengthening its infrastructure while building on its workforce advantage to attract investment and support increasingly specialised, high-value work. Nipuna Karnataka puts industry needs at the centre To help workers prepare for evolving job requirements, Kharge highlighted Nipuna Karnataka, the state’s industry-led skilling initiative. The programme brings industry partners into the training process, allowing companies to identify the capabilities they need and help shape relevant curricula. The government and industry then work together to prepare candidates for emerging roles. Under the model, government support for eligible training costs is linked to employability and employment outcomes. The aim is to ensure training responds to actual hiring needs rather than leaving candidates with skills that employers may not require. Since AI reshapes how businesses operate, the minister stressed the importance of closer industry participation in identifying emerging skill gaps and preparing the workforce accordingly. Karnataka’s ability to stay competitive will depend on how well its workforce keeps pace with changing technology. As AI changes job roles and the skills employers look for, continuous learning could prove just as important as technical expertise in helping professionals stay relevant.

title: Info Edge reports steady business growth ahead of leadership transition
content: Info Edge (India), which owns and operates internet-led businesses, delivered steady business growth in the second quarter ended September 30, 2026. Consolidated revenue from operations rose 12.2% year on year (YoY) to Rs 903.9 crore, while profit after tax was up 87% YoY at Rs 649.8 crore. Growth was supported by the recruitment business, faster expansion at property portal 99acres, and continued momentum in the matchmaking business. However, the education segment remained under pressure. Profitability improved as expenses grew more slowly than revenue, although higher other income also contributed to the increase in reported profits. There is also a leadership transition in the offing. Hitesh Oberoi is due to leave the full-time role of Managing Director and CEO on December 2 this year, after nearly 27 years with the company. Founder Sanjeev Bikhchandani is slated to assume an expanded executive role from December 3, subject to shareholder approval. Operating growth improves Info Edge operates the brands Naukri (online recruitment), 99acres (property listings), Jeevansathi and Aisle (matchmaking), and Shiksha (education services). It also invests in other businesses. So its financial results reflect both operating performance and changes in investment values. Consolidated total income, including other income, increased 37.7% YoY to Rs 1,332.3 crore. Other income rose 164.8% to Rs 428.4 crore from Rs 161.8 crore, while total expenses increased 4.5% to Rs 588.6 crore from Rs 563.5 crore. Profit before tax, before exceptional items, rose 85.2% to Rs 747.7 crore. Consolidated PAT reached Rs 649.8 crore, up 87% YoY from Rs 347.5 crore. This includes profits attributable to non-controlling interests in subsidiaries. The portion attributable to Info Edge’s shareholders was Rs 479.7 crore, up 51.6% from Rs 316.4 crore. Based on consolidated revenue, expenses, depreciation and finance costs, operating EBITDA (earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation) comes at approximately Rs 354 crore, up 27.4% YoY, with a margin of 39.2%, compared with 34.5% a year earlier. Standalone revenue from operations rose 12.8% to Rs 841.7 crore, while operating profit before tax increased 29.8% to Rs 347.3 crore. Its margin expanded to 41.3% from approximately 35.9%. Standalone PAT, however, fell 92.9% to Rs 333.8 crore from Rs 4,720 crore. The previous year’s quarter included an exceptional gain of Rs 5,200 crore arising from an unrealised investment valuation gain following the amalgamation of Makesense Technologies with PB Fintech. The decline therefore does not represent a comparable deterioration in operating performance. Revenue streams diverge Recruitment remained the largest revenue contributor. The company's earnings presentation, which includes acquired businesses in its operating-business breakdown, puts recruitment revenue at approximately Rs 682 crore, or 75.4% of the total. Standalone recruitment revenue grew 13.3% YoY to Rs 632 crore, while operating profit before tax increased 19.9% to Rs 374 crore. Its operating margin reached 59.1%. Recruitment billings grew 12.6% in Q2 and 14.9% in the first half of FY27. Candidate Services billings increased 37%, while AI and data products for recruiters and job seekers accounted for a high single-digit share of recruitment topline. Real estate contributed approximately Rs 134 crore, or 14.8% of revenue. 99acres revenue grew 16.7% YoY, while billings increased 21.2%. Property enquiries rose over 33% and app daily active users grew 25%. Operating losses narrowed 93% to Rs 1.6 crore, while cash from operations rose to Rs 22 crore from Rs 2.3 crore. These figures indicate improving business economics, although sustained operating profitability remains a test. Matchmaking contributed around Rs 53 crore, comprising Rs 40 crore from Jeevansathi and Rs 13 crore from Aisle. Jeevansathi revenue grew 16.5% and it reported operating profit of Rs 2 crore. Aisle revenue increased 35.1% and billings rose 40%, but it recorded an operating loss of Rs 3 crore. Combined matchmaking billings grew 23.1% YoY. Education remained the weakest business. Shiksha generated approximately Rs 35 crore in revenue, down 8.5% YoY, while billings fell 27.2%. The company attributed the pressure to AI-related traffic headwinds, declining Google-referred search traffic and subdued student interest in studying in the US, with preferences shifting towards the UK, Australia and Europe. The business reported negative operating cash flow of Rs 16 crore. Cash and transition Standalone cash generated from operations before tax rose 27.4% YoY to Rs 372.8 crore. The company reported a cash balance of approximately Rs 4,976 crore as at September 30, 2026, including balances held by wholly owned subsidiaries. The company board has declared an interim dividend of Rs 3 per share and approved an investment of approximately Rs 150 crore in wholly owned subsidiary Redstart Labs. It has also approved exits from the stakes in Medcords and Unnati Online, investments that had been fully impaired in earlier years. Edited by Swetha Kannan

title: Meesho narrows loss by 68% while revenue rises 34% in Q2 of FY27
content: Ecommerce company Meesho reported a 68% decline in net losses even as revenues rose by 34% on a year-on-year (YoY) basis for the second quarter of FY27. Meesho reported a net loss of Rs 132.44 crore for the three months ending September, 2026 which is the second quarter of FY27 as compared to Rs 411.36 crore recorded in the similar period a year ago. Revenue for the second quarter touched Rs 4131.58 crore as compared to Rs 3073.67 crore a year ago. On the performance of the company, Meesho CEO Vidit Aatrey said, “Our Q2 performance reflects the strength of Meesho's operating model, with NMV (net merchandise value) growing 23% year-on-year to Rs 12,911 crore and annual transacting users reaching 284 million. More consumers are shopping on Meesho, and they are shopping more frequently, even as first-time buyers grew 16% quarter-on-quarter.” According to the company, annual transacting users grew 21% YoY to 284 million while annual purchase frequency increased 7% YoY to 10.4 transactions per user. Meesho said NMV grew 23% YoY. Meesho said festive-aligned NMV grew 33% YoY over the 90 days preceding Dussehra. The annual transacting sellers increased 60% YoY to 1.13 million. The e-commerce company said over 4 lakh sellers are now part of its Content Commerce ecosystem, enabling entrepreneurs to reach consumers through creator-led product discovery. For Meesho, artificial intelligence (AI) has emerged as a big differentiator as it transitions towards an agent-led software development with engineering productivity increasing 171% between March and September 2026 and the number of experiments rising 73%. It noted that approximately 65% of engineering pods now operate with a single engineer directing AI agents. “Our focus remains on reinvesting these efficiency gains into better consumer and seller experiences, accelerating innovation and building a larger, more efficient marketplace that can generate sustainable free cash flow over the long term,” Aatrey said. Meesho said as of September 30, 2026, it had a cash balance of Rs 7,048 crore, providing flexibility to pursue long-term growth opportunities while maintaining financial discipline.
