title: Workshaala targets Rs 1,000 Cr revenue as it scales enterprise workspace business
content: India's offices are being reinvented, and Workshaala wants to be the company that runs them. The enterprise workspace provider has set out a Rs 1,000 crore revenue vision for its next phase of growth, built on a footprint that already spans 3.5 million sq ft of serviceable area: 75,000 seats across 25 centres in 10 Indian cities. The announcement follows a landmark moment for the company. Workshaala recently delivered what it describes as the world's largest service-platform workplace transaction, a deal that is now live within its existing footprint. For the company's leadership, that transaction is less a finish line than a proof point. It shows the model works at the very top end of enterprise demand, and that it is ready to be replicated across the country. From proof point to growth platform Workshaala is clear that the Rs 1,000 crore target is not a fundraising story or a projection built on potential. It is a revenue roadmap anchored in a model the company has already tested at the largest scale in its category. The timing reflects a market at an inflection point. India's technology and services economy is expected to add millions of white-collar seats over the next decade. Grade-A workspace demand is outpacing supply in every major city. And enterprises are taking a hard look at the economics of traditional real estate, seeking flexibility, cost predictability and operational efficiency without the weight of long-term leases. That is precisely the gap Workshaala was built to fill. With execution already proven, the company sees scaling not as an option, but as the logical next step. Four pillars to Rs 1,000 crore Rather than a single bet on one city or one client segment, Workshaala's growth plan rests on four pillars, each already in motion. 1. Pan-India expansion. The company is growing across Bengaluru, Hyderabad, Pune, Chennai and Mumbai, with emerging Tier II hubs such as Indore, Coimbatore and Chandigarh close behind. Enterprises increasingly want a single partner that can deliver consistent workspace standards in every city they operate in. Workshaala's playbook is designed to travel. 2. A technology layer beneath the real estate. Workshaala runs a platform that manages occupancy, utilization, service delivery and facility operations in real time. This lets it operate 75,000 seats across 25 centres with the discipline of a technology business rather than the margins of a facilities operator, and allows revenue to scale faster than headcount. 3. Enterprise-grade service delivery. Large corporates do not switch workspace partners lightly. They need assurance on uptime, compliance, safety, and consistency at scale. Workshaala's landmark transaction gives prospective clients a live reference they can visit before they sign, rather than a promise in a pitch deck. 4. Strategic ecosystem partnerships. Instead of competing with developers, landlords and corporate real estate teams, Workshaala works alongside them. It positions itself as the operating layer that makes large commercial assets enterprise-ready, a model that compounds as more partners plug into the platform. Taken together, the pillars describe a company that is not chasing growth for its own sake, but extending a model it has already validated at scale. Built for the GCC wave No discussion of enterprise workspace demand in India is complete without Global Capability Centers, and this is where Workshaala sees its sharpest fit. GCCs come with distinct expectations. Parent companies mandate strict security and compliance standards. Headcount plans can double within a year. And the space has to feel world-class from day one. Workshaala's answer is to pair real estate execution with its live occupancy and service-delivery platform. Instead of waiting months for a customized build-out, a GCC can move into managed, technology-enabled space that is enterprise-ready from the outset. It can then grow from 200 seats to 2,000 without renegotiating its entire real estate strategy. Standardized service levels across 25 centres in 10 cities mean every GCC location runs on the same playbook, with the uptime guarantees, compliance rigor, and reporting discipline a global headquarters expects. As India cements its role as the world's hub for innovation and operations, GCCs are emerging as one of the fastest-growing segments of Workshaala's enterprise pipeline. The road ahead The next decade will decide how enterprise India works, and where. Companies want space that scales with them, runs reliably in every city and frees capital from long leases. Workshaala is betting that the winners in this market will be operators who combine physical execution with a technology backbone, and that a model proven at the largest scale can be repeated city by city. The Rs 1,000 crore milestone is the company's way of measuring that bet. With 75,000 seats already live, a reference transaction enterprises can walk into, and a growing GCC pipeline, Workshaala is entering its growth decade from a position of proof rather than promise. (Disclaimer: The views and opinions expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the views of YourStory.)

title: 5 lessons to learn from Sorrow and Bliss by Meg Mason
content: Sorrow and Bliss by Meg Mason is a moving novel about mental health, marriage, family relationships, and the complicated experience of living with emotional pain. The story follows Martha Friel, a woman in her forties who struggles with an unnamed mental illness that affects her relationships, her sense of identity, and her ability to navigate everyday life. Through Martha's experiences, Mason explores the challenges of understanding oneself when one's emotions feel difficult to explain. The novel also examines how mental health struggles can affect loved ones and how compassion, patience, and acceptance can help people navigate difficult periods in their lives. Rather than offering simple answers, Sorrow and Bliss presents an honest portrayal of a woman trying to understand herself while learning to live with uncertainty. 5 Important lessons readers can learn from Meg Mason's novel 1. Mental health struggles are not always visible One of the most significant lessons from Sorrow and Bliss is that emotional pain is not always easy to recognise from the outside. Martha often struggles internally in ways that other people cannot fully understand. Her behaviour, relationships, and reactions are shaped by difficulties she cannot easily explain, making it challenging for those around her to understand what she is experiencing. The novel highlights how someone can appear functional in certain areas of life while privately struggling to cope. It challenges the assumption that people who seem capable, articulate, or outwardly comfortable are necessarily doing well emotionally. This lesson reminds us to approach others with empathy rather than making assumptions about their lives. We rarely know the full story behind someone's behaviour, and a little patience can make a meaningful difference. Mental health deserves the same compassion and understanding as any other aspect of a person's well-being. 2. Love does not always mean understanding someone completely Relationships are central to Martha's story, particularly her marriage to Patrick. Their relationship illustrates how love can coexist with confusion, frustration, and emotional distance. Sometimes, the people closest to us genuinely care about us but struggle to understand what we are going through. They may want to help without knowing what to say or how to respond. Sorrow and Bliss explores the difficult reality that loving someone does not automatically give us the ability to understand every part of their experience. Relationships can become complicated when emotional struggles affect communication, expectations, and everyday responsibilities. The novel encourages readers to recognise that meaningful relationships require more than affection. They also need honesty, patience, communication, and a willingness to acknowledge what we do not understand. Love may not solve every problem, but a willingness to listen and learn can help people feel less alone in their struggles. 3. You do not have to have everything figured out Martha's journey is not a straightforward story of personal growth in which every problem eventually disappears. Instead, she navigates uncertainty, difficult emotions, and questions about who she is and what she wants from life. Her experiences remind readers that personal growth rarely follows a perfect timeline. Some people understand themselves early in life, while others spend years trying to make sense of their emotions, relationships, and choices. There is no universal deadline for becoming confident, finding stability, or understanding what makes us happy. The pressure to have a successful career , a healthy relationship, and a clear sense of identity can make people feel as though they are falling behind. Martha's story challenges this expectation by showing how complicated real life can be. The lesson is to permit yourself to be a work in progress. You can make mistakes, change your mind, and take time to understand yourself without treating uncertainty as a personal failure. 4. Family relationships can be complicated and imperfect Family plays an important role in Sorrow and Bliss, particularly through Martha's relationships with her parents and sister, Ingrid. The novel portrays family as a source of both comfort and conflict. Family members may care deeply about one another while still misunderstanding each other's needs, struggling to communicate, or carrying unresolved tensions. These relationships demonstrate that affection does not automatically remove differences or prevent people from hurting one another. Sometimes, family members have difficulty recognising experiences that are different from their own. Mason presents these dynamics with humour and emotional honesty, showing that family relationships are rarely as simple as they appear from the outside. The lesson is that understanding within a family requires effort. Listening without judgement, recognising individual differences, and acknowledging past hurt can help create healthier relationships. It is also important to remember that complicated family dynamics do not mean that every relationship is beyond repair. With willingness and appropriate boundaries, people can find new ways to relate to one another. Also Read 5 Non-fiction books you must read before 2026 ends 5. Happiness does not mean living without sorrow The title Sorrow and Bliss captures one of the novel's central ideas: life can contain happiness and pain at the same time. Martha's experiences challenge the belief that a fulfilling life must be free from sadness, uncertainty, or emotional difficulty. Her journey is not simply about eliminating suffering but about understanding how her struggles fit into her larger experience of living. People often postpone happiness until they believe everything is in order. They may think they can only feel content once their relationships improve, their careers become stable, or their emotional difficulties disappear. However, life rarely unfolds so neatly. The novel encourages readers to recognise that difficult emotions do not erase moments of connection, humour, love, or joy. A person can experience pain while still appreciating meaningful parts of life. This does not mean ignoring suffering or pretending that everything is fine. Instead, it means allowing room for different emotions without believing that one difficult chapter defines an entire life. Final thoughts Sorrow and Bliss by Meg Mason is a deeply human novel about mental health, relationships, family, and the complicated process of understanding oneself. Through Martha Friel's experiences, it explores the realities of emotional suffering without reducing them to easy answers or simple solutions. The five lessons from the novel remind us to approach mental health with empathy, recognise that love requires understanding, give ourselves time to grow, accept the imperfections of family relationships, and make space for both sorrow and happiness. Ultimately, the book offers a compassionate reminder that people are more complicated than their struggles. Understanding ourselves and others may take time, but patience, honesty, and empathy can help us navigate the uncertainty of being human.

title: Lessons in Chemistry: 5 Takeaways from Bonnie Garmus’ Novel
content: Lessons in Chemistry by Bonnie Garmus is a thought-provoking novel about ambition, gender inequality, motherhood, and the courage to challenge social expectations. Set in the 1960s, the story follows Elizabeth Zott, a brilliant chemist whose professional ambitions are constantly challenged by a society that believes women belong in the kitchen rather than the laboratory. When Elizabeth unexpectedly becomes the host of a cooking television show, she uses the opportunity to teach more than recipes. Through science, she encourages women to think independently, question established beliefs, and recognise their own abilities. The novel offers several meaningful lessons about self-worth, equality, and the importance of refusing to let society define who we can become. 5 Powerful ideas in Lessons in Chemistry by Bonnie Garmus 1. Never let society define your potential One of the most important lessons in Lessons in Chemistry is that your potential should never be determined by society's expectations. Elizabeth Zott is an exceptionally talented scientist, but she faces discrimination because she is a woman working in a male-dominated field. Instead of being judged solely on her knowledge and abilities, she repeatedly encounters people who underestimate her because of her gender. Her experiences highlight how social stereotypes can prevent talented individuals from reaching their full potential. Elizabeth refuses to accept these limitations as the truth about herself. She continues pursuing her interests and challenges the assumptions that attempt to hold her back. The lesson is simple: your abilities are not limited by what others believe you can achieve. Whether in your career, education, or personal life, you deserve the opportunity to explore your potential without being restricted by outdated expectations. 2. Question everything instead of accepting it blindly Elizabeth approaches life with the curiosity of a scientist. She believes in examining evidence, asking questions, and understanding why things happen rather than accepting conventional wisdom without thinking. This mindset becomes particularly important when she begins hosting her cooking show, Supper at Six. Although the programme is designed around cooking, Elizabeth introduces scientific explanations and encourages her audience to understand the processes behind everyday tasks. Her approach transforms an ordinary television show into an opportunity for women to learn, think critically, and develop confidence in their own intelligence. The novel reminds readers that questioning established ideas is not necessarily an act of rebellion. Sometimes, it is the first step towards progress. In everyday life, this means examining the beliefs we inherit, questioning unfair traditions, and making decisions based on reason rather than fear of judgement. Independent thinking allows us to recognise when something needs to change. 3. Women deserve equal opportunities and respect Gender inequality is a central theme throughout Lessons in Chemistry. Elizabeth encounters professional discrimination, unequal treatment, and assumptions about what women should do with their lives. Her experiences reflect a broader social problem: women's achievements have often been overlooked simply because they do not fit traditional expectations. Through Elizabeth's journey, Bonnie Garmus illustrates how exhausting it can be to prove one's competence in an environment where others are unwilling to offer equal opportunities. Elizabeth must work harder to have her knowledge recognised, even when her qualifications speak for themselves. However, the novel also demonstrates the importance of women supporting one another and recognising their shared potential. The lesson extends beyond the workplace. Equality means respecting women's choices, valuing their contributions, and allowing them to pursue careers and ambitions without being forced into predefined roles. A person's capabilities should determine their opportunities, not their gender. Also Read 7 Things to Accept About Yourself Before You Turn 30 4. Intelligence and confidence can change the way people think Elizabeth's transformation into a television personality demonstrates that knowledge can be a powerful tool for challenging social attitudes. Rather than abandoning her scientific background to fit the expectations of a cooking show, she brings science into the kitchen. She explains cooking through chemistry and treats her viewers as intelligent individuals capable of understanding complex ideas. Her approach challenges the assumption that domestic responsibilities and intellectual pursuits must exist separately. It also gives women a platform to engage with science in a way that traditional institutions have often denied them. Elizabeth's confidence is not about proving that she is better than everyone else. It comes from knowing the value of her knowledge and refusing to make herself smaller to satisfy other people's expectations. This lesson encourages readers to embrace their expertise, communicate their ideas clearly, and trust their ability to make a difference. Sometimes, changing people's perspectives begins with one person who is willing to challenge the familiar and present a different way of thinking. 5. Family and personal identity can exist beyond traditional roles Another meaningful lesson from Lessons in Chemistry is that people should be allowed to define family and identity on their own terms. Elizabeth's life challenges conventional ideas about motherhood, relationships, and women's responsibilities. Her experiences show that being a mother does not mean abandoning one's ambitions, just as pursuing a career does not make someone less capable of caring for a family. The novel explores how people navigate grief, parenthood, relationships, and the expectations placed upon them. It presents a more nuanced understanding of what it means to build a fulfilling life . Elizabeth refuses to accept that she must choose between being intellectually ambitious and being a devoted parent. Instead, she creates a life that reflects her circumstances, values, and priorities. For readers, the lesson is that there is no single formula for a meaningful life. People have different ambitions, responsibilities, and definitions of happiness. Rather than measuring ourselves against conventional milestones, we can focus on building lives that align with our own values and allow us to grow. Final thoughts Lessons in Chemistry by Bonnie Garmus is more than a novel about a scientist navigating a world that underestimates her. It is a story about challenging inequality, embracing curiosity, and refusing to let other people's assumptions determine your future. Through Elizabeth Zott's experiences, readers are reminded that intelligence deserves recognition, women deserve equal opportunities, and personal ambition should not be sacrificed to satisfy society's expectations. The five lessons from the book encourage us to question outdated beliefs, trust our abilities, and create lives that reflect who we truly are. Whether you are navigating your career, questioning social norms, or discovering your own identity, Elizabeth's journey offers a powerful reminder that you do not have to fit into someone else's definition of success. Ultimately, Lessons in Chemistry encourages readers to approach life with curiosity, courage, and the confidence to challenge what they have been told is possible.

title: Rotoris bags Rs 70 Cr to expand its luxury watch business
content: Gurugram-based independent luxury watchmaker Rotoris has raised Rs 70 crore (~$8.5 million) in a Series A funding round led by early-stage investment firm Blume Ventures. 9Unicorns and Centricity also participated, bringing in family-office investors including Diwakar Goel, BlackRock’s global head of data, former Coca-Cola Asia-Pacific group president Atul Singh and Adhiraj Burman of the Dabur family. Actor and television host Rannvijay Singha also invested. The company plans to use the funds for research and development, expanded production, and growing its Rotoris House, its appointment-based space for meeting clients, presence in India and overseas. The Gurugram-based watchmaker claims its first collection of 2,100 numbered timepieces sold out within days of its February 2026 launch. It asserted that nearly 1,00,000 people have since registered for access, while 40% of demand comes from outside India, including the US, Dubai, and Australia. Blume Ventures sees an opportunity to build an Indian luxury brand with international ambitions. “We are backing their vision to make an Indian brand shine amongst global icons, and the timing has never been better,” said Karthik Reddy, co-founder and managing partner of Blume Ventures. Rotoris produces limited-run analogue watches, releasing collections as named chapters with published production numbers. Its Manifesta collection features natural-stone dials, including lapis lazuli and imperial jade, making each dial distinct. Astonia is a 42mm chronograph, a watch with a stopwatch function, made using steel, titanium and carbon and powered by a Swiss movement. Each timepiece is assembled and tested by hand at the company’s Gurugram Atelier, with movements sourced from Switzerland or Japan depending on the collection. “The design creates the desire, but the engineering, assembly and attention to detail earn the trust,” co-founder Prerna Gupta said. Co-founder Aakash Anand described a Rotoris watch as “a symbol of ambition, worn on the wrist”. He said the company plans to open Rotoris House in New York because many of its customers live there. The expansion comes as Indian consumers increasingly trade up to higher-priced watches. Luxury and high-end watches accounted for 70% of sales in FY25, up from 48% in FY20. Younger buyers are showing greater interest in mechanical watches, distinctive designs and limited editions. Trade policy could also reshape competition. The India-EFTA Trade and Economic Partnership Agreement, which took effect in October 2025, is expected to reduce import duties on qualifying watches from member countries, including Switzerland, over time. This could support greater access for international brands while raising competitive pressure on domestic manufacturers. Other Indian watchmakers are pursuing international growth. In September, Bangalore Watch Company raised $1.4 million from its own customers, including family-office principals and high-net-worth individuals. Rotoris had previously raised $3 million in seed funding in December 2025.

title: Healthtech startup Cent raises $15M in Series A
content: Healthtech startup Cent has raised $15 million in a Series A funding round through a combination of debt and equity, led by Blume Ventures and existing investor South Park Commons. The round also saw participation from individual investors, including Arun Sarin, former CEO of Vodafone; Srinivas Narayanan, former CTO (B2B) of OpenAI; and Sharath Narayana, Krishna Sridhar, and Aprameya Radhakrishna. Cent said it will use the funding for R&D and to build out its AI, engineering, and clinical teams. Cent was founded by Shashank ND, Arpit Garg, and Anshul Khandelwal in 2025 and is positioned as a preventive health intelligence company. Shashank ND is the founder of Practo, while Anshul Khandelwal was the former CMO of Ola Electric, and Arpit Garg was the former product head at Lenskart. Cent is building a vertically integrated preventive health platform that combines purpose-built hardware, AI-driven radiology and diagnostics, and bioinformatics. The startup says the platform can help detect diseases well before symptoms appear. Cent has also acquired Medsee, an AI-powered radiology reporting workflow platform founded by Chitra Singh and designed for qualified medical professionals. The platform drafts structured reports and highlights findings for radiologist review, enabling Cent to deliver faster, more consistent reporting as scan volumes grow. "India's healthcare system is still built to treat illness, not to find it early. We believe the next shift is preventive care that is precise and accessible at scale. This investment lets us go deeper into AI, medical imaging and clinical research, and build preventive health infrastructure in India that can serve the world," said Anshul Khandelwal, Co-Founder, Cent. According to Cent, it has completed 10,000 preventive whole-body scans across Bengaluru, Mumbai and Delhi since inception. It is targeting 10 million scans by 2035. “We are believers in the Cent's vision to extend this from India to the world over time, and it is in line with our conviction around health tech for a decade now," said Karthik Reddy, Co-founder and Managing Partner, Blume Ventures.

title: Google Cloud’s Gemini voice AI wants to do more than just talk
content: Imagine asking an AI assistant to find a customer, negotiate a price and help close a sale, all without typing a single prompt. Voice AI is moving beyond answering questions to taking on tasks, and Google Cloud wants businesses to put it to work. At TechSparks 2026, Naren Kachroo, Head of AI Go-to-Market at Google Cloud, demonstrated how Gemini’s voice AI capabilities could help businesses handle customer conversations, restaurant bookings and sales negotiations. From talking to taking action Until now, much of the AI experience has revolved around asking questions and getting answers. Kachroo said the next step is AI that can access information, use tools and take action on a user’s behalf. “We don't want to focus on voice AI just being an experience to talk to AI,” he said. “We want voice AI to be powered through agentic experiences where the task is actually accomplished with AI.” To show what that means, Naren Kachroo played a demonstration of an AI assistant booking a restaurant table for eight. The assistant answered questions about bringing a birthday cake, identified a dish from an image, discussed vegetarian options and switched between English and Spanish during the conversation. In other words, it did more than take a booking. It handled the questions that came with it, too. Kachroo also introduced Gemini Live voice capabilities, alongside models for text-to-speech, speech-to-text and translation. He showcased Live Avatar, which combines voice interaction with a visual AI presence. Meet the AI sales assistant The standout demonstration involved a fictional safety equipment business with 500 helmets sitting in its inventory. Its owner, Rajesh, wanted to sell them quickly and instructed an AI voice agent to find a suitable lead, contact the customer and negotiate a price above Rs 400 per helmet. The assistant checked the business’s leads, identified a construction company that needed 500 helmets and initiated a call in Hindi. When the prospective buyer pushed for a lower price, the AI negotiated while sticking to the owner’s pricing instruction. It was a glimpse of how AI could help small businesses manage sales without handling every step themselves. The agent could draw on internal business information, speak to a customer and respond to objections, rather than simply recommend what the owner should do next. Kachroo said the demonstration showed how the agent maintained context as it moved from internal information to a customer conversation. Why India needs voice AI Voice could be particularly useful in India, where people speak many languages and have different levels of comfort with typing or navigating digital interfaces. “I believe that India and Indian consumer is continuing to go as voice first,” Naren said. He highlighted Google’s work on Indian languages, accents and cultural nuances, and pointed to Equal AI, an Indian company building voice assistants that can handle calls on users’ behalf. For Kachroo, the goal is to make voice AI useful in everyday business processes, not just impressive in a demo. That means building systems that understand context, handle interruptions and follow instructions while completing tasks. The real test, then, is not whether AI can hold a conversation. It is whether it can get the job done. And for businesses exploring voice AI, that could be the difference between another chatbot and a genuinely useful assistant.

title: Healthy snack brand Troovy raises Rs 100 Cr in Series B round led by Fireside Ventures
content: Troovy, a food and snacks brand, has raised Rs 100 crore in a Series B round of funding led by Fireside Ventures, with participation from Sharrp Ventures and other investors. The Gurugram-based brand will use the funding for R&D, expanding its manufacturing capacity, and scaling distribution across quick commerce and offline channels, as it looks to launch a wide range of products. Troovy was founded in 2023 by Mansi Baranwal and Aditya Mukherjee with the goal of providing nutritious food. Its portfolio spans categories such as snacks, sauces and spreads, and millet pasta. It says its vacuum-cooked potato chips have 10-12% oil and high protein, compared with 35-40% oil in mainstream chips. It also promises clean-label ketchups and seasonings without synthetic additives or preservatives. Troovy's co-founder & CBO Aditya Mukherjee said, " This backing (investment) is a vote of confidence in a model most food companies don't use: building with the people who'll actually eat what you make. When you build with users, you have to push innovation, because users don't settle. It's not enough to replace the oil and sugar; you have to reduce them dramatically.” Troovy says it has engaged with over 100 mothers and their children through community-led discussions, recipe brainstorming, and product tastings. These conversations have helped shape the brand’s approach to creating snacks with good ingredients, without harmful preservatives or additives, while maintaining the taste that children expect, the company said. Ankita Balotia, Principal, Fireside Ventures, said, "Troovy grew 5x in the eight months following our last investment, and that is what made us double down. The team has executed incredibly well on growth, and the backend supply chain.” Troovy had raised $5 million in a Series A round of funding in January this year.

title: AI startup Simplismart raises $14M from Dallas Venture Capital, Nvidia, and others
content: AI inference infrastructure startup Simplismart has raised $14 million in a Series B funding round led by Dallas Venture Capital, with participation from NVIDIA, Accel, Shastra VC and Micromax. The company will use the funds to further develop its AI inference platform, expand its partnerships with cloud providers and sovereign AI initiatives, and strengthen its presence in North America and other global markets. Simplismart builds software that connects AI models with GPU infrastructure. Its modular inference engine enables businesses to configure models based on their speed, cost and performance requirements, while its orchestration platform manages deployment and scaling across cloud and on-premises infrastructure. “We have spent four years building the software layer between the model and the GPU, helping customers optimise how their workloads are deployed and operated. This funding will allow us to take that platform to more enterprises and cloud providers globally,” said Amritanshu Jain, Co-founder and CEO, Simplismart. The company said its annualised revenue run rate has grown 14-fold over the past six months. It counts companies such as HeyGen, Higgsfield, InVideo, Shiprocket, Apna and Ema among its customers, which use its platform to run production workloads across video, voice, multimodal and enterprise AI applications. For its cloud-provider offering, Simplismart works with NVIDIA to deploy AI infrastructure. Unlike inference providers that purchase or reserve GPU capacity and resell it, Simplismart does not own compute infrastructure. Instead, it provides the software layer that enables third-party GPU fleets to run production AI workloads, positioning itself as a data centre enabler. The platform allows cloud providers to offer managed AI services under their own brands without having to build the underlying software stack from scratch. “ Simplismart is rapidly emerging as a global player helping enterprises run AI workloads more efficiently, while enabling cloud providers to turn GPU capacity into scalable services. We are backing this fast-growing company because of its proven technical prowess in addressing a critical need in the AI infrastructure ecosystem globally, as well as the strong execution capabilities of its founding team,” said Dayakar Puskoor, Managing Partner, Dallas Venture Capital.

title: Rs 10,000 Cr into restaurants. But why do 80% fail? Here's the Hotshare F&B investment playbook
content: India's restaurant industry is attracting serious capital, but building a profitable restaurant remains one of the most difficult businesses to crack. According to Lavanya Jayashankar, Founder and CEO of Hotshare, an F&B investment platform, around Rs 10,000 crore was deployed into the F&B business in 2025, while organised food services are expected to account for more than half the market by 2030. Yet, despite growing consumer demand and investor interest, Lavanya points to an uncomfortable statistic: 80% of restaurants close within their first five years. Hotshare funds restaurant businesses with a range of Rs 50 lakh to Rs 5 crore. For the investment platform, which raises capital for profitable restaurants and bars at the outlet level, the opportunity is not necessarily to change that statistic, but to identify and fund the businesses that have already demonstrated their ability to survive. "My play here is to say, let's identify those 20," says Lavanya. One example is Beyondburg, one of Hotshare’s portfolio companies. The burger brand began in Bengaluru in 2017 as a four-seater kiosk selling 40 to 50 burgers daily. Today, according to co-founder Mohammed Anas, the brand sells approximately 3,000 burgers a day and has just opened its sixth location Its journey offers a practical illustration of what Lavanya believes separates a successful restaurant from an attractive but financially unsustainable concept. The Rs 50 lakh to Rs 5 crore funding gap India's F&B industry has traditionally attracted two types of capital: institutional investors backing large, scalable chains and informal investors financing individual restaurants through personal networks. Lavanya believes a significant opportunity exists between these two categories. "There is a vast middle of profitable, successful entrepreneurs who are under-capitalized," she says, arguing that investors frequently evaluate restaurant businesses using frameworks borrowed from technology and direct-to-consumer companies. The distinction is fundamental. A restaurant chain can create enterprise value through expansion, but an individual outlet generates value primarily through its operating cash flows. Hotshare therefore evaluates outlets as income-generating assets rather than businesses dependent on a future acquisition or exit. According to Lavanya, opening a restaurant typically requires Rs 50 lakh to Rs 5 crore, an amount that can be too small for institutional investors but substantial enough to demand professional financial oversight. She says Hotshare's selected outlets offer a projected 15% to 20% post-tax internal rate of return over five to seven years, with returns distributed through profit sharing. She also describes the possibility of higher effective returns when investors reinvest those distributions, although these remain investment projections rather than guaranteed outcomes. Why great food is not enough For Lavanya, the economics of running a restaurant are more important than its popularity. She outlines specific financial benchmarks across restaurant formats. Quick-service restaurants should aim for food costs below 18% of revenue, manpower costs below 15% and EBITDA margins above 18%. Casual dining restaurants can accommodate food costs of 18% to 22%, but should still target EBITDA margins exceeding 15%. Rent is another critical variable. "Whatever category you are in, it's not great business if your rent is more than 12 to 15% of your revenue," she explains. These numbers help explain why a restaurant with excellent food, strong social media visibility, and crowded tables can still struggle financially. Lavanya believes first-time founders frequently spend too much on their initial outlet before establishing product-market fit. A restaurant requiring Rs 5 crore in capital expenditure is not necessarily better positioned than one requiring Rs 2 crore. It may simply be a more expensive experiment. Beyondburg followed a different approach. Beyondburg: From 50 to 3,000 burgers a day Anas recalls arriving in Bengaluru on a holiday and meeting his future co-founders, Ajmal and Nishaf. Together, they decided to start a small burger business near Christ College in Koramangala. "We used to do, uh, 40 to 50 burgers a day," he recalls. The founders operated the kiosk for almost three years before deciding to rebuild Beyondburg as a scalable brand, beginning with a flagship outlet in Calicut. Rather than attempting to establish a large restaurant chain immediately, the team used its initial years to understand the product, customer preferences and operating requirements. Lavanya considers this approach one of Beyondburg's biggest strengths. "They didn't start with a five crore capex," she says, explaining how the founders first tested the concept before committing to larger outlets. By the time Beyondburg began expanding, it had already invested in central procurement, vendor relationships and operational systems. For Lavanya, the brand demonstrated that expansion could follow operational readiness rather than precede it. Why Beyondburg refuses to sell pasta Anas identifies three priorities behind Beyondburg's growth: product, people and operations. Despite customer requests to introduce additional dishes, the company has resisted expanding beyond its core burger proposition. "If they want to try pasta, they can go to somewhere else, right?" he says. The decision is not simply about brand positioning. Every additional menu item introduces complexity into procurement, inventory, kitchen operations and service. Beyondburg has instead focused on reducing unnecessary stock-keeping units and improving kitchen throughput, particularly during busy weekends. Anas explains that the company works with kitchen consultants to estimate peak demand and design its outlets accordingly. At the Bengaluru location in Indiranagar where the podcast was recorded, he says the business sells 700 to 800 burgers a day. The company has also built a structured approach to training. New employees are paired with experienced colleagues, while a dedicated trainer travels between outlets to maintain consistency. The challenge, Anas explains, is ensuring that a growing business delivers the same product and customer experience regardless of location. What made Beyondburg investable? Lavanya first met Anas in December 2024, when Hotshare was still developing its investment framework. Beyondburg subsequently became one of its portfolio brands, and she credits the business with helping shape Hotshare's evaluation checklist. "Gold standard of operations data was available from day one," she explains. The company maintained historical financial information, treated outlet-level profitability as non-negotiable and developed central systems before they were essential for its existing scale. Its vendor relationships were also designed to support future expansion rather than simply meet immediate requirements. But Lavanya's conviction was not built on financial information alone. During her first visit to Beyondburg, before meeting Anas, she noticed that her water glass was consistently refilled without asking. At the end of the meal, employees offered a complimentary dessert without seeking management approval. For her, these were indicators of a culture in which employees understood hospitality and had the freedom to improve customer experiences. The combination of financial discipline, repeatable operations, and service quality made Beyondburg particularly attractive. The real test of restaurant success Lavanya believes the restaurant industry's next phase of growth will require founders and investors to rethink how they define success. Opening more outlets is not necessarily evidence of a stronger business. A restaurant that expands rapidly while sacrificing profitability may ultimately destroy value rather than create it. Beyondburg's experience illustrates an alternative approach: establish demand with limited capital, build operating systems, maintain product focus and expand only when the underlying economics support it. For aspiring restaurateurs, Lavanya also emphasises the importance of working with experienced operators rather than assuming that culinary ability translates into business expertise. "Hospitality is an execution business, it is not an ideas business," she says. Beyondburg's journey from a four-seater kiosk to thousands of burgers a day shows why that distinction matters. The visible success is a popular consumer brand. Behind it are years of disciplined decisions about costs, people, procurement, kitchens and profitability. For Hotshare, those are precisely the businesses worth backing.

title: Infosys AI revenue jumps 29%; Apple’s foldable iPhone fully pre-booked in week 1
content: Dear Reader, Cybercriminals wasted little time turning a software disclosure into an opportunity. Cloudflare detected millions of attempts to exploit vulnerabilities in PHP soon after they were made public, underscoring how quickly attackers can move to target exposed systems. The surge in attacks has renewed concerns about the security of widely used systems and the urgency of patching vulnerabilities before they can be exploited. Meanwhile, Apple appears to have struck a chord with India’s premium smartphone buyers. The company’s first foldable smartphone, the iPhone Duo , has reportedly seen its first week’s inventory fully booked through pre-orders. The response signals continued appetite for high-end devices as Apple enters the foldable phone market. But not every digital trend brings good news. The Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) has cautioned investors against fraudulent WhatsApp groups promising stock tips and profits. Such groups may use fabricated testimonials and misleading claims to gain trust before pushing unauthorised trading advice or suspicious apps. Investors have been advised to verify intermediaries before acting on recommendations. On the jobs front, India’s healthcare global capability centres (GCCs) are expected to create 67,000 job openings in 2026, according to a Quess Corp report. Demand for specialised talent across technology and healthcare operations is expected to support this growth, reinforcing the sector’s shift towards more technology-driven work. In today’s newsletter: Infosys sees 6.2% rise in Q2 net profit, AI revenue jumps 29% QoQ How AI is democratising creativity: Canva India’s Chandrika Deb Here’s your trivia for today: Which is the world’s oldest known surviving epic poem? (Scroll down for the answer) Corporate Infosys sees 6.2% rise in Q2 net profit, AI revenue jumps 29% QoQ Infosys reported steady growth in Q2 FY27, with AI emerging as a key revenue driver amid continued macroeconomic uncertainty. However, soft demand in North America and sector-specific challenges weighed on its outlook. The IT major lowered its full-year revenue growth guidance to 1-2% from 1.5-3% despite strong large deal wins. Key takeaways: AI revenue grew strongly, accounting for a larger share of Infosys’ overall revenue, even as automation puts pressure on revenues. Infosys lowered its FY27 revenue growth guidance amid demand softness and macroeconomic headwinds, particularly in North America. The company’s large deal wins are expected to provide a cushion for growth, while Infosys continues to hire fresh graduates. TechSparks How AI is democratising creativity: Canva India’s Chandrika Deb AI is making creativity more accessible by helping people overcome barriers of skill, resources and confidence. At TechSparks 2026, Canva India’s Chandrika Deb discussed how AI is reshaping creative workflows and workplace collaboration. She emphasised that human judgement and intent remain critical to creating relevant content. Key takeaways: AI tools help people turn ideas into creative outputs faster, without requiring specialised skills or large teams. While AI can generate content, human intent, cultural understanding and audience awareness determine its relevance and quality. AI enables teams across marketing, sales, product and leadership to participate in creative work, while specialists continue to ensure quality and brand consistency. News & updates Social Media: Greece’s parliament has passed a law banning children under 15 from using social media, citing concerns over minors’ health and safety. The ban will take effect on January 1, 2027, requiring platforms to introduce age-verification systems that protect users’ privacy. The move is part of wider efforts across Europe to curb excessive screen time and protect children from online harm. AI Diagnosis: Microsoft has developed an AI tool that diagnoses patients through a step-by-step process, achieving more than twice the accuracy of physicians in complex medical cases. Published in Science, the research will be followed by real-world testing at Boston’s Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center to assess its use in emergency departments. title: Why India’s flying taxi revolution begins with electric air ambulances
content: For most deeptech entrepreneurs, the hardest lesson is not solving complex physics but overcoming their own technical fascination. Professor Satya Chakravarthy, Founder and technical lead of The ePlane Company, explained this clearly at TechSparks 2026 , YourStory's flagship event. “The biggest challenge that a deep tech entrepreneur normally would face is what I call the technology trap,” he said. “We have to actually ask the question who cares, and the moment you actually ask the question who cares... even your wife doesn’t care.” Chakravarthy, an aerospace professor at IIT Madras, founded the company to develop electric vertical takeoff and landing aircraft, or eVTOLs. These are battery-powered flying vehicles capable of hovering, taking off, and landing vertically without a runway. In a sector often driven by academic prestige, Chakravarthy insists that financial fundamentals must lead engineering ambitions. For deeptech startups, companies built on breakthroughs in science and engineering, long development timelines and heavy capital commitments mean that technological novelty alone cannot survive. In aerospace, he notes, becoming a unicorn is merely the minimum baseline, and founders must build business cases capable of reaching decacorn scale through healthy revenues and margins. The inspiration for ePlane stemmed from a visit to Toulouse, France, where Chakravarthy discovered that 50 smaller aircraft manufacturers existed alongside global giants. “If there are 50 plane companies in France, maybe plane making is not so difficult... why don’t we give a shot at it?” he recalled. Coming from an academic institution accustomed to international standards, he aimed to build a world-class aircraft directly out of India. The air ambulance strategy To avoid the economic traps that have sunk rival aviation ventures, ePlane has designed a phased commercial rollout. Instead of launching directly into intracity air taxis, which represent a high-volume but low-margin business, ePlane is prioritising electric air ambulances. Emergency medical transport offers higher profit margins at lower production volumes, providing early positive cash flow while supply capacity scales up. This approach also solves the challenge of demand modulation, preventing consumer frustration when early aircraft supply is limited. “First of all don’t let the bubble grow in the first place... be realistic about what is the customer that you can actually cater to,” Chakravarthy explains. Deploying five air ambulances in a congested city like Bangalore transforms emergency healthcare without overwhelming fleet capacity. Only after establishing economic stability will ePlane expand into short-haul air cargo and urban air taxis, where commuters can achieve a five-to-eightfold reduction in travel time for roughly double the cost of an Uber ride. Global standards, Indian economics Crucially, Chakravarthy rejects the notion that Indian innovations must settle for discounted quality. Because gravity and flight dynamics are identical everywhere, aircraft must satisfy rigorous international regulatory benchmarks, such as those set by the Directorate General of Civil Aviation. Building to global safety standards while keeping production costs low creates a distinct export advantage. As Chakravarthy asserts, “what’s good for India is good for the world.” Engineering decisions at ePlane have been tailored specifically for practical certification and urban operation. The team deliberately avoided the tilt-rotor mechanism, a design where propellers rotate between vertical hover and horizontal flight, because single points of mechanical failure complicate regulatory approval. Instead, they selected a multi-rotor layout backed by redundant systems to ensure a straightforward path to certification. Public anxiety regarding urban air mobility is often misplaced when compared to everyday transit risks. Aviation regulators demand a failure rate of less than one in a billion before granting commercial approval. “If you are driving a car, you are actually driving something that can kill you... planes are much, much safer,” Chakravarthy remarks. Furthermore, by engineering the smallest aircraft footprint in its class, ePlane ensures its flying vehicles can land on existing hospital helipads and urban rooftops, including Metro station plazas. With commercialisation targeted for 2028, ePlane represents a critical test case for the maturing Indian deeptech ecosystem. While government grants have provided crucial runway, private venture capital continues to struggle with long development cycles. “Patient capital still is more or less an oxymoron,” Chakravarthy reflects. Yet by pairing aerospace innovation with disciplined business strategy, India’s deeptech sector is proving that moonshot technologies can land firmly on commercial ground.

title: 5 Lessons to learn from Nexus by Yuval Noah Harari
content: Information has always shaped human civilisation. From ancient stories and religious texts to newspapers, television and social media, the way people share information influences what they believe, how they make decisions and whom they trust. In Nexus, historian and author Yuval Noah Harari examines how information networks have shaped human history and how they may influence our future. Published in 2024, the book explores the relationship between information, power, truth and the development of artificial intelligence. Harari challenges the assumption that having more information automatically makes societies wiser or better informed. What matters is how information is organised, who controls it and whether the systems that distribute it help people correct their mistakes. Here are five important lessons to learn from Nexus and how they apply to the world we live in today. 5 Lessons to learn from Nexus by Yuval Noah Harari 1. More information does not always mean more truth One of the most important lessons from Nexus is that the availability of information does not automatically make people better informed. We often assume that access to more facts, news and opinions will help us understand the world more accurately. However, information can also be misleading, incomplete or deliberately manipulated. Throughout history, information networks have helped societies organise themselves, preserve knowledge and cooperate on a large scale. Yet the same networks have also spread myths, propaganda and misinformation. Harari explores this tension through historical examples ranging from religious institutions to modern political systems. The same challenge exists today. Social media allows us to access information within seconds, but it can also expose us to misleading headlines, unverified claims and content designed to provoke emotional reactions. The lesson is to become more thoughtful about the information we consume. Instead of believing something simply because it appears frequently online, examine the source, look for supporting evidence and consider alternative explanations. What to remember: Being informed is not just about knowing more. It is about learning to distinguish reliable information from misleading narratives. 2. The stories we believe shape society Human beings depend on shared stories to build communities, establish institutions and coordinate their actions. These stories can include national identities, cultural traditions, political ideologies and ideas about how society should function. In Nexus, Harari examines how information networks help these shared narratives spread across generations and large populations. Such stories can bring people together around common goals, but they can also reinforce divisions when people accept different or conflicting versions of reality. Consider how a single event can be interpreted differently by different communities. The facts may overlap, yet people's beliefs, experiences and sources of information can lead them to completely different conclusions. Understanding this helps explain why disagreements are not always resolved by presenting more facts. Sometimes, people are also defending a larger story about their identity, values or place in the world. What to remember: Question the narratives that influence your thinking . Understanding why you believe something is an important step towards forming independent opinions. Also Read 6 Books that teach lessons from ordinary everyday life 3. Information is closely connected to power Information has always been an important source of power. Those who control how information is collected, recorded and distributed can influence public opinion, shape decisions and determine which perspectives receive attention. Harari traces this relationship through historical examples, examining how empires, religious institutions and political regimes have used information networks to maintain authority or influence society. He also considers how modern information systems affect the distribution of power. Today, this relationship extends to digital platforms, search engines and algorithmic systems that determine what people see online. The information presented to us can influence what we consider important, which issues we discuss and how we understand current events. This does not mean every information system is deliberately manipulative. Rather, it highlights the importance of asking who controls a system, what incentives shape it and whose interests it serves. What to remember: Whenever information influences an important decision, consider who created it, who distributes it and who benefits from the way it is presented. 4. Artificial Intelligence makes information networks more complicated Artificial intelligence is one of the most significant themes in Nexus. Harari explores how AI differs from earlier information technologies and why systems capable of generating content and making decisions could change the way information networks operate. Unlike traditional tools that primarily store or transmit information, AI systems can generate persuasive text, images and other content at enormous scale. They can also perform tasks that previously required human judgement, raising questions about accountability and control. These developments create opportunities in areas such as education, research and healthcare. At the same time, they raise concerns about fabricated information, automated manipulation and the difficulty of identifying who is responsible when AI systems cause harm. The lesson is not to reject technology outright. It is to recognise that technological progress needs to be accompanied by critical thinking, appropriate safeguards and clear accountability. What to remember: AI can help us process information, but we should not automatically treat its outputs as accurate or allow automated systems to make consequential decisions without appropriate oversight. 5. Human responsibility matters more than technological progress alone A central concern in Nexus is that technological advancement does not guarantee that societies will make wise decisions. Humans have developed increasingly powerful tools and information networks, but the consequences depend on how these systems are designed, governed and used. Harari argues that the future of information networks is not predetermined. The choices made by individuals, institutions and governments can influence whether new technologies strengthen society or create additional risks. This is particularly relevant as AI becomes more integrated into everyday life. Decisions about privacy , misinformation, automated systems and the concentration of technological power will affect how people interact with information in the years ahead. Responsibility therefore cannot rest entirely with technology companies or governments. Readers, citizens and technology users also have a role to play by checking claims, recognising uncertainty and thinking carefully about what they share. What to remember: Progress is not simply about developing more powerful technology. It is about making responsible choices about how that technology affects human lives. Final thoughts Nexus: A Brief History of Information Networks from the Stone Age to AI explores how information has shaped human civilisation, from shared beliefs to artificial intelligence. The book argues that more information does not always mean more truth or wisdom. For readers navigating social media, digital news and AI-generated content, it highlights the need to question claims, examine evidence and think critically about how information shapes decisions.

title: As chip prices surge, EV maker Ultraviolette is working on ways to absorb costs
content: The global shortage of memory chips has driven up costs, placing a huge strain on electric vehicle makers in the country. Bengaluru-based Ultraviolette—which produces high-performance electric motorcycles—says it will not pass on the high input costs to customers and is exploring other ways to tide over the situation. Memory chips are a critical component of an electric vehicle, used to store data, run control software, and manage real-time operations across critical systems. According to Ultraviolette’s Founder and CTO, Niraj Rajmohan, RAM (random access memory) alone adds Rs 20,000 to the cost of a vehicle. With global companies building very large data centres, there has been a surge in memory chip consumption, he added. AI data centres are projected to consume 70% of global memory chip production in 2026. The data centre boom has led to a supply crunch, subsequently shoring up costs of chips. But it would not be fair to pass on the costs to customers, said Rajmohan, adding that a threefold jump in memory prices in recent times cannot translate into a threefold jump in the price of an electric bike, and customers cannot be asked to suddenly pay far more. The company is working on alternatives to absorb costs. For now, Ultraviolette is scouting for alternative parts, including software, components and technologies, and alternative manufacturers to partner with. The company is also relying on partners who hold a stake in the company, including TVS, TDK Ventures, and Intel, for their knowhow and expertise, said Rajmohan. He, however, did not elaborate on the alternatives. Rajmohan was speaking at the launch of X-47 Venom, Ultraviolette’s first bike built on its new platform ‘VX-100’, What is VX-100? VX-100 is a 100V electric powertrain architecture that seeks to improve performance and efficiency in electric two-wheelers. An electric powertrain architecture is the integrated system of energy storage, electronics, and mechanical components that converts stored electrical energy into mechanical motion to propel the vehicle. Rather than upgrading the parts one at a time, Ultraviolette has redesigned the battery, motor, and control electronics together, as one system. The X-47 Venom is the first bike built on this new architecture. The company claims it offers better battery cooling, lighter components, and stronger power delivery, along with support for DC fast charging at up to 12 kW. Most electric two-wheelers run on 48V, said Rajmohan, adding that the telecom industry and Southeast Asian manufacturers built their systems around it. At 100V, X-47 Venom’s system draws lower current, and hence produces less heat. The objective is to provide high speed and better performance without the heat, energy loss, and extra weight that usually come with electric vehicles. Currently, Qualcomm supplies the chips that power the bike's new dashboard, while TDK provides the RF (radio frequency) components and capacitors. The X-47 Venom is priced at Rs 2,65,000 for the first 5,000 buyers. Bookings opened on October 22, and deliveries are set to start in November. The European launch will happen on November 3 at EICMA, an international motorcycle expo in Milan. The bike has undergone extensive test rides covering 150 to 200 km a day for several months, said Rajmohan. Ultraviolette’s product portfolio includes the F77 sports bike that is targeted at sports enthusiasts, while the X-47 Crossover is intended to appeal to a broader set of customers, including sports, adventure and street riders. The Crossover makes up about 90% of the company’s sales. The new VX-100 platform will go into all of Ultraviolette’s forthcoming products. Four launches are expected next year, including the Tesseract (a scooter) and Shockwave (an Enduro motorcycle), and an upgraded F77 bike. Roughly 90% of sales come from India and 10% from abroad, including the European market, where the company has been expanding. There are more than 7,000 Ultraviolette bikes on the roads worldwide today. Ultraviolette was founded in 2016 by Narayan Subramaniam and Niraj Rajmohan. Its backers include Lingotto, TDK Ventures, Qualcomm Ventures, Zoho Corporation, TVS Motors, Yali Capital, and Speciale Invest. Edited by Swetha Kannan

title: Autonomy and control are not opposites, they go together: EY GDS at DevSparks Chennai
content: Ask a room of developers about agents today and you will get plenty of answers. Almost everyone has built one, and most have a demo they are proud of. The harder question is what happens after that, when the agent has to hold up against real customers, real data, and real consequences. At DevSparks Chennai 2026 , Arvind Purushothaman, Global Cloud Consulting, Microsoft Practice and Alliances Leader at EY GDS , opened with a version of it. He asked how many people in the room had built an AI agent, and plenty of hands went up. Then he asked how many had built one that made it to production for a business-critical system. "I think that's where the numbers dramatically drop," he said. "Not because of anybody's fault, but that's how it is." That gap is the whole problem, and it is not a model problem. Cloud, low code tools, and open model APIs have pushed the entry barrier close to zero. What has not changed is the difficulty of industrializing what you build. "Access to intelligence is not the bottleneck, but the ability to industrialize is going to be the bottleneck," said Arvind Purushothaman. From the nets to the match Drawing on a cricket analogy, he said that hackathon builds are like net practice, where a few lines of Python and an API key let you rehearse your reverse scoop all afternoon. The match is different. You need 12 runs off six deliveries under pressure, and the strokes only matter alongside the ability to read the situation. For agents, that pressure arrives when the demo meets regulated data, compliance requirements, integration points, and business-critical workflows. Skip the rigor and the exposure is concrete: a bad transaction, financial loss, reputational damage, security and privacy failures. The question itself changes, Purushothaman said, from does it work in a demo to "can we trust it repeatedly under real operating conditions." More autonomy means more engineering Traditional software ran on deterministic rules and stage gates that everything had to clear before production. Agents behave differently. They interpret context, reason about a goal, and decide for themselves which tools to use to reach an outcome. The instinct is to read it as less work for engineers. Purushothaman argued the opposite. More freedom for the agent means more engineering responsibility for the people around it, because the system has to constrain, restrict, and verify what the agent does. "Autonomy and controls … they are not the opposite of each other in this world," he said. He offered three maturity levels to locate yourself against. Task-based agents automate specific steps and return an output. Goal-oriented agents are handed an objective, such as how much credit limit a customer should get, and assemble their own data and policies to reach a recommendation. The third horizon is humans and agents as one team, with judgment reserved for critical calls. Ontologies, controls, and platform Three foundations make production deployment possible, and they only work together. Domain context and ontologies codify business knowledge, taxonomy, and decision logic, and mature vendors now ship them by industry. Controls evaluate outcomes for quality, bias, and risk, and produce traceability. The platform makes execution repeatable and scalable. Ontologies without controls create chaos, controls without a platform are not repeatable, and a platform without domain context is generic. The same logic scales up. The model is only one part of the system, so the engineering has to cover data context, cloud and compute, integration APIs, security and identity, responsible AI, and FinOps discipline around cost. "The outcome is only as strong as the weakest link in your chain," Purushothaman said. Every agent needs a passport Take a customer asking a bank to raise their credit limit. The agent has to establish identity, retrieve the applicable risk policy before anything else so it knows which boundary it is operating under, pull the relevant data, and interpret context. The recommendation has to stay inside policy guidelines, and if the risk is high, it should transfer to a human. Every step has to be auditable. Without that preserved history, he said, it is not a production-ready system. Hence the agent passport. Every agent gets an identity, a named business owner and technical owner, defined permissions covering where it can operate, and escalation points. Organizations already carry deprecated software they cannot account for, and agents will multiply that problem faster. Production systems also need circuit breakers: anomaly detection, the ability to halt execution, roll back, and escalate to humans. What value actually looks like Asked how to measure return, Purushothaman pushed back on counting agents deployed and tokens consumed. The number that matters is cost per governed business outcome, counting cloud and agent running costs, the human effort still in the loop, and the risk profile. "You don't want to over-engineer a simple ask, and you don't want to under-engineer a complex ask. It should be right for the outcome." Testing, he added, has to shift from fixed test cases toward simulating production like runtime conditions. Asked whether robustness holds as attackers keep evolving, he conceded that the how will change while the fundamentals will not. "We talked about the why. We talked about the what. The how will evolve." He closed on the sharpest line of the session. "Intelligence is abundant, but trust, accountability, and repeatability, we must still engineer."

title: Startup news and updates: Daily roundup (October 23, 2026)
content: YourStory brings you today’s headlines with the latest developments across sectors. Funding news GVFL leads Rs 3.7 Cr seed funding round in SpectraGaze Systems GVFL has led a Rs 3.7 crore seed round in Ahmedabad-based SpectraGaze Systems, with participation from angel investors. Founded in 2023 by former ISRO scientist Arup Banerjee, the startup develops indigenous optical imaging sensors and electro-optical payloads for space, defence and scientific applications. SpectraGaze's customers include ISRO, Physical Research Laboratory, and Kaynes Technology. It has delivered an infrared detector and test system to ISRO and secured an image sensor development contract for its HRSAT programme. The funding will support product development, engineering expansion, testing infrastructure and existing customer projects. The company is also developing a hyperspectral imaging camera for a 3U satellite. haf.vc invests Rs 3 Cr in conversational AI startup Hunar.AI Hyderabad-based venture capital fund haf.vc has invested Rs 3 crore in Hunar.AI, a conversational artificial intelligence startup focused on frontline workforce management. The investment will support AI infrastructure, product development, sales and market expansion as the company targets businesses managing large, multilingual workforces across locations. Founded in 2022 by Krishna Khandelwal and Shantanu Bhattacharyya, Hunar.AI develops conversational AI agents that help enterprises hire, onboard, train and engage frontline workers through voice and WhatsApp. Kalyan Sivalenka, Managing Partner at haf.vc, said the company’s understanding of workforce challenges and its technology-driven approach made it an attractive investment. Hunar.AI co-founder and CEO Krishna Khandelwal said the funding would strengthen its presence in Hyderabad and Telangana’s logistics, retail and services sectors. Other news India’s GCCs are projected to grow to about 3.7M employees by 2031 India’s global capability centres (GCCs) are projected to grow from 2.3 million employees to 3.3-3.7 million by 2031, adding 1-1.4 million net jobs and generating 150-170 million sq ft of additional office demand, according to an Embark report. Based on a survey of 100 GCC leaders, the report found that 92% have moved beyond selective AI adoption, but realised productivity gains remain below 15%. Around 80% of workforce additions are expected from existing centres, while demand shifts towards specialised AI, data and cybersecurity roles. Bengaluru and Hyderabad account for 67% of Tier I GCC leasing, while BFSI and technology, media and telecom are expected to drive 54% of incremental office demand. Read more Honasa Consumer elevates Vipul Maheshwari to CPTO Honasa Consumer has elevated Vipul Maheshwari to chief product and technology officer, overseeing product, technology, engineering and analytics. He will lead the company's AI-led transformation and development of agentic AI systems. Maheshwari has spent six years at Honasa, building its data and product capabilities. His new role will focus on developing AI-powered workflows to automate processes, improve decision-making and increase operational efficiency. Before joining Honasa, he held roles at Delhivery and Global Analytics India. He holds a master's degree in mathematics and computer science from IIT Delhi. Microsoft, MeitY Startup Hub, 1M1B launch CoE in Hyderabad Microsoft, MeitY Startup Hub and 1M1B Foundation have launched a Green Skills and Applied AI Centre of Excellence at SAS iTower, Hyderabad, with a dedicated AI and Green Pharma training track. The centre will provide practical training in applied AI, pharmaceutical manufacturing, solar energy, electric vehicles and wind energy, alongside industry mentoring, internships and employment pathways. At the launch, 1M1B Jobs Express reported 100 job offers on its first day. The Hyderabad facility is part of a planned network of five centres aiming to train 100,000 young people in AI and green skills by 2030. Purple Finance posts 101% AUM growth Purple Finance's standalone assets under management rose 101% year-on-year to Rs 329.21 crore in H1 FY27. The NBFC's board has approved exploring entry into affordable housing finance through an acquisition, investment or subsidiary, subject to regulatory approvals. The company has introduced two MSME lending products, PURPLE SARAL, offering loans of Rs 75,000 to Rs 2 lakh, and SAKSHAM LAP, providing mortgage loans of Rs 2 lakh to Rs 4 lakh. It has also launched institutional lending to NBFCs serving MSMEs. Gross non-performing assets remained below 2.5%. Following its acquisition of Saksham Gram Credit, combined AUM reached Rs 853 crore across 205 branches. Lenskart opens its first concept flagship store in India Lenskart has opened its first concept flagship store in India, Lenskart evolv, at Worli, Mumbai. The store combines eyewear retail with design, technology and fashion, featuring chrome-finished interiors and interactive installations Lenskart evolv's services include AI-assisted eye testing, remote optometrist consultations, and a digital shopping assistant. The store also uses Tango Eye technology to support the shopping experience. Lenskart CEO Peyush Bansal said the concept store aims to expand how customers discover and experience eyewear. The company plans to explore a limited number of similar stores in the future. Delhivery, Peak XV Partners launch Demo Day Delhivery and Peak XV Partners have launched Demo Day, powered by Amazon Web Services, to support startups developing technology for supply chains and logistics. The initiative will focus on artificial intelligence applications in logistics, robotics and industrial automation. Selected startups will present their solutions to Delhivery and Peak XV leaders and may access mentorship, cloud infrastructure support, potential investment and opportunities to test technologies in live logistics environments through Delhivery’s network. The programme is open to startups developing solutions for the Indian market, with an emphasis on technologies that can be deployed in real-world operations. Unicorn India Ventures launches US operations to support Indian deeptech startups Deeptech venture capital firm Unicorn India Ventures has launched operations in the US, appointing former Google executive Kishore Kanakamedala as Venture Partner. He will lead the expansion, build a team of mid-to-senior professionals and develop relationships with investors and technology ecosystems in the US to help Indian portfolio companies expand internationally. The move follows the firm’s closure of its third fund of Rs 1,200 crore earlier this year. The fund said it had observed significant interest among US investors in Indian deeptech startups during its fundraising process. Kanakamedala will also help build the US investor base and track global technology developments. Unicorn India Ventures invests in early-stage Indian deeptech companies across sectors including semiconductors, space, defence, healthcare, robotics and agritech. The firm manages approximately $350 million across its funds and has backed 54 companies. ZFunds launches US stocks and ETFs, opens 5,000 accounts on day one Wealth management platform ZFunds has launched US stocks and exchange-traded funds (ETFs), enabling Indian investors to access securities listed in the US market. The platform opened around 5,000 new accounts on the first day of the launch. Investors can access US-listed companies, including Apple, NVIDIA, Amazon, Microsoft, Meta and Berkshire Hathaway, along with ETFs. The offering brings international investing into ZFunds’ wealth manager-led model, allowing customers to manage global investments through the financial professionals handling their other wealth requirements. Manish Kothari, CEO and Co-founder of ZFunds, said global diversification could improve risk-adjusted returns and provide exposure to investment themes such as artificial intelligence and semiconductors. The company cited Reserve Bank of India data showing that overseas equity and debt investments under the Liberalised Remittance Scheme rose 56% to approximately $2.65 billion in FY26. Cortex DC plans 2 GW data centre capacity across India Cortex DC, the AI-focused subsidiary of The Chatterjee Group (TCG), has entered the data centre sector with plans to develop 2 GW of capacity across India. The company aims to serve hyperscalers, cloud service providers and advanced artificial intelligence workloads amid growing demand for computing infrastructure. Cortex DC is targeting operational readiness for its first data centre within 18 months of construction commencing. It also plans to source 51% of its energy from green sources, incorporating renewable power into its infrastructure strategy. Rahul Sharma, CEO of Cortex DC, said the company aims to deliver scalable, resilient and AI-ready infrastructure for domestic and international customers. The company has assembled a leadership team with experience in engineering, construction and digital infrastructure. Its investments are also expected to generate direct and indirect employment across construction, engineering, supply chains and facility operations.
