title: Building a New Foundation for Education: Anshu Kumar’s Neev Ki Eent Foundation for Children of Bihar’s Brick Kiln Workers
content: Every year, thousands of families in Bihar move from one place to another in search of employment. A significant number of these families work at brick kilns. For them, migration is not simply about changing locations. It means changing homes and workplaces. In the process, children’s education often takes a back seat. When a family leaves its village for a few months to work at a brick kiln, its children usually move with it. Schools may be located far away, and a lack of essential documents can make it difficult to access government services. Limited awareness of welfare schemes adds to the challenges. The impact is felt not only in children’s education but also in the entire family’s access to social security. Anshu Kumar Jaiswal from Bihar had not encountered this challenge for the first time through a report or a set of statistics. He had witnessed it on the ground. Between 2019 and 2021, while working with the Piramal Foundation as a Gandhi Fellow, he arrived in Sheikhpura. It was here that he came face to face with the lives of families living and working at brick kilns. This experience changed the direction of his work. He eventually went on to establish the Neev Ki Eent Foundation (NKEF). Today, the NGO works to improve access to education for children of brick kiln workers, help families obtain essential documents, connect them with government welfare schemes, and strengthen local leadership. A change that began in Sheikhpura Anshu’s early education and career gradually led him towards development and public institutions. He studied mass communication and later earned a master’s degree in social work, specialising in youth and community development. He also had opportunities to represent India at international youth programmes. These included the ASEAN-India Youth Summit and a youth exchange programme in China under the Government of India’s Ministry of Youth Affairs and Sports. His subsequent work brought him into contact with various government and development institutions. He worked with the Aspirational Districts Programme, Parliament, the Ministry of Labour and Employment, and the Ministry of Panchayati Raj. These experiences helped him understand how government schemes are designed and how they are implemented on the ground. However, his experience in Sheikhpura was different. Here, he had the opportunity to understand policies and ground-level needs more closely. While working among families employed at brick kilns, he identified several opportunities to improve children’s education and help them connect with schools. He realised that if education could be made more accessible to these families and adapted to their circumstances, children would have a better chance of continuing their studies. Also Read ShuruKar: Your next business could start in your hometown Speaking to YourStory, Anshu Kumar Jaiswal explains, “After meeting families working at brick kilns, I realised that children’s education is not just a school-related issue. Wherever a family works, the child often stays there too. If the family keeps moving from one place to another, the child’s education is likely to suffer. Therefore, simply trying to send a child to school is not enough. Family documents, access to government schemes, and community participation are equally important.” This realisation motivated him to work towards educating the children of brick kiln workers. The initiative is being implemented under Project Swabhimaan, led by Sheikhpura Collector and District Magistrate Shekhar Anand, an IAS officer from the 2018 batch. Launched in February 2026, the initiative has been implemented across the district. While working under this project, Anshu observed that many families lacked essential documents such as birth certificates, Aadhaar cards, ration cards, and bank accounts. The consequences of missing documents extended beyond administrative procedures. They directly affected access to education, ration supplies, healthcare, and social security services. Another question also emerged: if a child must stay with their family at a brick kiln for a certain period, why should education not be made accessible there? Taking Education Where the Children Are After 2022, Anshu began spending time with migrant workers and families employed at brick kilns. Gradually, his focus shifted towards developing a model that could address educational needs alongside other challenges faced by these families. In 2023, he established the Neev Ki Eent Foundation. The NGO works to reduce the social and economic challenges faced by migrant workers and families employed at brick kilns. Its primary programme is Project Swabhimaan. The initiative focuses on education, documentation, access to government schemes, community mobilisation, and preparing young people to take on leadership roles. An important component of this initiative is the Akshar Learning Centre. Through these centres, the organisation attempts to bring education closer to children at the locations where their families work. Children receive foundational instruction in reading, writing, and mathematics. They are also prepared to transition into the formal education system. The distinctive feature of this model is that it takes children’s actual circumstances into account. When families move elsewhere for work, efforts are made to ensure that education remains accessible to their children. Anshu says, “For us, education does not simply mean that a child’s name is entered into a school register. The real question is whether the child continues to learn. The biggest challenge for children of migrant workers is that their lives keep changing. Therefore, we need a system that understands their circumstances and keeps them connected to education. Our effort is to create that continuity.” Under Project Swabhimaan, the foundation also works with children’s families. The NGO assists them in obtaining essential documents, including birth certificates, Aadhaar cards, caste certificates, ration cards, bank accounts, and Ayushman cards. This work goes beyond helping families obtain paperwork. Essential identity documents enable families to establish their presence within the government system. They also open up opportunities to access public services and welfare schemes. That is why the Neev Ki Eent Foundation’s model does not treat education and civic identity as separate issues. Bridging the Gap Between Communities and the Administration One of the challenges faced by grassroots organisations is that their impact can remain limited to a small geographical area. From the beginning, Anshu emphasised working alongside government institutions. Sheikhpura is an example of this approach. The district where he first encountered brick kiln communities as a Gandhi Fellow has now become a place where the Neev Ki Eent Foundation is working with the district administration on a larger scale. Currently, around 55 brick kilns in Sheikhpura have been brought within the initiative’s scope. Efforts are underway to reach thousands of migrant workers and children. Alongside education, the programme focuses on documentation, access to government welfare schemes, community participation, and connecting children with formal schools and Anganwadi services. According to Anshu, more than 15,000 documentation-related needs have been identified or addressed with assistance across different categories. These include birth certificates, Aadhaar cards, caste certificates, ration cards, Ayushman cards, and bank accounts. Another aspect of this work is protection from extreme heat. People working at brick kilns often have to work for long hours in intense heat. Children also live in the same environment. In response, the Neev Ki Eent Foundation has worked with public institutions towards developing heat-resilient spaces. These spaces aim to bring together cooling facilities, children’s education, care, and community-related activities. Anshu explains, “Our objective is not to create a parallel system separate from the government. Government institutions have both the resources and the responsibility. Our role is to reduce the distance between communities and the system. When a family’s needs reach the right department and a department’s scheme reaches the right person, its impact becomes visible. We believe that if communities, civil society organisations, and the administration work together, the model can be scaled up.” This approach is also connected to Anshu’s earlier experience with public administration. He has seen first-hand that having a scheme on paper and ensuring that its benefits reach a family are two different things. Empowering Young People to Lead Change Anshu’s work is not limited to providing external assistance. He also wants to develop people within communities who understand local challenges and can play an active role in addressing them. With this objective, the Swabhimaan Fellowship was launched. Through the fellowship, local young people are trained to support children’s education, inform families about government schemes, and work closely with their communities. The goal is to enable these young people to become voices for their communities and play an important role in bringing about change. Trust plays a crucial role when working with brick kiln workers. Someone from outside the community may understand a family’s problems, but a young person from within the same community is more familiar with its language, relationships, and everyday difficulties. Also Read Taruwar Agro: Three Bihar Friends Built a Rs 2.5 Crore Business from Banana Waste Anshu believes that local leadership is essential to making social change sustainable over the long term. He says, “If change within a community depends entirely on people coming from outside, it will have its limitations. We want young people from the community to step forward themselves. They can support children’s education, inform families about government services, and communicate with the administration when necessary. This ensures that the community is not merely receiving assistance but becomes an active participant in its own transformation.” This is where the energy of Bihar’s youth can be connected to the need for social change. From Sheikhpura to the Rest of Bihar As its work in Sheikhpura expands, Anshu is also looking towards other brick kiln communities across Bihar. The Neev Ki Eent Foundation is working on a model that can be replicated in different parts of the state. Seasonal migration is not new to Bihar. For decades, families have moved from one place to another in search of employment, making migration a longstanding feature of the rural economy. Therefore, the solution to this challenge cannot be limited to a single project or district. For Anshu, the larger question is whether it is possible to create a system in which children can continue their education even when their families must migrate for work. Essential family documents should remain accessible, access to government schemes should continue, and workers should be recognised not merely as labourers but as citizens with rights. Anshu says, “Our efforts are not limited to changing the situation at a single brick kiln. The bigger question is whether children can continue their education despite seasonal migration. Can families retain their identity documents and access to government services wherever they go? If we can find practical answers to these questions, the model could also be used for other migrant communities across Bihar.” A New Approach, A New Bihar The story of Anshu and the Neev Ki Eent Foundation did not begin in a large office or with a major project. It started with his work in Sheikhpura as a fellow. There, he encountered families whose lives are often reduced to a number in government statistics. A few years later, he returned to the same place in a different role. This time, he had his own organisation, the experience he had gained over the years, and a model that brought communities, young people, and the administration together. This shift represents an important aspect of Bihar’s evolving development story. The state’s development is no longer defined solely by infrastructure, roads, or employment statistics. Access to education, digital and civic identity, government welfare schemes, local leadership, and community participation are also becoming increasingly important. Young people like Anshu Kumar are playing a significant role in this transformation. They are not simply identifying problems but also exploring new ways for communities, public policies, and administrative institutions to work together. The Neev Ki Eent Foundation’s work is ongoing, as are its efforts to expand beyond Sheikhpura into other parts of Bihar. However, the significance of this journey lies in more than its current reach. It represents a larger possibility. When government policies and welfare schemes are combined with local knowledge and the participation of young people and grassroots organisations, social change can become more effective and sustainable. Such efforts matter because development does not happen only from the top down. It becomes stronger when policies reach the ground and the voices of communities reach policymakers. Anshu’s journey, which began among the brick kilns of Sheikhpura, is an example of this dialogue. A young man witnessed a problem, understood its underlying causes, and began working towards a solution. Today, Bihar increasingly needs young people, local organisations, and administrative initiatives that connect development with people’s everyday lives. When education, identity, social security, and employment are addressed collectively, the impact can extend beyond a single family. Gradually, it can change the direction of an entire community. Perhaps this is one of the most important aspects of Bihar’s changing development story: the foundation of progress is not built solely through large projects. It is also built through small but consistent efforts that give people access to opportunities, dignity, and a path towards a better future. title: 5 Lessons from Prithvi Raj Banerjee’s Mindful Thinking
content: Anxiety, distraction and overthinking can make everyday life feel overwhelming. In Mindful Thinking: Simple Ways to Let Go of Your Anxiety, Boost Your Productivity and Rewire Your Thoughts , technologist and mindfulness coach Prithvi Raj Banerjee explores how people can understand and gradually change unhelpful thinking patterns. As the founder of the MindGym Initiative, Banerjee approaches mindfulness as a practical skill rather than an abstract spiritual concept. Drawing on mindfulness, cognitive science and everyday exercises, he explains how people can improve their focus, manage anxious thoughts and respond more consciously to life's challenges. 5 Lessons from Prithvi Raj Banerjee’s mindful thinking 1. Train your attention like a muscle Attention can be strengthened through regular practice. Instead of becoming frustrated whenever your mind wanders, recognise the distraction and gently return to the task at hand. Like physical exercise, consistent practice can help you develop better focus over time. The lesson: Focus is a skill you can build through small, consistent efforts. 2. Learn to observe your thoughts without believing them Not every thought reflects reality. Anxiety can make ordinary situations seem threatening, encouraging you to believe worst-case scenarios without questioning them. Banerjee's approach encourages you to observe thoughts without immediately accepting or reacting to them. The lesson: Recognising that thoughts are not always facts can help you respond more thoughtfully. 3. Practise mindfulness through small exercises Mindfulness does not always require long meditation sessions. Techniques discussed in the book, such as Belly Breathing, Bumblebee Humming and the Sensation Scan, offer practical ways to bring attention back to the present moment. You can experiment with these exercises and find what works for your routine. The lesson: Small mindfulness practices can make awareness part of everyday life. Also Read 7 insightful books on anxiety, identity, and online chaos 4. Protect your attention in a digital world Notifications, social media and constant screen-switching can make sustained concentration difficult. Banerjee also highlights the importance of using artificial intelligence thoughtfully rather than accepting its outputs without questioning them. Setting boundaries around technology can help preserve focus and independent thinking. The lesson: Use technology intentionally instead of allowing it to dictate your attention. 5. Pause before reacting to stress Stress can trigger impulsive responses and unnecessary worry. Taking a few deliberate breaths and identifying your emotions before reacting can create space to consider your options. Mindfulness does not eliminate difficult feelings; it encourages you to respond to them more consciously. The lesson: A brief pause can help you make more thoughtful decisions. Final thoughts Prithvi Raj Banerjee's Mindful Thinking presents mindfulness as a practical way to understand thoughts, manage distractions and strengthen attention. Its central message is that you do not need to eliminate every negative thought to think more clearly. By practising awareness, questioning assumptions and making deliberate choices, you can gradually develop a healthier relationship with your mind.

title: [Weekly funding roundup Oct 17-23] VC funding falls below $100M amid lack of big deals
content: Venture capital funding for Indian startups saw a steep decline in the third week of October, primarily due to a lower number of deals and the absence of any large-value transactions. Venture capital funding during the week stood at just $96 million across 15 deals. In contrast, startups raised a total of $180 million in the previous week. This sharp drop in venture capital funding highlights the challenges the Indian startup ecosystem continues to face in raising a steady flow of capital. This is also the eighth time so far this year that weekly venture capital funding has fallen below the $100 million mark. The only large deal during the week was Even Healthcare’s $50 million raise. The other deals were worth $11 million or less. While transactions during the week saw investors place their bets across segments such as healthcare, consumer and AI, there were no other significant deals. The biggest challenge for the Indian startup ecosystem so far this year has been the low number of large-value deals. In fact, there have been just 16 deals worth $100 million or more. This does not bode well for the ecosystem as 2026 draws to a close. However, there is hope for a revival in 2027. Key transactions Even Healthcare raised $50 million from Khosla Ventures and Alpha Wave. The Pant Project , a premium menswear label, raised Rs 109 crore ($11.4 million approx.) from Mirae Asset Venture Investments, Sorin Investments, Alteria Capital, and family offices. Rural healthcare platform CureBay raised Rs 100 crore ($10.4 million approx.) from IvyCap Ventures, Trifecta Capital, Alteria Capital and VentureSoul Partners. Chapter Home , a home and kitchen consumer brand, raised Rs 63 crore ($6.6 million approx.) from Bessemer Venture Partners, Stride Ventures, influencer Tanmay Bhat, and select family offices. Traveltech startup TravClan raised $5 million from Flipkart, August One, and Trifecta Capital. AI startup Hunar AI raised Rs 40 crore ($4.2 million) from Blume Ventures, Hyderabad Angels Fund, Together Fund, Seedstars, AVNM Ventures and startup founders.

title: Tonbo Imaging shares make stellar market debut; jump 66%
content: Shares of Tonbo Imaging India, a defence electronics maker, on Friday listed with a premium of 66% against the issue price of Rs 700. The stock made its debut at Rs 1,162 apiece, registering a premium of 66% from the issue price on the BSE. Later, it traded at Rs 1,059.05, down 8.86% from its listing price, still maintaining a premium of 51.28% over its issue price. On the NSE, the shares opened at Rs 1,160 apiece, a jump of 65.71% over the issue price. It was later trading at Rs 1,058.30, down by 3.64% from the opening level, but 51.18% higher than the issue price. Following the listing, the company's market capitalisation stood at Rs 6,191.91 crore on the BSE and Rs 6,060.45 crore on the NSE. The broader equity market was trading in the red, with the BSE Sensex falling 409.06 points, or 0.56%, to 72,840.33, while the NSE Nifty dropped 173.65 points, or 0.77%, to 22,514. The Rs 852.18-crore initial public offering (IPO) was subscribed nearly 136 times on the final day of bidding on Monday. The public issue was fully subscribed on the first day of bidding on Thursday last week. The issue comprises an offer-for-sale (OFS) of 1.22 crore equity shares by promoters and existing shareholders, with no fresh issue component. Since the IPO is entirely an OFS, the company will not receive any proceeds from the issue. The price band for the IPO has been fixed at Rs 665-700 per share. The Bengaluru-based Tonbo Imaging designs and manufactures sensing, processing, communication and guidance systems used in surveillance, reconnaissance, targeting and control applications. Its product portfolio includes thermal imaging cores, weapon sights, targeting systems, missile seekers, fire control systems and missile guidance systems. As of June 30, 2026, the company has deployed over 28,000 tactical systems and served customers across 24 countries. According to the F&S Report, Tonbo Imaging competes with the likes of Epirus and Teledyne FLIR (US), Hensoldt (Germany), Theon International, and Controp (Israel), which represent established players in electro-optical/ infrared, thermal imaging, and advanced defence electronics in the global market.

title: Swiggy’s Q2: Net loss drops nearly 16%, revenue rises 36%; What sells? The celebrity or the product?
content: Dear Reader, Shiprocket expands into the food commerce market. The company’s AI-native commerce platform fastrr has partnered with Vegorama Group, which operates Punjabi Angithi, and Bikkgane Biryani, to help the restaurant brands manage direct orders, customer engagement, and hyperlocal deliveries. In recent times, restaurants have been exploring ways to drive orders through their own digital channels instead of relying solely on third-party food aggregators. Direct channels give restaurants greater access to customer data and more opportunities to engage with diners after a purchase. Meanwhile, Bengaluru-based digital trust company eMudhra has decided to exit its global website security certificate business, following a security incident involving weak cryptographic keys that prompted action from Google and Mozilla. In a regulatory filing on Thursday, the company said its board had decided to voluntarily withdraw from the business, citing rising compliance costs, increasing data sovereignty requirements and diminishing commercial returns. In other news, rural healthcare platform CureBay has raised Rs 100 crore in a pre-Series C funding round led by IvyCap Ventures. The round comprises Rs 69 crore in equity from IvyCap Ventures and existing investors, and more than Rs 30 crore in debt from Trifecta Capital, Alteria Capital, and VentureSoul Partners. CureBay will use the funds to expand its operations across India, strengthen its healthcare delivery network, and develop its technology and AI capabilities. Amid increasing AI threats, here’s a new one. Major US banks have detected AI agents lurking inside customer accounts. Some of these ​unauthorised third-party agents are even ‌attempting to act independently, Axios reported. Banks including ‌Morgan ⁠Stanley, Bank of America, JPMorgan, and Wells Fargo ​are working to curb these risks. Lastly, what’s PHP and why did companies worldwide scramble to fix flaws in the programming language used to build websites? Here’s the lowdown . In today’s newsletter, we will talk about Swiggy’s Q2: Net loss drops nearly 16%, revenue rises 36% What sells? The celebrity or the product? (Scroll down for the answer) Earnings Swiggy’s Q2 net loss drops nearly 16%, revenue rises 36% Food and grocery delivery platform Swiggy narrowed its net loss by 15.6% year on year (YoY) in the second quarter of FY27. Its revenue rose 36% during the same period. The company reported a loss of Rs 922 crore in Q2 of FY27, compared with a loss of Rs 1,092 crore in the same period a year ago. Revenue for the quarter was Rs 7,571 crore, up from Rs 5,561 crore a year ago. Key takeaways Losses at Instamart, Swiggy's quick commerce business, widened to Rs 764 crore, compared with Rs 739 crore a year ago, thus impacting the overall numbers of the company. Instamart’s revenue for the second quarter was Rs 1,306 crore, up from Rs 980 crore in the corresponding year-ago period. The gross order value of the food delivery business grew 17.7% YoY to touch Rs 10,054 crore for the second quarter. The adjusted EBITDA for the quarter was Rs 341 crore, an improvement of Rs 101 crore over the last one year. In comparison, Swiggy’s rival Eternal reported a 92% rise in net profit at Rs 125 crore, while revenue grew 78% to Rs 24,138 crore in the second quarter of FY27. TechSparks Celebrities don’t sell, the product does: Ananth Narayanan The froth has gone out of D2C, and brands that want to last will have to play the patient game. This was the key message from Ananth Narayanan, Founder and CEO of BRND.ME, at the 17th edition of YourStory’s TechSparks event. In a fireside chat with Shradha Sharma, Founder and CEO of YourStory and The Bharat Project, Narayanan said, without product-market fit, merely scaling, which a lot of D2C brands used to do, is not valued anymore. “You need real cash flows, you need real product love, which is very hard,” he said. Key takeaways A celebrity may add recall to a brand, but it’s the product that sells, said Narayanan. “A face can give you initial momentum, but I don’t think it can get you repeat consumers.” He advised founders to build with heart. “Build products that you love. Otherwise you are becoming a bit of a machine that churns out unit economics.” On India as a brand, Narayanan said the country stands for talent and should now move on to culture, from yoga and Ayurveda to mindfulness. “Why can’t we make the Indian way of living the most important thing in the digital age?” <Funding Alert> Startup: Chapter Home Amount: Rs 63 Cr Round: Equity & Debt Startup: TravClan Amount: $5M Round: Undisclosed News & updates PHP patch: Companies and governments worldwide rushed on Thursday to patch critical flaws in the widely used PHP programming language, as a cybersecurity company reported millions of hacking attempts after the ​vulnerabilities were disclosed. title: How AI Is democratising creativity, according to Canva India’s Chandrika Deb
content: As AI-generated creators and near-identical AI visuals flood social feeds, the question of what is left for humans to do has become hard to avoid. At TechSparks 2026 , Chandrika Deb, Country Manager, India, Canva, offered a clear answer: judgement, intent, and point of view. In a fireside chat titled "Tool to Co-creator: How AI is rewriting the creative process,” with Aditya Gurwara, Co-Founder and Head of Brand Alliance, Qoruz, Chandrika said that Canva sees itself as "a collaborator, a partner and an enabler" in the creative process. According to her, AI removes barriers of skill, resources, and knowledge. She drove the point home with an interesting statistic. “We've heard from 97% of the marketers we have surveyed that they use AI in some form. But it's about understanding whether this is the best output I can get from the prompt I've generated. So it's about having that judgement and intent in place, and that only comes from human nature. It ensures you are using AI in the best possible way and getting output that is relevant for your audience,” she said. Asked whether generative AI is moving from democratising design to democratising creativity itself, Chandrika replied, “ I think it's about democratising the ability to act on your creativity. All of us have inherent creativity. AI helps you realise it by overcoming barriers. Maybe it's a mental block: I want to create a video, but I don't know what to create it on. AI helps you overcome that ideation barrier. Or maybe it's a resource barrier: I need so many team members to make that video for me,” she explained. A small business owner may have an idea of what they want to build but may not be able to visualize how the product should look and feel. Chandrika believes AI lets you get to that output much faster and iterate more easily than before. She framed this as the next phase of Canva's story. She said the company's first decade brought fragmented, expensive design tools into one online editor. The current decade is about doing the same for scattered AI platforms and workflows, so businesses can work more efficiently. Chandrika expects AI to reshape team structures, mainly by widening participation. Founders, marketers, product staff and salespeople can now start shaping creative work before specialist design teams step in. “Historically, we've relied on design teams to produce much of the creative output companies work on. AI makes it easier for a founder, a marketer, someone on the product team, or a salesperson to get involved much faster. So the structure of teams is evolving. It's about who steps into the journey earlier,” she said. Specialists who understand craft, cultural nuance and audiences remain essential, she added, as do creative-operations experts who keep output on brand. She also flagged the need to be mindful when working with early talent, because years of experience often bring judgement. “As leaders, it's our job to shape early talent, give them feedback and mentor them, so that those just starting out with AI in the workplace get a better sense of how to use their judgment, and use AI more efficiently and more responsibly,” she added. Chandrika also addressed the risk of AI-driven personalisation becoming noise rather than relevance. “Personalisation becomes noise when your audience sees no benefit,” she said, emphasising that AI should make content more relevant to the people it seeks to reach. AI, she explained, lets brands scale personalisation across more audience segments, formats, and languages, rather than creating assets for a limited number of groups. Tools such as Canva AI can generate multilingual content, helping brands tailor communication to different audiences while accounting for cultural nuances. However, technology alone cannot guarantee relevance. “At the end of the day, you have to make it relevant for them. Otherwise, it just becomes noise,” Chandrika said. Chandrika believes AI will overturn the assumption that creativity is a skill reserved for a select few or those with access to resources. “What AI has shown is that anyone with a sense of judgement and an idea can produce a good creative. We recently launched a new campaign for Canva called Aap aur Canva, Jodi Wah Wah, to communicate this: Canva is your partner. It helps you overcome the lack of confidence you may feel about exploring your creativity,” she elaborated. According to her, AI can play a huge role in removing self-doubt or inhibition people may have about exploring their creativity. It can help everyone go from idea to output more seamlessly and iterate on their ideas. “The other thing is that in businesses today, AI empowers everyone to be part of the creative process, and part of the process that takes an idea to a product to a business. We are seeing a lot of organic, bottom-up adoption of AI tools within businesses because they solve a real problem for employees. Nobody has to come in and force it on them. 95% of the Fortune 500 companies use Canva and our AI features, so we see real value and real impact. It is delivering ROI for these businesses,” she added.

title: Sebi cautions investors against fraudulent stock-tip WhatsApp groups
content: Markets regulator Sebi has cautioned investors against fraudulent WhatsApp stock-tip groups that use 'astroturfing'–fake endorsements and profit claims–to create a false impression of credibility and lure investors. In a statement, Sebi said certain unregistered persons were offering stock recommendations to investors through invitation-only WhatsApp groups in the name of free investor education. The operators of these fraudulent groups often use overseas WhatsApp numbers posing as market experts. “To make these calls look credible, certain members, acting in concert with the operators, post false claims of profit and praise the 'expert'. This practice, known as astroturfing, creates a false impression of genuine support and induces unsuspecting investors to act on the call,” Sebi said. The regulator also highlighted a tactic used by such groups after enforcement agencies or regulatory bodies take action against them. The Securities and Exchange Board of India (Sebi) noted that members are often contacted from a new number and invited to join another group, with operators claiming that the previous group had been banned due to social media platform restrictions. One such message cited by Sebi reads, "Due to social media platform's risk control measures, our previous group has been banned. This new group will provide daily recommendations of quality stock information and trading guidance. Please join the group.” Advising investors to exercise caution, Sebi said they should not join invitation-only WhatsApp groups operated by unknown persons or individuals claiming to be stock market experts, particularly those using overseas numbers. Investors have also been advised not to be influenced by messages containing praise, profit claims or trade confirmations posted by other members, as such posts could be planted to create a misleading impression. The regulator said messages claiming that a group had been suspended, closed or banned, and inviting members to join a new group should be treated as red flags. It further advised investors against opening accounts on, or transferring money to, trading platforms or applications recommended by such groups. ​ Investors should also refrain from sharing their investment holdings or trading account details with the operators, the regulator advised. “Deal only with Sebi-registered intermediaries and use only authentic trading apps,” the regulator said, adding that investors could verify the registration status of intermediaries through its official website. Sebi said the statement was intended to caution investors against acting on stock tips and trading calls circulated through such closed fraudulent WhatsApp groups and urged them to remain vigilant while dealing in the securities market.

title: Experts discuss how AI can bridge gaps in India’s public healthcare system
content: From remote monitoring and early disease detection to tools that help frontline health workers make better decisions, startups are developing solutions to address gaps in healthcare delivery. The bigger challenge, however, lies in integrating these technologies into India’s public health system and making them accessible. At TechSparks 2026, Dr Geetha Manjunath, Founder and CEO, Niramai Health Analytix; Debraj Banerjee, Global technology investor and General Partner, Fundamentum Frontier Advisors; and Shekar Sivasubramanian, Head, Wadhwani AI; discussed on healthcare innovation and AI, and why promising innovations often struggle to achieve widespread adoption. According to the panel, startups face three interconnected challenges: rigorous clinical validation, integration with existing public health infrastructure, and the patience capital required to scale solutions across India’s diverse healthcare ecosystem. “There are no gaps in the system,” said Shekhar Sivasubramanian, Head of Wadhwani AI, arguing that innovators must learn to design solutions around real-world constraints rather than treat them as obstacles. Internet connectivity may be inconsistent, data may be incomplete, and solutions may need to work across languages and cultural contexts. These are realities that developers must account for, he said. “If you cannot solve a problem with these realities, then you shouldn’t be in this business,” he added. Clinical validation remains a critical hurdle Geetha Manjunath said one of the biggest barriers to adoption is the tendency to prioritise rapid product development over clinical validation. AI tools can now be built in days using readily available datasets and development platforms. But a model that performs well in a laboratory does not necessarily deliver reliable results when deployed in real-world healthcare settings. “The question is not whether you build your model. The real problem is to see if your algorithm actually works on real people,” she said. Retrospective studies, which use existing hospital data with known outcomes, can provide an initial assessment. Prospective studies go further by testing a technology in a live clinical setting without allowing its predictions to influence treatment decisions. The results are subsequently compared with established clinical findings. However, she added that even these stages may not be enough for public health deployment. A technology tested in a hospital must also be evaluated in the settings where it is intended to be used, including rural areas where diagnostic infrastructure may be limited. The cost of implementation, feasibility of deployment and clinical performance must all be considered before a technology can be recommended for wider use. “Healthcare requires more patience,” she said, adding that founders need resilience and a long-term commitment. Integrating with public health systems Beyond clinical validation, integrating new technologies into existing government systems remains a significant challenge. Sivasubramanian of Wadhwani AI said companies looking to work in public health must understand the systems used by both central and state governments. His organisation has teams embedded in state health offices across 17 states, with teams of around five to seven people working within these offices. The approach is necessary because implementing a technology requires more than developing a functional product. Teams must train users, understand local requirements and adapt their solutions to existing workflows. He added that each application requires integration with frontline healthcare infrastructure. “India has around 150,000 primary health centres, and innovators must be prepared to work at that scale. Without patience, perseverance and sufficient financial resources, a company may reach a halfway point, become disappointed and walk away. Deep commitment is essential.” He added that government officials implement these solutions, while innovators act as facilitators. “Technology companies must work with them rather than assume they can independently deliver change.” Making AI affordable and accessible For healthcare technologies to reach underserved populations, affordability and accessibility must be built into their design. Geetha Manjunath cited Niramai’s breast cancer screening technology as an example. The company uses thermal imaging and AI to assess breast cancer risk through a non-invasive screening process. The company aims to bring the cost of screening below Rs 50 at scale. The technology is also designed to address barriers that discourage women from seeking screening, including discomfort with procedures involving physical contact or breast compression. Manjunath identified affordability, accessibility, acceptability, and accuracy among the key requirements for successful AI adoption in public health. Timely results and clear accountability are also important. Scaling still remains difficult For investors, the challenge extends beyond determining whether a technology works. They must assess whether the business can navigate regulatory approvals, financing requirements and the complexities of reaching customers. Banerjee, a general partner at Fundamental Frontier Advisors, said deep-tech companies need an ecosystem that supports the journey from product development to commercialisation. “There is no single formula for scaling healthcare innovation.” He added, “When evaluating AI products, we look at the underlying principles and whether several of them apply to the product. It should be appropriately segmented, nested within the relevant system and hyperlocalised. Those are some of the factors that can help us assess whether an investment is likely to work.” “Venture capital represents only one part of the entire ecosystem,” he said, emphasising that the wider network of healthcare providers, regulators, investors and commercial partners must also develop. The broader challenge, he said, is not simply creating better technology but building the systems that allow it to reach users. From India to global markets For Niramai, the opportunity extends beyond India as the company has screened around seven lakh women and is working towards expanding access to its technology. “Our goal is to reach every woman,” Geetha Manjunath said, acknowledging that achieving this would take sustained effort over many years. The company has also expanded into international markets. The same technology can also be relevant in developed markets, where healthcare systems are seeking ways to manage costs. Niramai has six centres in the US using its solution and that the company received US FDA approval for use alongside existing screening methods. However, expansion requires a different approach in each market, she added. Regulatory requirements, reimbursement structures and pricing models vary, and a solution cannot necessarily be deployed in the same way everywhere. For Indian healthcare innovators, she said, building for local needs should not prevent them from pursuing international opportunities.

title: Apple iPhone Duo's entire first week stock pre-booked in India
content: Apple is learnt to have exhausted the first week’s stock of its most expensive iPhone, the iPhone Duo, which is scheduled to go on sale in India on October 23, sources aware of the development said. Apple Stores in BKC (Bandra Kurla Complex), Mumbai, and Saket, New Delhi, have recorded the highest number of pre-bookings for the ultra-premium, first-ever foldable iPhone from the company. "First week stock of iPhone Duo is entirely sold out in India. Apple Stores located in BKC and Saket are very close in terms of booking numbers," sources aware of inventory movement told PTI . This implies that the iPhone Duo will not be available for walk-in purchases at Apple Stores. Pre-orders for the iPhone Duo opened in India on October 16. An emailed query to Apple did not elicit an immediate response. With the Duo, Apple has entered the foldable smartphone category. The device will be priced between Rs 3 lakh and Rs 4.5 lakh in India, putting it in the same price range as some of the country’s top-selling Maruti Suzuki hatchback models. Analysts estimate that the iPhone Duo will capture around 24% of the foldable device market, where it will compete with the Samsung Z Fold 8 series, which is available in India at prices ranging from Rs 1.79 lakh to Rs 2.6 lakh per unit for the 1TB storage variant. Counterpoint Research Director Tarun Pathak said the initial adoption of Duo will be driven by an excellent form factor, the bigger screen value proposition and a great UI experience, which will make loyal Apple users and early adopters of technology go for it, especially those who have been waiting for an Apple foldable form factor for a long time. "Overall, we believe that the iPhone Duo is set to expand India's foldable segment by value rather than volume initially and bring the spotlight on the foldable segment," he said. In its folded state, the iPhone Duo will have a 5.4-inch display, offering 90% of the screen area of the iPhone 18 Pro. When unfolded, it will have a 7.6-inch display, which is 50% larger than that of the iPhone 18 Pro Max. The iPhone 18 Pro has a 6.3-inch display, while the iPhone 18 Pro Max has a 6.9-inch display. Apple has been posting record performance in India. Its revenue in India is estimated to have crossed $10 billion, driven by record iPhone shipments in FY26. In rupee terms, this translates to revenue of nearly Rs 1 lakh crore. According to Counterpoint Research, Apple’s iPhone shipments in FY26 rose to 14 million units, up 24% year-on-year. The iPhone accounts for the majority of Apple’s revenue in India and is also the country’s top-exported smartphone.

title: Deeptech startups in India must have global ambitions, urge panellists at TechSparks
content: The deeptech sector in the Indian startup ecosystem has emerged out of the shadows and carved a niche for itself. Many aspects are falling in place for the growth of deeptech startups, and despite various challenges companies from India must cultivate global ambitions, concurred experts at a panel discussion at TechSparks, YourStory’s tech-startup summit. The panel comprised founders from the domains of robotics, precision manufacturing, and semiconductors, and an executive from a policy think-tank. The session was moderated by Shivani Muthanna, Senior Director - Strategic Content & Video, YourStory. Despite the challenges in the sector, the panellists agreed that the overall environment was changing for the better. Kaushik Mudda, Founder & CEO, Ethereal Machines, a high precision manufacturing startup, said, “We have most things in place that enable us to compete globally.” According to Shweta Rajpal Kohli, President & CEO of Startup Policy Forum, the deeptech ecosystem has found its rightful place with the government making key contributions in terms of capital and policies. “I think the government's done a lot of things right in terms of providing that enabling environment. This is India's moment to push deeptech.” Today, the deeptech sector is keen on building or possessing technologies that are critical to the sovereignty of the country. Agnit Semiconductors’ co-founder and CEO Hareesh Chandrasekar said, “We need to build across the ecosystem but this will only be built over time.” Agnit Semiconductors is India’s first vertically integrated gallium nitride semiconductor product startup. Challenges in the sector Commenting on the challenges that deeptech startups are facing in the country, Gokul N A, the founder of robotics startup CynLr said, especially in the space they are present in, the ecosystem is still absent. There is also a shortage of talent, especially at the mid-management level, he added. “We don’t churn that much volume of quality engineers in the country as we are still very service oriented,” he remarked. The panellists were of the view that the country needs to have clear focus areas in the deeptech segment, which is a fairly vast subject. “We need to start building the basic building block of what it takes to become a manufacturing superpower,” Mudda said. Chandrasekar remarked that, in the current environment where semiconductors have been weaponised, it is important for the country to develop sovereign capability. Availability of capital is another roadblock, although the situation is much better now than in the past. According to Gokul, while seed-stage funding has improved, a lot needs to be done to get patient capital into the segment. Kohli said the capital challenge is being solved, especially with the government coming out with a Rs 1 lakh crore Research, Development and Innovation Fund. Mudda opined that funding up to $5 million is not much of a challenge for deeptech startups but there is still a scarcity when it comes to the next level of fundraise—$10million to $15 million. Deeptech needs a global market On the government as a customer for deeptech startups in the country, the panellists said the government can be an enabler but startups should look at global markets. “That demand generation and the government as the first buyer is a big boost for any sector,” said Kohli. But the government’s procurement process is a bit complicated, he added. According to Chandrasekhar, while startups would like the government to be their first customer, it cannot be the only customer. Deep technology needs a global market, and cannot have India alone as its focus, said Gokul. According to Kohli, self-belief among participants in the ecosystem needs to improve to ensure deeptech grows bigger. “India has the talent, scale and everything going for it. We just need to accelerate it at a feverish pace now,” she remarked.

title: 5 Books you must read to learn how to say no confidently
content: Saying no can be surprisingly difficult, especially when you worry about disappointing others, damaging relationships or being perceived as selfish. Whether it is agreeing to extra work, accepting social invitations you would rather decline or constantly putting other people's needs before your own, the habit of saying yes can leave you feeling overwhelmed and emotionally exhausted. Learning to set boundaries does not mean becoming rude or uncaring. It means recognising your limits, respecting your time and understanding that you cannot meet everyone's expectations. The right books can help you understand people-pleasing, communicate your needs more clearly and become comfortable with the possibility that not everyone will agree with your decisions. If you find yourself struggling to say no without feeling guilty, these five books offer practical insights into building boundaries, protecting your energy and developing healthier relationships. 5 Books you must read to learn how to say no confidently 1. The Joy of Saying No by Natalie Lue If guilt often prevents you from saying no, Natalie Lue's The Joy of Saying No is a useful place to begin. The book explores people-pleasing, emotional obligations and the fear of disappointing others. It encourages readers to recognise when they agree to things out of guilt rather than genuine willingness. Lue also highlights the importance of understanding your limits and communicating them without overexplaining every decision. Learning to say no becomes easier when you stop treating everyone else's approval as a responsibility. The book reminds readers that protecting their time and emotional well-being is not an act of selfishness. 2. Set Boundaries, Find Peace by Nedra Glover Tawwab In Set Boundaries, Find Peace , therapist Nedra Glover Tawwab explains why healthy boundaries are essential for maintaining balanced relationships. The book explores how unclear expectations can contribute to resentment, frustration and emotional exhaustion. Through practical guidance, Tawwab helps readers identify their needs, communicate limits and respond when others struggle to respect them. It covers boundaries in family relationships, friendships , romantic partnerships and professional settings. For anyone who finds it difficult to refuse requests from loved ones, this book offers a helpful reminder that caring about someone does not require agreeing with everything they ask. 3. When I Say No, I Feel Guilty by Manuel J. Smith Manuel J. Smith's When I Say No, I Feel Guilty focuses on assertiveness and the ability to communicate your thoughts without becoming aggressive or unnecessarily apologetic. It helps readers understand how fear, social pressure and the desire for approval can make ordinary conversations difficult. The book introduces practical communication techniques for handling criticism, unreasonable requests and attempts to pressure you into changing your decision. Its central approach is to help readers express themselves calmly while respecting both their own rights and those of others. It is particularly useful for people who struggle to stand their ground during uncomfortable conversations. 4. Essentialism: The Disciplined Pursuit of Less by Greg McKeown Greg McKeown's Essentialism explores how to focus on what genuinely matters instead of spreading your time and energy across too many commitments. The book challenges the assumption that being productive means doing more and accepting every opportunity. Also Read 5 Teachings from Essentialism about doing less but better McKeown encourages readers to distinguish between essential priorities and activities that contribute little to their goals. This approach makes saying no easier because decisions become guided by what matters most rather than by pressure to please everyone. For professionals, students and anyone managing competing responsibilities, the book offers a practical way to protect time and make more intentional choices. 5. The Book of Boundaries by Melissa Urban Melissa Urban's The Book of Boundaries provides practical guidance for communicating personal limits in everyday situations. It addresses challenges involving family members, friends, colleagues and other people who may have expectations that conflict with your needs. One of the book's most useful aspects is its focus on what to say when setting a boundary. Having clear language can make difficult conversations less intimidating, particularly when you are accustomed to agreeing automatically. Urban encourages readers to communicate their limits clearly and follow through consistently, rather than relying on others to guess what makes them uncomfortable. Final thoughts Learning to say no is not about shutting people out or refusing every request. It is about understanding your priorities, recognising your limits and making decisions without constantly seeking approval. These five books approach the subject from different perspectives, including people-pleasing, assertive communication, healthy relationships and time management. Together, they offer practical ways to establish boundaries and become more confident about expressing your needs.

title: Swiggy's net loss drops nearly 16% to Rs 922 Cr in Q2, revenue rises 36%
content: Food and grocery delivery platform Swiggy narrowed its net loss by 15.6% year on year (YoY) in the second quarter of FY27. Its revenue rose 36% during the same period. The company reported a loss of Rs 922 crore in Q2 of FY27, compared with a loss of Rs 1,092 crore in the same period a year ago. Revenue for the quarter was Rs 7,571 crore, compared with Rs 5,561 crore a year ago. On the second quarter performance of the company, Swiggy MD & Group CEO Sriharsha Majety said, in a statement, “Our food delivery business delivered its highest ever profits and margins while we continue to unlock new category growth through Toing, our standalone offering for affordable meals. "In quick commerce, we delivered accelerated growth as guided and obtained necessary approvals to qualify as an Indian owned and controlled company - an important milestone for the business with the transition underway." The gross order value (GOV) of the food delivery business grew 17.7% YoY to touch Rs 10,054 crore for the second quarter. The adjusted EBITDA for the quarter was Rs 341 crore, an improvement of Rs 101 crore over the last one year. Swiggy's quick commerce business Instamart saw net order value grow 31.4% YoY to reach Rs 6,954 crore. Instamart added 69 darkstores in the quarter, equal to the cumulative additions of the last three quarters, bringing the total network to 1,240 stores covering 5.2 million sq ft. Instamart's revenue for the second quarter was Rs 1,306 crore, up from Rs 980 crore in the corresponding year-ago period. However, it clocked a loss of Rs 764 crore, compared with Rs 739 crore a year ago. In a shareholder letter, Majety said, “This was a quarter in which our businesses grew faster and our direction became clearer. At our first ever Capital Markets Day held on 6-Aug-26, we shared our long-term aspiration to build towards Rs 10,000 crore of adjusted EBITDA by FY31, at GOV of over Rs 2.5 lakh crore with ~4% margins.” “We see assortment as a curation game rather than a volume game, and our aim is to enable consumers to buy better, not just offer more," said Majety, in the statement. In comparison, Swiggy’s rival Eternal, which operates Zomato and Blinkit, reported a 92% rise in net profit at Rs 125 crore, while revenue grew 78% to Rs 24,138 crore in the second quarter of FY27.

title: eMudhra to exit global website security certificate business
content: Bengaluru-based digital trust company eMudhra has decided to exit its global SSL/TLS certificate business following a security incident involving weak cryptographic keys that prompted action from Google and Mozilla. In a regulatory filing on Thursday, the company said its board had decided to voluntarily withdraw from the business, citing rising compliance costs, increasing data sovereignty requirements and diminishing commercial returns. The decision follows the discovery of eight intermediate certificate authority keys linked to eMudhra that were found to be dangerously weak, potentially allowing attackers to impersonate legitimate websites. The keys were generated in April 2025, but the weakness remained undetected for about 18 months. Google and Mozilla subsequently moved to block the affected certificates to protect users. eMudhra Chairman V Srinivasan said the company had revoked the affected certificate authorities within 14 hours of discovering the incident and promptly disclosed the issue. The company maintained that its infrastructure had not been compromised, no data had been breached and none of the affected intermediate authorities had issued end-user certificates. Global SSL/TLS certificates, which help authenticate websites and secure online communications, contribute approximately 1% of eMudhra's global revenue. Srinivasan said increasing data sovereignty and compliance requirements had made the business more complex and expensive to operate. Competition from large providers offering SSL/TLS certificates free of cost had also reduced its commercial potential and return on investment. "The level of social media amplification around this incident has brought scrutiny that is out of proportion to SSL/TLS's place in our business," Srinivasan said. He added that the board, following detailed deliberations, had concluded that withdrawing from the global SSL/TLS business was the right decision for the company and its shareholders. eMudhra said it would now sharpen its focus on core enterprise solutions and digital trust services outside the SSL/TLS segment. What happens to existing customers? The company said its G1 RSA root certificates would continue to serve customers during the transition as it works with browser programmes and customers to facilitate the withdrawal. It will reach out to affected customers and arrange replacement certificates free of cost through partners. Revocation and certificate status services will continue until every issued certificate has expired or been replaced. eMudhra also committed to fulfilling its remaining obligations to browser root programmes, including submitting a full root-cause report on the incident. It has not specified a timeline for completing the exit. Other operations unaffected The company clarified that its global SSL/TLS infrastructure operates separately from its other businesses, including its Indian digital signature certificate (DSC) and eSign services. Its enterprise public key infrastructure platforms, including emCA and CertiNext, emSigner eSignature Suite and identity and authentication solutions such as SecurePass and emAS, will also continue operating normally. The incident has drawn scrutiny from global browser providers and Indian authorities. Google's Chrome Security team had warned that the weak keys could allow attackers to forge trusted HTTPS certificates, while Mozilla blocked the affected certificates in Firefox. India's Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In) also issued an advisory on October 21, flagging the risks associated with the compromised certificate keys. eMudhra, which provides digital identity, trust and security solutions across more than 35 countries, said the decision would allow it to concentrate resources on its broader enterprise technology portfolio.

title: Amazon bets on agentic AI to power enterprise ops; Is your marketing AI tool driving profit or just noise?
content: Dear Reader, The future points to agentic AI, and its implementation is gathering pace. Cognizant and Google Cloud are expanding their partnership to accelerate adoption of agentic AI. This includes a ‘Gemini Frontier Capability Group’, which brings together Google’s full-stack, enterprise-ready AI platform and Cognizant’s industry and engineering expertise as an AI-builder. The group will be supported by more than 18,000 dedicated Cognizant associates and a substantial joint investment. Meanwhile, ahead of its IPO , Jio Platforms’ anchor book has drawn Rs 2.5 lakh crore in bids. The company allotted 7.24 crore shares at a price of Rs 1,119 apiece to anchor investors, with LIC receiving the largest allocation. Moving on, Hunar.AI has raised Rs 40 crore in a Series A funding round led by Blume Ventures. The round also saw participation from Hyderabad Angels Fund, Together Fund, Seedstars, AVNM Ventures, PhysicsWallah co-founders Prateek Maheshwari and Alakh Pandey, and MediaMint co-founder Aditya Vuchi. The startup, which develops specialised AI tech for frontline-intensive industries, will use the funds for building AI infrastructure, product development, and go-to-market expansion. Lastly, a report by Redseer notes that the online retail market in the country is expected to cross $90 billion this year with grocery overtaking mobiles. The gross merchandise value of the ecommerce market expanded roughly 25% year on year to about $38 billion in the first half of 2026, marking its strongest H1 performance in four years. In today’s newsletter, we will talk about Amazon’s bet on agentic AI to power enterprise ops Marketing AI tool: Is it driving profit or just noise? Here’s your trivia for today: What was the first Mickey Mouse cartoon ever produced? (Scroll down for the answer) TechSparks Amazon bets on agentic AI to power enterprise ops Speaking at TechSparks 2026, Rajeev Rastogi, Vice President of Machine Learning at Amazon, highlighted the rise of agentic AI in the entire enterprise operating layer, marking a transition from static software to autonomous systems capable of understanding natural language instructions. “Agents prepare plans dynamically to solve a problem... and invoke the appropriate tools,” Rastogi explained during a fireside chat at the 17th edition of YourStory’s flagship tech-startup event. Driving transformation: Instead of relying on human intervention at every step, these autonomous agents evaluate queries, formulate a sequence of actions, and call specialised digital tools to complete complex tasks end-to-end. Within Amazon, this operating layer is active in systems like Rufus, a conversational shopping assistant that parses customer requests, applies price filters, invokes search engines, and guides users through product comparisons and checkout journeys. Similarly, autonomous seller assistants pre-fill product listings, monitor inventory levels, and guide small businesses through international export compliance. According to Rastogi, eventually the industry will advance towards genuine world models that possess an internal understanding of physical spaces and environmental behaviour, establishing a practical, cost-effective framework for enterprise automation. TechSparks Is your marketing AI tool driving profit or just noise? At TechSparks 2026, Anand Jain, Co-founder and Chief Marketing Officer of CleverTap, a customer engagement and marketing automation platform, explained why marketing teams must move beyond basic generative AI productivity tools and adopt autonomous, real-time decisioning systems that drive genuine business profit. Key takeaways: In a masterclass on marketing strategy, Jain urged leaders to look beyond simple shortcuts, and move from using AI for fun and games to generating actual business results. While creating content using AI makes the job faster and saves time, Jain questioned whether it truly drives growth. “Is it actually going to impact business results or is it just more of the same?” Instead of broadcasting generic promotions to large groups, modern marketing engines should interpret live customer actions to match individual needs. This approach marks a shift towards the highest level of AI maturity, known as ‘real-time decisioning’. News & updates Trade deal: The India-New Zealand Free Trade Agreement has come into effect. The agreement provides duty-free access to a range of Indian goods, including products from labour-intensive sectors such as textiles and leather. OYO IPO: OYO parent PRISM plans to nearly halve the size of the fresh issue in its proposed IPO to up to Rs 3,350 crore from almost Rs 6,650 crore. This follows strong cash generation and an improving balance-sheet position, people familiar with the matter told PTI . title: Jio Platforms' anchor book draws Rs 2.5 lakh crore in bids ahead of IPO
content: Jio Platforms has allotted shares worth Rs 8,109.85 crore to 212 anchor investors at the top end of its price band, after institutional demand for the offering exceeded Rs 2.5 lakh crore, more than 30 times the amount available in the anchor book, according to a stock exchange filing and people familiar with the matter. The allotment of 7.24 crore shares at Rs 1,119 apiece comes ahead of the initial public offering that opens for public subscription on Wednesday. The strong demand underscores institutional investor interest in what is expected to be India's largest IPO, although the extent to which it translates into broader public demand will become clearer once the offer opens. Life Insurance Corporation of India received the largest allocation, worth Rs 499.98 crore, accounting for 6.17 per cent of the anchor portion. New World Fund Inc was allotted shares worth Rs 486.27 crore, followed by the Government of Singapore at Rs 340.93 crore, SBI Focused Fund at Rs 315 crore and BNP Paribas Financial Markets - ODI at Rs 303.25 crore. Domestic mutual funds received 2.489 crore shares worth Rs 2,784.96 crore, representing 34.34 per cent of the anchor book, through 95 schemes across 25 fund houses. Life insurers and pension funds received 97.4 lakh shares worth Rs 1,089.95 crore, or 13.44 per cent of the total. Both categories exceeded the allocations reserved for them under the red herring prospectus dated October 14, which earmarked 33.33 per cent of the anchor portion for mutual funds and 6.67 per cent for insurers and pension funds. Global investment firms participating in the anchor book include BlackRock, Capital Group, Fidelity, T. Rowe Price, Schroders, JPMorgan Asset Management, Franklin Templeton and Janus Henderson. Sovereign and public investment institutions include the Abu Dhabi Investment Authority and the Monetary Authority of Singapore, alongside other long-term institutional investors. Some large overseas and domestic institutions bid for allocations worth $750 million to more than $1 billion each, people familiar with the matter said. Jio Platforms is seeking to raise about Rs 30,213 crore through a fresh issue of up to 27 crore shares, at a price band of Rs 1,065 to Rs 1,119 apiece. The offering values the company at around USD 108 billion, according to the offer documents. The IPO will open on October 21 and close on October 23.

title: OYO-parent PRISM to nearly halve IPO fresh issue size to up to Rs 3,350 cr: Sources
content: OYO parent PRISM is planning to nearly halve the size of the fresh issue in its proposed initial public offering (IPO) to up to Rs 3,350 crore from almost Rs 6,650 crore, sources said. People familiar with the matter told PTI the reduction in the issue size follows continued strong cash generation and an improving balance-sheet position, which has lowered the amount of capital the company needs to raise compared with what was originally envisaged. "The original issue was sized before the company's more recent financial performance came through. With cash generation remaining strong and the balance sheet improving, the funding requirement has come down, allowing the company to reduce the amount of primary capital it raises. "The objective is to raise what the business needs while keeping the capital structure efficient. The plan is to repay the residual debt over the next two to three years through cash flows generated by the business," a person familiar with the matter said. Earlier, OYO had planned to raise up to Rs 6,650 crore through an IPO, of which around Rs 5,000 crore was intended for debt repayment. The revised issue size comes with PRISM continuing to focus on reducing its outstanding debt. Under the revised structure, most of the issue proceeds are proposed to be used towards repayment or prepayment, in part or full, of certain borrowings. The revised issue comes as PRISM moves towards the next stage of its proposed IPO following its earlier filing of the uUpdated draft herring prospectus. Moody's Ratings has revised the outlook on PRISM to 'positive' from 'stable', while reaffirming the travel tech unicorn's B2 corporate family rating. Explaining the rationale behind ratings, Moody's said, "We expect OYO's EBITDA (earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation) to grow to around Rs 3,000 crore ($315 million) over the next 12-18 months as the company continues to scale and add new storefronts to its platform. For FY26, OYO's EBITDA more than doubled to Rs 2,630 crore from Rs 1,080 crore in FY25. OYO was founded in 2013 by Ritesh Agarwal, who currently holds a 30.52 per cent stake in the company. SVF India Holdings (Cayman) Ltd, a subsidiary of SoftBank Group Corp is the largest shareholder in the company, with a 40.04% stake.

title: India-New Zealand trade pact kicks in
content: The India-New Zealand Free Trade Agreement (FTA), signed on April 27, came into effect on Tuesday, providing duty-free access to a range of Indian goods, including products from labour-intensive sectors such as textiles and leather. It is the seventh trade pact to come into force in the last five years. The others are agreements with the UAE, Mauritius, the European Free Trade Association (EFTA) bloc, the UK, Oman and Australia. Signed on April 27, 2026, the agreement follows negotiations launched in 2010, stalled in 2015 and revived in March 2025. The pact becomes India's 17th operational FTA. According to experts, the sectors benefiting from the FTA are textiles and apparel, leather and footwear, engineering goods and auto components, gems and jewellery, agriculture and processed foods, pharmaceuticals, and other manufacturing industries. Gulzar Didwania, Partner, Deloitte India, said the deal is expected to support higher FDI inflows into India, but the scale of any increase remains uncertain and will depend on private-sector investment decisions. New Zealand has committed FDI worth USD 20 billion in over 15 years. "The FTA's provisions on duty-free access for certain inputs, bilateral cumulation, customs facilitation, and investment-promotion mechanisms may encourage deeper value-chain integration and improve investment conditions," he said. He added that the pact has significance beyond trade, strengthening India's strategic position in the Indo-Pacific, expanding its network of FTAs with developed economies. At a time of growing global trade uncertainty, the India-New Zealand FTA is a strong endorsement of open markets and predictable trade rules. Its target of doubling bilateral trade by 2030 sets an ambitious agenda for both countries. What makes this FTA particularly valuable is that it goes beyond goods to cover services, investment, skills and mobility, creating fresh opportunities for Indian professionals and businesses. With 100 per cent of Indian exports gaining duty-free access to New Zealand from day one, the agreement gives Indian exporters a significant competitive advantage. MSMEs in textiles, leather, footwear and engineering goods are particularly well placed to benefit. Economic think tank Chintan Research Foundation (CRF India) President Shishir Priyadarshi said that at a time of growing global trade uncertainty, the India-New Zealand FTA is a strong endorsement of open markets and predictable trade rules. "What makes this FTA particularly valuable is that it goes beyond goods to cover services, investment, skills and mobility, creating fresh opportunities for Indian professionals and businesses," he said. Trade expert and Hi-Tech Gears Chairman Deep Kapuria said the FTA operationalisation with New Zealand completes India's preferential market access in all major countries of the Asia-Pacific region. "New Zealand is a very open economy; India has very well crafted this trade deal by securing market access for new services such as Ayush, yoga instructors and student mobility, including post-study work visa," he said. Bilateral trade declined by about 11 per cent to USD 1.15 billion in 2025-26 from USD 1.3 billion in the previous fiscal year. India's exports stood at USD 566.51 million, while imports were USD 589.1 million, resulting in a meagre trade deficit of USD 22.59 million for India. Rani Singh, Indian-origin New Zealander, said the deal is an important step forward for both countries as it is not just about trade; it is about bringing the two countries closer, creating opportunities for businesses and people, and building a stronger relationship for the future. "India now has an opportunity to build its own strong partnership with New Zealand. With duty-free access to New Zealand for all Indian export tariff lines from day one, Indian businesses can become more competitive in this market," she said. Singh added that the benefits are not limited to goods as there is also scope for greater cooperation in education, tourism, technology, professional services and investment. Greater opportunities for eligible skilled professionals and young people can further strengthen these connections, she said.
