title: From implementation to innovation: The next step in your Gemini Enterprise journey
content: How do you move from a basic Gemini Enterprise setup to a live, identity-aware, data-protected AI platform? That is the question at the center of Google Cloud's next webinar, in partnership with YourStory. On October 23, Google Cloud's AI and ML experts return for the second edition of the Gemini Enterprise series, titled ‘Gemini Enterprise: Integrate, secure, and scale your AI strategy’. Where the first series focused on initial setup, this session moves into the technical connectivity that determines whether a Gemini Enterprise deployment actually works inside an organization's existing ecosystem. Attendees will get a practical look at bridging Gemini Enterprise with the tools already in use, while maintaining the security and compliance standards enterprises cannot afford to skip. Whether the challenge is navigating complex compliance requirements or automating workflows across multiple apps, the session is built to provide a clear roadmap for the next stage of the AI journey. What attendees will learn The session will open with a look at Workspace synergy, walking through how different Gemini Enterprise editions integrate with an organization's existing productivity suite to unlock more value from tools already in place. From there, the focus will shift to app connectivity. Attendees will see how to securely link Gmail, Calendar, and Drive, allowing Gemini to reason over internal data and automate workflows that span multiple applications, rather than working in isolation. The webinar will also cover identity and access, including a walkthrough of Workforce Identity Federation using providers like Okta or Microsoft Entra ID, to make identity management seamless across an enterprise's existing infrastructure. Finally, the session aims to address security in depth, covering Safety Filters, AI Defense policies, and Model Armor, the tools organizations need to defend against prompt injection and protect personally identifiable information as AI usage scales. Meet the speakers The session aims to bring together specialists across connectivity, identity, and security. Ria Patel, Platform Customer Engineer for SMB, Scaled, and Specialist accounts at Google Cloud, opens with a walkthrough on connecting Google Calendar to Gemini Enterprise. Janani Pandurangan, also a Platform Customer Engineer for SMB, Scaled, and Specialist accounts, follows with a session on connecting Gemini Enterprise to Gmail. Jared Houston, Security Customer Engineer at Google Cloud, covers connecting Google Drive to Gemini Enterprise. Derian Tungka and Graciella Liander, both Platform Customer Engineers for SMB, Scaled, and Specialist accounts, co-lead a deep dive into third-party identity provider integration, offering step-by-step guidance on Workforce Identity Federation using Okta or Microsoft Entra ID. Methasit (Most) Tuwawit, Platform Customer Engineer for SMB, Scaled, and Specialist accounts, leads a session on securing a Gemini Enterprise application. Eva Gao, Security Customer Engineer at Google Cloud, closes the technical program with a session on Model Armor, covering prompt injection and data leakage prevention through Safety Filters and AI Defense policies. Why this matters For organizations past the initial pilot stage, the risks shift. It is no longer just about getting Gemini Enterprise running, but about making sure it connects securely to the systems that hold sensitive data, respects existing identity infrastructure, and holds up against the kinds of attacks that come with wider AI adoption, such as prompt injection and data leakage. This webinar is built for that stage. Rather than a high-level overview, it offers specific, technical guidance from the engineers who work on these integrations directly, covering the connectivity and security groundwork that determines whether an AI deployment can scale safely across an organization. Register now to secure your spot and learn how to take your Gemini Enterprise deployment from basic setup to a fully integrated, secure, enterprise-ready platform.

title: Sahi’s Dale Vaz wants an AI financial team in every pocket
content: Opening a trading account in India now takes minutes. Knowing what to do once you’re in is much harder. This gap was the focus of Dale Vaz’s keynote at TechSparks 2026. The co-founder and CEO of fintech company Sahi argued that the last decade of fintech solved the issue of access, but not outcomes. “Everybody here has a broking app,” Vaz told the audience. “But when you think about outcomes, do people really feel confident about what to do with their money? The numbers indicate most of us are still struggling.” The intent-capability gap Vaz described a familiar pattern among retail investors. People start investing, then struggle to make sense of their portfolios. A bad day in the market leaves them unsure about whether to buy, sell, or quit altogether. The cause, he said, is complexity: too much jargon, too much data, and too many tools. Investors are left with two poor choices. They can spend years becoming experts, or they can trust someone promising guaranteed returns. Regulator-led investor education has helped, Vaz said, but a wide gap remains between people’s intent to grow their money and their capability to do it. Why generic AI falls short AI is increasingly pitched as the answer. But Vaz cautioned that general-purpose chatbots carry three serious flaws when money is involved. The first is hallucination. “A model is confidently wrong. It will never tell you it’s wrong,” he said. That might be acceptable for an essay, but not for financial decisions. The second is missing context. A chatbot can answer 'should I buy HDFC stock?' without knowing that half your portfolio is already in banking stocks. The third is accountability. If a general chatbot gives you bad guidance, there is no regulatory protection and no one to call. Meet Kyro: A purpose-built assistant Sahi’s answer is Kyro, an agentic AI assistant built into its app and web platform. Vaz called it a “vertical harness” around an AI model. If the model is the engine, the harness is the car. Kyro combines three things: personal context from a user’s activity on Sahi, 28 expert skills written by Sahi’s research team, and more than 100 tools. Those tools give Kyro “hands and legs," he said. Users can set price alerts, create conditional orders, build custom scanners, or describe a trading strategy in plain language and have Kyro turn it into executable code. Crucially, the AI model doesn’t do the calculations. It routes requests to Sahi’s backend APIs, which return deterministic results. “When you say add four plus five, the model calls the calculator that we have built,” Vaz explained. This design keeps numbers out of the model’s hands and reduces the risk of hallucination. A constitution for trust Sahi built Kyro around a set of rules it calls a constitution. Answers must be grounded in facts, and Kyro is designed to say “I don’t know” when it should. The user always presses the final buy or sell button. Every output must come with evidence a person can check. “If AI could just magically make money for everybody, the people making the models would have made all the money,” Vaz said. “AI can help augment our skills as investors, but it can never really replace the individual.” The system is designed to comply with SEBI regulations, with in-country inference, data logging, and full traceability of conversations. Early results Kyro has been tested with more than 11,000 traders in a closed user group. It has generated over 2.7 lakh responses at a 99.2% success rate, and 78% of users returned after their first interaction. Some use cases surprised the team. Many traders treat Kyro as a sounding board for losses and discipline problems. Others talk to it in Gujarati, Tamil, and Marathi. What Kyro won’t do yet Asked whether Kyro acts as an advisor, Vaz was direct: it does not. It has strict rules against buy or sell calls. Advisory features would require a separate SEBI investment advisory licence, which Sahi plans to pursue. Vaz also previewed a Discipline Score. Based on academic research into why retail traders fail, it will flag habits such as overtrading, oversized positions, and revenge trading. Looking further ahead, Vaz sees AI agents running exchange-approved algorithms for retail investors, and a future where every Indian has “a team of AI-enabled agents” watching their risk, portfolio, and taxes in their own language. “We are at the first minute of the first day,” he said.

title: Data, not chips, will decide India’s AI and biotech future, say deeptech founders
content: When people talk about technology infrastructure, they usually mean semiconductors, data centres, and AI models. But the layer that decides how well these technologies work is the data underneath them, and India still has to build it. At a panel discussion on 'The invisible infrastructure of the new tech order' at TechSparks 2026, moderated by Chhavi Mahajan, Chief Content Officer, YourStory, the panellists said India’s advantage will come from owning trusted, context-rich data in fields ranging from language AI to biotech. Arvind Pani, Founder, CoreMantle, an AI data intelligence startup, said data is the one part of the technology stack that cannot be swapped out. “You can continue to replace compute. You can continue to replace the application, but you cannot replace the data,” he said. Ankit Bagaria, Co-founder and CEO, Loopworm, an insect biotechnology company, said the gap is especially wide in biopharma, where too much work still happens through trial and error. Better data, he said, could cut the time it takes to bring a product to market. Bagaria said biotech deserves the same attention as AI, quantum and chips, particularly after the COVID-19 pandemic. He noted that India still imports about 73% of its key materials, including active pharmaceutical ingredients and reagents, from China. And although the country supplies a large share of the world’s vaccines by volume, that accounts for only about 5% of the market by value. “We have operated in the biosimilar space for a very, very long time, where somebody else is discovering the molecules for us,” he said. He argued that India now needs to move into drug discovery. Pani said the same need for local context applies to language. India’s internet was built for English users, which put up two barriers at once for most citizens, who had to learn the technology and a new language. Only about 4 to 5% of India’s population is comfortable using English alone, he noted. He added that even English is not a solved problem for AI. Models trained mostly on American English often struggle with Australian or regional accents, and English as spoken across Indian states varies widely. “These are the nuances that nobody else will understand, that India will understand,” he said. Both panellists agreed that a bigger dataset is not necessarily a better one. Pani said AI models built on smaller amounts of enriched, contextual data outperform those trained on large volumes of raw data. Many Indian language datasets are recorded in studios from scripts, he noted, so models trained on them perform well in controlled settings but fail in real-world conversations. Bagaria said that across biological data, “it’s garbage in, garbage out.” Loopworm spent about 12 to 13 months cleaning existing data while building a digital tool that maps the inner workings of the silkworm. The work had to be tailored to Indian silkworm strains and the pathogens that affect them. Loopworm uses silkworms to produce sustainable animal feed and high-value recombinant proteins. Bagaria said Loopworm chose silkworm because silk is over 98% protein, which makes the insect one of nature’s most efficient converters of plant leaves into protein. The silkworm has been domesticated for about 4,000 years, its genome was sequenced in 2007, and around 175 institutes in India teach sericulture and related biotech. He added that this data-led approach has already cut a set of experiments from 10 months and Rs 25 lakh to two and a half months and about Rs 4.5 lakh. “I am sure that in 10 years’ time, all of us would be saying that the largest impact of AI has come on biotech,” he said. Pani said proprietary data is already becoming a competitive moat. He cited legal AI company Harvey, which has changed both its models and its compute while keeping its domain-specific data as its core advantage. On what needs to change, Pani said India must design technology for its own needs. He recalled that his previous company brought Indian language support to Android in 2011 through a partnership with Qualcomm, before Google did. “If we continue to think that somebody else is going to solve our problem, then we will always be behind the curve,” he said. Bagaria welcomed government initiatives such as the BioE3 policy and the Research, Development and Innovation Fund. But he called for more public and foundational funding for basic data generation, such as the in-depth sequencing and characterisation of Indian organisms, because traditional investors are unlikely to fund fundamental science.

title: Is your marketing AI tool driving profit or just noise? CleverTap co-founder Anand Jain weighs in
content: Most marketing teams today use AI to save time on tasks such as drafting emails, creating image variants, and summarising long documents. However, Anand Jain, Co-founder and Chief Marketing Officer of CleverTap, a customer engagement and marketing automation platform, says basic tools that do these jobs rarely improve company profits. In a masterclass on marketing strategy at TechSparks 2026, Jain urged leaders to look beyond simple shortcuts. “We are going to talk about how you go from using AI for fun and games all the way to using AI to generate actual business results," he said. While creating content using AI makes the job faster and saves time, Jain questioned whether it truly drives growth. "Is it actually going to impact business results or is it just more of the same?” Traditional digital campaigns usually operate on a push model wherein companies decide what they want to sell instead of understanding what consumers want to buy. Whereas, a local shop assistant in an offline channel remembers a customer’s personal taste, notices immediate reactions, and suggests items tailored to their budget and style. Digital marketing must adopt a similar mindset. “Not what I want to sell, (but) what my customer wants to buy. So you flip this around,” Jain said. Instead of broadcasting generic promotions to large groups, modern marketing engines should interpret live customer actions to match individual needs. This approach marks a shift towards the highest level of AI maturity, known as 'real-time decisioning'. Marketing technology generally progresses through three stages. Level 1 focuses on basic time-saving tasks, level 2 covers experimentation such as A-B testing (comparing two ad versions to see which works better), and level 3 achieves true automated decisioning. “You start with productivity, then you do experimentation, and the hardest thing is decisioning. When you actually are building an entire system for a party of one and that one person could be one out of several million that show up on your app or your website,” Jain noted. Instead of bombarding users with discount codes, decisioning offers gentle helpful steps first, such as establishing brand trust or explaining product benefits. Real-time decisioning relies on a single data hub that combines a customer’s historical profile with their immediate live actions. Traditional A-B testing usually stops after selecting one fixed winner, but decisioning uses reinforcement learning, a smart system that learns continuously from user responses and adjusts offers on the fly. Furthermore, instead of relying only on propensity scoring (calculating how likely someone is to buy), decisioning uses uplift modelling. This method identifies the specific nudge, message, or channel needed to encourage an individual user to take their next positive step. As automated systems manage campaign delivery across thousands of message options, the role of the marketer shifts from execution to strategic direction. Rather than manually drafting creative variants, marketers define high-level goals and establish strict operational limits. “Your job is to create budget guardrails, brand guardrails, regulatory guardrails. Do not use the word 'free' if you are offering something, if you are a bank,”Jain emphasised. By establishing clear boundaries, marketing leaders empower smart decisioning engines to work independently, keeping brand messaging safe while driving genuine commercial profit, he added. Edited by Swetha Kannan

title: Angel One, Zerodha expand US stock investing access for Indian investors
content: Angel One and Zerodha are expanding access to the US stock markets for Indian investors, as domestic brokerages look to tap into the growing demand for international equities and portfolio diversification. Angel One has begun rolling out US stock investing on its app, allowing users to invest in US-listed stocks and exchange-traded funds (ETFs) alongside their Indian portfolios. The facility is currently available to a limited group of users, with a wider rollout expected by mid-November. Investors will be able to buy shares of companies such as Apple, Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon, Nvidia, Netflix, Spotify and Toyota. The platform will also support fractional investing, allowing users to purchase a portion of a share rather than an entire unit. Meanwhile, Zerodha has also launched US stock investing in beta, offering access to around 2,000 US-listed stocks and 1,000 ETFs through its platform. The move gives Indian investors another avenue to access global businesses, particularly in sectors such as artificial intelligence, cloud computing, and semiconductors. The expansion follows regulatory approval from the International Financial Services Centres Authority for brokers to offer international investing through GIFT City in Gujarat. Angel One will waive brokerage charges until December 2026. From January 2027, it will charge 0.1% per trade, subject to a minimum brokerage of $0.99. Account opening, maintenance, deposits, and withdrawals will be free, although regulatory charges, GST, and foreign-exchange conversion costs will apply. Zerodha's offering is being introduced in beta, with brokerage and other applicable charges governed by its published pricing structure. Investments through these platforms are subject to the Reserve Bank of India's Liberalised Remittance Scheme and applicable regulatory requirements. Angel One has also said eligible US securities will carry Securities Investor Protection Corporation protection of up to $500,000, subject to applicable conditions. The launches reflect a broader push by Indian investment platforms to expand beyond domestic equities as retail investors seek exposure to global markets. Platforms including Groww, Upstox and INDmoney also offer routes to international investing, intensifying competition in the segment.

title: Beyond the GenAI hype: Amazon's Rajeev Rastogi bets on agentic AI to boost enterprise operations
content: “Clearly the entire operating layer is becoming agentic,” said Rajeev Rastogi, Vice President of Machine Learning at Amazon, pointing to a decisive transformation in business technology. This marks a transition from static software to autonomous systems capable of understanding natural language instructions. Unlike conventional software that follows rigid, pre-programmed scripts, agentic systems possess dynamic execution paths. “Agents prepare plans dynamically to solve a problem... and invoke the appropriate tools,” Rastogi explained during a fireside chat at the 17th edition of YourStory’s flagship tech-startup event, TechSparks. Instead of relying on human intervention at every step, these autonomous agents evaluate queries, formulate a sequence of actions, and call specialised digital tools to complete complex tasks end-to-end. Within Amazon, this operating layer is active in systems like Rufus, a conversational shopping assistant that parses customer requests, applies price filters, invokes search engines, and guides users through product comparisons and checkout journeys. Similarly, autonomous seller assistants pre-fill product listings, monitor inventory levels, and guide small businesses through international export compliance. Beyond the generative AI hype Despite intense market enthusiasm surrounding generative artificial intelligence (Gen AI), Rastogi emphasised that generative models are not a universal cure for every computing challenge. Generative AI excels at complex reasoning, text summarisation, review analysis, and creative tasks such as editing product image backgrounds. However, it struggles with high-volume, low-latency applications. “For certain applications, Gen AI models will never match the performance that you can get from traditional machine learning models,” Rastogi pointed out. Traditional machine learning relies on classical algorithms such as gradient-boosted decision trees or standard neural networks that process structured numerical data with extreme speed. For large-scale operational needs such as ecommerce product search handling tens or hundreds of billions of items, generative models suffer from prohibitive computing costs and slow response times, he said. High-performance architectures therefore use agentic orchestrators to parse human intent while relying on underlying traditional search engines for lightning-fast data retrieval. Where generative capabilities are genuinely required, enterprise leaders do not need to rely exclusively on massive foundation systems. Frontier models, which represent the largest, most computationally heavy artificial intelligence architectures, carry substantial operational overheads. Rastogi highlighted a far more economical alternative, noting, "Fine-tuning some of the open-base models... can give you models that perform a lot better than some of these large models out there... at one-fifth or one-tenth of the cost.” Fine-tuning involves taking a smaller, publicly available open-source model, such as Qwen, and training it on specific proprietary application data. By adopting fine-tuned open models, businesses can achieve equal or superior accuracy for specialised classification or prediction tasks compared to giant closed models like Claude or ChatGPT, while dramatically lowering their computational expenses. Unlocking the white spaces For technology entrepreneurs and enterprise architects, the most compelling opportunities lie in vertical workflow automation rather than attempting to construct foundational models. Developing new frontier models requires unsustainable financial capital and computational infrastructure. Instead, Rastogi advises that "building on top of the frontier models, using agentic AI to automate workflows in domains... that’s definitely promising.” Taking inspiration from coding tools like Cursor, major opportunities exist across specialised domains including law, finance, healthcare, agriculture, and human resources. A particularly valuable white space lies in automating standard operating procedures, which are natural language documents detailing step-by-step instructions for human workers to resolve complex operational issues. An agentic automation platform can clarify poorly written instructions using internal knowledge bases, break down long procedures into manageable sub-tasks, and delegate them to networks of specialised sub-agents that automatically browse internal tools, extract document data, analyse images, and resolve issues. Looking ahead, the underlying design of AI models must evolve to remain sustainable. Current frontier models face severe physical and financial constraints. “The frontier models today are massive, computationally super expensive, consume a lot of energy and resources... and I don’t think that’s sustainable,” Rastogi noted. Furthermore, today’s monolithic models function primarily as statistical next-token prediction engines, guessing the most likely next word in a sequence without a genuine understanding of physical laws, 3D spatial geometry, or cause and effect. According to Rastogi, to overcome these boundaries, the future landscape will transition toward networks of smaller, domain-specific models directed by central routing orchestrators. Rather than storing vast amounts of world knowledge inside giant model parameters, future AI architectures will separate core reasoning capabilities from data storage, relying on external, high-speed search engines for information retrieval. Eventually, the industry will advance towards genuine world models that possess an internal understanding of physical spaces and environmental behaviour, establishing a practical, cost-effective framework for enterprise automation.

title: How Operation Sindoor reshaped India's private defence tech industry
content: Following Operation Sindoor, India's private defence technology sector is seeing a shift in how the armed forces engage with domestic manufacturers. The transformation is marked by faster procurement, greater private-sector participation, and renewed emphasis on developing critical military technologies domestically, according to industry executives. At TechSparks 2026, Ankit Kumar, Co-founder and Chief Business Officer of Tonbo Imaging; Priyanka Singhal, Founder and CEO of Ammunic Systems; and Radhika P, Co-founder of Pinaka Aerospace; discussed how Indian private companies contributed to recent military operations and what the country must prioritise to prepare for the battlefield of 2035. In a panel discussion titled 'War Room 2035: What technologies must India build for the battlefield' moderated by Adith Charlie, Managing Editor of YourStory and The CapTable, the founders pointed to growing opportunities for indigenous companies in night-vision systems, electronic warfare, smart munitions, and autonomous defence platforms. Operation Sindoor and the private sector's growing role Priyanka Singhal, Founder and CEO of Ammunic Systems, a defence R&D firm specialising in electronic fuzes and munition technologies, described Operation Sindoor as a turning point for the industry. “The operation was an eye opener,” she said, adding that it had exposed the limitations of traditional defence procurement cycles. Singhal said Ammunic supplied loitering munitions and gravity-drop bombs during Operation Sindoor, working with drone platform partners to integrate its weapons into systems used in the operation. According to her, the armed forces have begun moving away from an excessive focus on procedural compliance towards deploying equipment that meets immediate battlefield requirements. Initiatives such as iDEX and emergency procurement mechanisms have helped accelerate the process, she said. Radhika P of Pinaka Aerospace echoed this assessment. Previously, private defence companies often worked through defence public sector undertakings (DPSUs), the Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO), and other established channels. Following Operation Sindoor, she said, the armed forces had increasingly engaged directly with private companies, particularly in electronic warfare, avionics, and sensor technologies. Radhika said Pinaka had contributed to the indigenisation of missile systems that were deployed during the operation. She argued that the effectiveness of military equipment increasingly depends on its payloads, including sensors and electronic warfare systems, rather than the platform alone. “If there is an electronic countermeasure system, it can neutralise a platform which is probably 10 times more expensive,” she said, underscoring the strategic importance of developing indigenous payload technologies. Kumar of Tonbo Imaging, which specialises in electro-optical and infrared technologies, said the shift towards indigenous defence procurement had begun even before Operation Sindoor, particularly following developments along India's eastern border. That had encouraged the armed forces to reduce their dependence on technologies sourced from countries sharing land borders with India. Tonbo, which has spent nearly two decades developing indigenous imaging systems, was positioned to benefit from that shift, Kumar said. Its night-vision technologies have been deployed across several Indian military operations, including Operation Sindoor, when air-defence systems used the company's capabilities, he added. Kumar said close engagement with the armed forces, including product trials and feedback from users, had helped Tonbo develop its technologies. “We've learned things the hard way. We've learned things on the ground. We've learned things with the customers,” he said. What India must build by 2035 Looking towards 2035, Kumar said defence systems would increasingly move towards autonomy, reducing the need for direct human involvement in certain operations. He pointed to the potential use of autonomous systems in air combat and on the ground, including the possibility of humanoid robots supporting border operations. As military platforms become more autonomous, sensors and intelligence will become critical to their ability to detect threats, interpret their surroundings and respond without constant human intervention. “For autonomy, sensors, intelligence, both are very critical, very important,” Kumar said. He argued that India had strengths in both areas, particularly in developing intelligence capabilities that can operate directly on military platforms. Such technologies, he said, could improve operational efficiency and reduce dependence on human operators, but they needed to be developed as sovereign capabilities rather than sourced from overseas suppliers. “Intelligence, connectivity, sensing, these will be the mainstay of how the wars will be fought tomorrow,” he said. For Radhika, a key battlefield priority is control over the electromagnetic spectrum, which underpins radar, communications, electronic warfare, and several other military capabilities. She argued that future military advantage would increasingly depend on how effectively forces detect, interpret and disrupt electromagnetic signals. That also makes ownership of the underlying technology critical. Developing or assembling defence platforms in India is not sufficient if the software, electronics architecture and intellectual property remain controlled by foreign suppliers. “It is very important to have good control on the source code, the board design, and things like that,” Radhika said. She also emphasised that technology transfer should strengthen India's ability to develop and integrate systems independently, rather than create continued dependence on overseas suppliers. Control over intellectual property and systems integration would be especially important in reducing the risks associated with foreign supply chains, she added. Closing the gaps in research and deployment Singhal, meanwhile, called for greater integration across the three armed services. She argued that the Army, Navy and Air Force needed better-connected platforms and weapons systems to coordinate effectively during emergencies. She also highlighted materials research as an area requiring greater attention. Advanced materials would play an increasingly important role in developing next-generation weapon systems, including those requiring greater effectiveness and stealth capabilities. India, she said, needed to place more emphasis on materials R&D alongside investments in autonomous systems and other defence technologies. The founders also identified persistent challenges in bringing together the armed forces, government research institutions and private industry. Singhal said startups and smaller defence companies could move faster than government research programmes, which often face bureaucratic delays. Radhika said the challenge stemmed partly from differing expectations. The armed forces want sophisticated systems delivered quickly, research organisations operate through lengthy validation cycles and private manufacturers need commercially viable development timelines. One way forward, she suggested, was to involve private industry from the prototype stage, with the armed forces funding development projects, research organisations working alongside manufacturers and clearer pathways to production orders. She pointed to the Development-cum-Production Partner model as a mechanism that could help bridge the gap between research, development and large-scale manufacturing if implemented effectively. For India's private defence technology industry, the next challenge is not simply to manufacture more equipment domestically. It is to develop and control the technologies that make military platforms effective, while building a procurement and research ecosystem capable of moving those technologies from the laboratory to the battlefield.

title: Startup news and updates: daily roundup (October 19, 2026)
content: From India’s artificial intelligence (AI) opportunity to how a Bengaluru hospital is paying doctors for recovery, not procedures, here are the latest developments across sectors. Featured Stories India's next tech edge according to CTOs India’s technology industry has long relied on talent, cost efficiency and scale. But as artificial intelligence makes advanced tools more accessible, these advantages alone may no longer be enough to differentiate companies. The next edge, according to technology leaders at TechSparks 2026, will come from how effectively companies use AI to solve specific problems, understand customers and build products that are difficult to replicate. Read more Funding News Even Healthcare raises $50M in Series B round Bengaluru-based managed care company Even Healthcare has raised $50 million in a Series B round led by existing investor Khosla Ventures. Alpha Wave also participated in the round. According to the company, the round values it at three times its valuation 18 months ago and brings its total funding to more than $120 million. The money will go towards five new Even hospitals in Bengaluru over the next six months, beginning with Indiranagar. The company runs two hospitals in the city at present. Read more The Pant Project bags Rs 109 Cr to accelerate retail expansion The Pant Project, a premium menswear label specialising in trousers and other bottomwear, has raised Rs 109 crore in a Series B funding round led by Mirae Asset Venture Investments. Existing investor Sorin Investments also participated, alongside family offices and angel investors including Anisha Saraf, B&K Securities, MGA Ventures and B2V Ventures. The company has also secured venture debt from Alteria Capital, with IndigoEdge advising on the equity transaction. Founded by brothers Dhruv and Udit Toshniwal, The Pant Project began as a digital-first business focused on fit, fabric performance and comfort for Indian men. Its products include Malai Pants and Inklock No Fade Black Jeans, and it sells through its website, Myntra, Amazon and physical stores. Read more Other News AngelBot AI launches TeamSync to secure enterprise knowledge with AI-powered search AngelBot AI has launched TeamSync, an AI-native platform designed to help enterprises securely search, manage and extract insights from fragmented documents and information repositories. The platform combines natural-language document interaction, semantic search and permissions-aware AI, with citations and audit trails to support reliable information access. Its capabilities also include metadata extraction, electronic signatures, contract lifecycle management and eDiscovery. Targeting mid-sized and large enterprises across regulated and document-intensive sectors, TeamSync offers subscription-based software, platform licensing and implementation services. The launch builds on AngelBot AI’s document management work, including IMIR, which has received recognition from the Indian Air Force. VETO launches sports carnival, offers 300+ hours of subscription-free live sports VETO, India’s subscription-free OTT platform, has launched the VETO Sports Carnival, offering more than 300 hours of live sports streaming across cricket, football, weightlifting and tennis during October and November. The line-up includes an international ODI tri-series, Test matches, the IWF World Senior Championships, SAFF Championship, Billie Jean King Cup Play-offs and Davis Cup Finals. The initiative expands VETO’s live sports portfolio as it seeks to make international sporting events accessible to Indian audiences without a subscription fee. The platform also offers 60+ live TV channels across 12 languages and more than 10 content genres. Yes Madam revenue hits Rs 402 Cr annualised run rate, grows 3.9x in two years At-home beauty and wellness platform Yes Madam has reported a 3.9-fold increase in revenue and 3.5-fold growth in Net Transaction Value (NTV) between Q2 FY25 and Q2 FY27. The company’s annualised revenue run rate reached Rs 402 crore, while its NTV run rate stood at Rs 836 crore. In Q2 FY27, revenue rose 69% year-on-year to Rs 79.4 crore, while NTV grew 75% to Rs 165.8 crore. Founded in 2016, Yes Madam operates across more than 55 cities with a network of 10,000-plus service professionals. The company plans to expand services, strengthen its network and invest in technology. So/Facet raises Rs 10 Cr seed funding led by Sauce to build lab-grown diamond jewellery brand So/Facet, a premium lab-grown diamond jewellery brand founded by former Unilever executives Aarushi Agrawal Naulakha and Abhishek Naulakha, has raised Rs10 crore in a seed funding round led by Sauce. The company will use the capital for brand building, design, technology, hiring and an omnichannel retail expansion. Set to launch online in November 2026, So/Facet plans to open more than 30 premium stores over three years. The brand aims to position lab-grown diamonds as expressions of personal style rather than jewellery reserved for traditional milestones. Its six launch collections feature IGI-certified diamonds and contemporary, in-house designs. Guttify targets Tier II markets in three states, eyes 5x growth in annual recurring revenue Gut-health startup Guttify plans to expand into select Tier II markets across Uttar Pradesh, Rajasthan and Punjab through pilot initiatives in FY27, targeting fivefold growth in annual recurring revenue (ARR). The company has served over 30,000 consumers and reported 67% quarter-on-quarter growth. Its Rs 399 DIY Gut Scan Kit sold approximately 15,000 units between January and August 2026, with around half of buyers subsequently purchasing other products. Guttify plans to expand its portfolio with products including Poopie, a fibre-based constipation-support product, and RISE, a morning greens blend, while strengthening personalised recommendations, consumer education and expert guidance. As You Asked raises Rs 45 lakh pre-seed funding to expand children’s nutrition products As You Asked, a nutrition startup focused on children aged 2–12, has raised Rs 45 lakh in an equity-funded pre-seed round backed by ISB D-Labs and angel investors. The company will use the funds to support its market launch, product development, manufacturing and distribution. Its planned portfolio includes daily nutrition powders, hydration mixes and micronutrient gummies without added sugars. The startup has engaged more than 100 parents, conducted over 200 child taste tests and run an early pilot involving 200-plus customers to inform its product development. It aims to make everyday nutrition simpler, accessible and easier for families to incorporate into daily routines. (The copy will be updated through the day)

title: Data is not a moat: What India’s CTOs say will define the next tech edge
content: India’s technology industry has long relied on talent, cost efficiency and scale. But as artificial intelligence makes advanced tools more accessible, these advantages alone may no longer be enough to differentiate companies. The next edge, according to technology leaders at TechSparks 2026, will come from how effectively companies use AI to solve specific problems, understand customers and build products that are difficult to replicate. During a panel titled The New CTO Playbook: India’s Next Tech Advantage , Nitin Jain, CTO of ShareChat and Moj; Ajit Narayanan, CTO of Angel One; Srividhya Srinivasan, CTO of Amagi; and Ankit Maheshwari, founder and CTO of Innovaccer, discussed how Indian technology companies can remain competitive in an AI-driven market, at the 17th edition of YourStory’s flagship tech-startup event, TechSparks. India’s complexity is an advantage For ShareChat and Moj, India’s linguistic and cultural diversity offers an opportunity to build products for varied audiences. Nitin Jain said companies must account for differences in languages, devices, network quality and user preferences. ShareChat, which Jain said has around 200 million monthly active users, uses audience behaviour to improve content recommendations and identify emerging preferences. He said the challenge is to deliver experiences comparable with global platforms while operating within India’s cost constraints. Building flexible technology that accommodates diverse users, he added, can help companies expand faster. Data alone is not enough In healthcare, Innovaccer’s Ankit Maheshwari said proprietary data is valuable but does not automatically create a competitive moat. Healthcare information is often fragmented across medical records, billing systems and medication databases. Connecting these sources is only the first step; the real challenge is using the information to determine what action should follow. “Data in itself, or having proprietary data, is not a moat,” Maheshwari said. He argued that companies need a context and intelligence layer that understands industry workflows, exceptions and operational requirements. In healthcare, this means moving beyond general-purpose AI to solutions that can work reliably across hospitals, providers and complex processes. Trust must be built into AI For Angel One’s Ajit Narayanan, trust can be a differentiator in financial services, where technology failures can have direct financial consequences. He cited the example of a trading order for which a customer receives no acknowledgement. Without knowing whether the order was processed, retrying could result in duplicate positions and potential losses. Narayanan said trust must be embedded in system design through accurate information, safeguards and accountability, rather than treated merely as a brand promise. He also outlined three considerations for AI automation: the cost of an incorrect decision, whether it can be reversed, and whether it can be audited. Human oversight, he argued, should focus on meaningful safeguards rather than simply assigning responsibility when systems fail. Building in India, scaling globally Amagi’s Srividhya Srinivasan said India’s complex media environment has helped the company develop products for global markets. Multiple languages, subtitles, audience demographics and advertising formats expose technology providers to challenges that also arise in international media operations. Srinivasan said Amagi developed solutions for India before taking some of them global. Emerging AI applications, including real-time dubbing, subtitling and short-form content creation, offer further opportunities. However, she said expansion should depend on market readiness rather than a fixed India-first strategy. Companies must identify where customers are prepared to adopt a product and where it solves an immediate need. The advantage lies in execution Jain said AI is helping ShareChat accelerate content production and improve recommendations by analysing how users engage with videos and other formats. The platform can use these signals to test content ideas, understand audience preferences and refine recommendations. The ability to feed user responses back into AI systems quickly creates a continuous improvement cycle. The broader message from the panel was that access to AI alone will not guarantee a lasting advantage. Companies must combine technology with specialised knowledge, customer understanding, reliable systems and the ability to execute at scale. For India’s technology industry, talent, cost and scale remain important foundations. But the next competitive edge will depend on how effectively companies turn those strengths into products that solve complex problems and deliver measurable value."

title: FMCG firms grapple with input cost inflation in Q2, brace for margin pressure
content: FMCG companies face sustained margin pressure in the second half of the current fiscal year, as rising input costs squeeze profitability, with firms weighing post-Diwali price hikes against the risk of hurting consumer demand, particularly in price-sensitive mass-market and rural categories. Input-cost pressures intensified in the September quarter, reversing some of the moderation seen in the preceding quarter, which squeezed margins even as companies absorbed part of it to protect consumer demand during the festive season. The increase has been uneven across commodities, with crude-linked derivatives, packaging materials, palm oil and sugar emerging as key pressure points, said Naveen Malpani, Partner and Consumer Industry Leader at Grant Thornton Bharat. "In rupee terms, palm oil prices were approximately 21% higher year-on-year in September, while sugar prices remained around 18% higher year-on-year despite correcting 8% month-on-month," he said. Higher costs have not been fully offset by price increases and operational efficiencies, putting pressure on operating margins, Malpani said. "Pre-results analyst estimates projected operating-margin compression of approximately 45 basis points year-on-year across a group of major consumer staples companies, with some estimates indicating declines of up to 150 basis points for the companies covered," he said. Companies operating in mass-market categories had limited room for aggressive price increases due to affordability concerns, making cost optimisation, procurement efficiencies and calibrated pricing crucial to protecting profitability without hurting demand. "The sector should therefore prepare for continued margin pressure through H2, with recovery contingent on actual commodity movements rather than an assumption that the cost cycle has peaked," Malpani added. Parle Products Chief Marketing Officer Mayank Shah told PTI that rising inflation was a major concern for the FMCG industry, which is "definitely worrisome". However, he also said companies were trying to absorb a bit of "margin shock" by offsetting higher input costs through efficiency improvements and cost cuts rather than immediately raising prices. Shah said demand remained robust across urban and rural India as companies refrained from passing on the entire increase in costs to consumers. However, he indicated that price increases could be considered after the festive season, depending on the movement of agricultural commodity prices and the broader geopolitical situation. “Most decisions on price hikes would be taken only post festive season… So, you may see some sort of thing happening from December onwards,” Shah said. Companies are also looking at reducing discounts and advertising expenditure to manage costs, Shah said, adding that protecting demand remained a priority. Nestle India Chairman and Managing Director Manish Tiwary also acknowledged the issues last week and said "rising inflation, particularly food inflation" is a "reality". In its commodity outlook, Nestle India said coffee and wheat prices were expected to remain range-bound, while sugar and edible oils would stabilise at elevated levels in the December quarter. Cocoa remained volatile because of weather-related crop concerns in key producing regions, while milk prices had strengthened seasonally but were expected to ease with the arrival of flush supplies, it said. Moreover, this inflationary environment poses a challenge for FMCG companies in the second half of FY27, when festive-season demand gives way to the need to sustain consumption momentum and restore profitability. "Outlook for H2 FY27 remains cautious," said Malpani, adding, " Companies may continue to face cost pressures, with any meaningful margin recovery dependent on commodity prices easing and earlier pricing actions flowing through. The risk is particularly relevant for packaged foods, home and personal care products and other categories exposed to edible oils, crude derivatives and agricultural commodities. The potential strengthening of El Niño conditions during October-December also adds uncertainty to the outlook for agricultural production and food prices. Its impact on Indian agriculture, however, will depend on broader ocean-atmosphere conditions and regional weather patterns, and higher food inflation is a risk rather than a certainty. The impact on consumer demand will be another key factor to watch. While price increases can support value growth, they may not translate into higher underlying volumes if consumers cut purchases, shift to cheaper brands or opt for smaller packs. “If food inflation rises or rural incomes weaken, consumers may trade down to lower-priced brands, choose smaller packs, reduce purchase frequency or defer discretionary purchases. The uneven monsoon and potential El Niño impact add uncertainty to rural purchasing power,” he said.

title: Cabinet approves Go-Delhi Foundation to help young innovators, startups
content: The Delhi government has approved setting up Go-Delhi Foundation with a corpus of Rs 50 crore to empower young innovators and startups, said a CMO statement on Sunday. The approval was given in a recent Cabinet meeting chaired by Chief Minister Rekha Gupta, sanctioning the fund to help turn ideas into products and take them to market. Delhi is home to nearly 21,000 startups recognised by the Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade (DPIIT). The foundation aims to promote startups, innovation and entrepreneurship in the capital while providing young people, researchers and entrepreneurs with integrated support to turn their ideas into practical products and successful enterprises. The government has also committed an initial budget outlay of Rs 50 crore for the foundation. Through the Go-Delhi Foundation, these resources will be brought together on a common platform, with a focus on developing new enterprises, attracting investment and creating employment opportunities, said the Delhi CMO statement. Gupta said the foundation would help startups and micro, small and medium enterprises (MSMEs) access product engineering, prototyping, laboratories and testing facilities. It would also provide technical guidance, mentorship, incubation, business support and opportunities to connect with investors, helping turn early-stage ideas into market-ready products. The initiative would support entrepreneurs at different stages, from product development and testing to certification preparation and market access. Its aim is to reduce dependence on scattered facilities for different needs and make it easier to set up and grow enterprises in Delhi, she added. The government departments would be able to bring their real-world challenges to Delhi's innovators through the foundation, Gupta said and added that the products and technologies developed to address these challenges could be tested through pilot projects, with successful solutions taken forward for adoption. This would give government departments an opportunity to access new technologies and practical solutions, while allowing startups to demonstrate the usefulness of their products, she added. The foundation will also work with industry, educational institutions, investors and other partners. It will adopt a hub-and-spoke model, delivering programmes through existing facilities and partner institutions across Delhi, the statement said. The foundation will be established as a not-for-profit company under Section 8 of the Companies Act, 2013, and will function under the Delhi government's Department of Industries, it added.

title: Health, inclusion, computing: Test your business creativity with Edition 254 of our weekly quiz!
content: Lateral Sparks, the weekly quiz from YourStory, tests your domain knowledge, business acumen, and lateral thinking skills (see the previous edition here ). title: How art platforms, exhibitions and awards strengthen the creative economy
content: Launched in 2014, PhotoSparks is a weekly feature from YourStory, with photographs that celebrate the spirit of creativity and innovation. In the earlier 1,020 posts, we featured an art festival , cartoon gallery . world music festival , telecom expo , millets fair , climate change expo , wildlife conference , startup festival , Diwali rangoli , and jazz festival . Lalit Kala Akademi (LKA) in New Delhi recently hosted its 65th National Exhibition of Art. It showcased over 270 artworks from around the country, selected by a jury from 6,175 submissions. Twenty artists were also conferred with the Lalit Kala Akademi Awards. The artists include Pooja Rajpoot, Praveen Kumar, Pritam Madhukar Deuskar, Rajendra Prasad, Ramesh Vithal Thorat, Raviram Ramakrishnan, and Sanjay Kumar. Also Read Year in Review: The great Indian consumer reset powered by protein, pickleball and micro-dramas Such exhibitions and awards help transform artistic talent into livelihoods, creative businesses, tourism, and international recognition. By connecting artists with audiences, buyers, institutions, and markets, they strengthen the creative economy while preserving a country’s cultural identity. Exhibitions provide artists with platforms to showcase, promote and sell their work. They connect creators with the broader ecosystem of collectors, galleries, curators, cultural institutions and potential investors, thus creating opportunities for income generation and professional growth. In the case of national exhibitions in India, opportunities are also created to showcase traditional crafts, indigenous knowledge, and contemporary artistic practices. Cultural assets thus go beyond elements of nostalgia into sources of sustainable economic value. Also Read Year in Review: Top 10 celebrity-backed ventures of 2025 Art competitions in turn encourage excellence, experimentation and creative risk-taking. When conducted annually, they identify emerging talent, provide visibility to underrepresented artists, and create pathways to grants and residencies, as shown in LKA's activities and centres across India. Art exhibitions delight and inspire art lovers while also spurring artists to develop new techniques, materials and ideas. At a broader level, this strengthens a country’s creative skills base and encourage innovation across design, fashion, architecture, digital media, and other creative industries. Awards conferred by national institutions like LKA provide credibility and elevate the profiles of artists and creative enterprises. National awards also help establish benchmarks of excellence, celebrate cultural achievement, and build a distinctive national creative identity. Also Read Breaking barriers in 2025: Women’s progress at work and what the road ahead demands As shown in this photo essay, the diverse artworks featured help emerging artists realise what is possible with current practices. It also opens the door to explore how other media can extend creative frontiers, such as digital technologies. Together, exhibitions, competitions and awards contribute to the creative economy of India. Regional creators can connect to national and international buyers, galleries, cultural institutions, and digital marketplaces. Traditional art forms and indigenous knowledge can be sustained while encouraging new creative expressions. The LKA annual exhibition encourages cultural institutions and private-sector partners to invest in accessible venues, professional development, and fair artist remuneration. Also Read How IIT Madras Incubation Cell is powering India’s next-gen deeptech startups Particular attention should be given to emerging artists, regional creative communities, women, youth, and indigenous practitioners. Success should be measured not only by attendance or media coverage, but also by artist earnings, tourism spending, repeat market opportunities, and international partnerships. In sum, sustained investment and effective partnerships via platforms like LKA can ensure that India’s artistic and cultural wealth generates lasting social, cultural and economic value. Now what have you done today to pause in your busy schedule and harness your creative side for a better world? (All photographs taken by Madanmohan Rao on location at Lalit Kala Akademi.)

title: Vance defends 'indentured servants' remark on H-1B workers, admits 'rhetoric' has been 'imperfect'
content: US Vice President J D Vance has admitted that his rhetoric has been "imperfect" when he referred to foreign professionals holding H-1 B visas as "indentured servants". He also clarified that he meant US companies and the visa system, not H-1B visa holders. India had objected strongly to the language used to describe foreign professionals calling the terminology "deeply offensive" and saying it carries painful historical and colonial legacy connotations. Speaking at the CBS News Townhall event, Vance insisted his criticism targeted the visa system that gives employers too much power over foreign employees, who can be sent back to their country of origin and effectively treated as "indentured servants". "I would say, and to the extent that my rhetoric has been imperfect here, that's on me," Vance said in response to a question from an Indian immigrant, who became a US citizen five years ago and voted for President Donald Trump. The Vice President said his comments were "not a criticism of the H-1B holder". "...Is when they come in on an H-1B, they're very often coming in, and the company is certifying that they're doing a job that they can't find an alternative American labour applicant for. And importantly, their visa is their only lifeline to the United States of America. So when I say an indentured servant, that's not a criticism of the H-1B visa holder. That's a criticism of a company that brings a person in," Vance said. "It's a criticism of the visa system that allows people to be treated effectively as indentured servants that can be shipped back to their country of origin." He also mentioned his South Indian in-laws, while calling for a balance between welcoming foreign professionals and protecting American workers. "You know where my family comes from, and I love my mother-in-law and father-in-law who immigrated from South India, and obviously their daughter, born in the United States of America, is now the second lady, and I’m very proud of her, and I love her very much." His wife, Usha Vance, is the daughter of Indian immigrants. "I will tell you that nobody's perfect, certainly not me. But my goal here is not to dehumanise any immigrant, and in fact, I love a number of immigrants,” Vance said. Earlier this month, the US suspended several firms, including Indian IT companies, from a programme that lets foreign workers apply for green cards, arguing that the practice has shut Americans out of the job market. Vice President Vance made the announcement. Indian professionals account for over 70% of all approved H-1B petitions annually. Vance referred to foreign workers hired on H1-B visas as "foreign indentured servants” and the companies using the programme as "visa mills”.

title: Cancellation: A creator’s biggest turning point; Scaling India’s research multiplier
content: Dear Reader, Food safety has come under intense scrutiny in recent times. The ​Food Safety and Standards Authority of India has now proposed a ban on adding sucrose and fructose to food products for infants up to the age of six ​months. The measure aims to reduce infants’ exposure to added sugars and tackle health risks linked to childhood obesity. In other related news, Maharashtra’s Food and Drug Administration has named officials of Reliance Group entities and Eternal’s Blinkit and Hyperpure units, including Blinkit CEO Albinder Dhindsa, in a probe over expired food ​products. The products have allegedly re-entered the food supply chain, according to case documents reviewed by Reuters . Meanwhile, amid rising concerns of AI safety, Anthropic has pitched its own safety bill to Capitol Hill lawmakers. According to the proposal , the government could block release or deter deployment of an AI model if it poses an imminent risk of causing more than $1 billion in damages or killing or seriously injuring more than 50 people, Politico reported, citing three people. Moving on, French carmaker Renault is betting big on hybrid and CNG technology in India. Renault India CEO Stephane Deblaise believes both technologies could account for almost half of the automaker’s powertrain sales mix over the next 2-3 years. On Saturday, the automaker launched its first strong hybrid offering on the Duster SUV; it plans to launch factory-fitted CNG models in the future. In today’s newsletter, we will talk about Cancellation: A creator’s biggest turning point Scaling India’s research multiplier Here’s your trivia for today: In which country was the world’s first ATM installed? (Scroll down for the answer) Content creation Cancellation: A creator’s biggest turning point At TechSparks 2026, Varun Mayya, Founder and CEO of AEOS, a content and media-tech company, spoke about how online backlash can free creators to speak their minds, why founders need to get comfortable with reinvention, and why there is no secret formula for going viral. Finding an audience takes more than posting regularly on social media. It requires years of experimentation, a willingness to stand apart, and the ability to adapt as technology and audience expectations change, according to the content creator and entrepreneur. Key takeaways: For Mayya, brand building comes down to two things. The first is simply having the courage to put yourself out there. The second is differentiation. When young founders stand out, they can even raise funding at a time when they have few other markers of success. Speaking on cancellation and criticism, Mayya said, “Once you've been cancelled, then you can say whatever you want. And I think that has been really valuable. As long as you understand that not everyone’s going to be on your side, then you’re okay.” When it comes to viral content, Mayya doesn’t believe there’s a secret formula to crack. He argued that recommendation algorithms largely reflect what people want to watch. Creators need to understand and mirror what their audience cares about. R&D Scaling India’s research multiplier India cannot afford to replicate the 75-year evolutionary timelines of Western institutions like the US National Science Foundation or DARPA, according to Shivkumar Kalyanaraman, Chief Executive Officer of the Anusandhan National Research Foundation. To boost India’s R&D spend toward 3% of GDP, Kalyanaraman reveals a patient-capital architecture combining private investment, open IP licensing, and national mission programmes. Key takeaways Speaking at TechSparks 2026, YourStory’s annual summit, Kalyanaraman outlined how the nation is altering its approach to scientific research and technology commercialisation. Formalised by Parliament in 2023 following recommendations in the National Education Policy 2020, the Anusandhan National Research Foundation operates as an autonomous statutory body presided over by the Prime Minister of India. The organisation, he said, must bypass traditional bureaucratic friction and drive scientific discovery into the real economy at unprecedented speed. At the centre of transformation is the Research, Development, and Innovation fund, a government-backed pool of Rs 1 lakh crore. Designed as a patient capital instrument, the fund provides long-term financial support tailored to research-intensive and deeptech enterprises that require extended gestation periods without demanding immediate short-term returns. title: ixigo Q2 profit at Rs 63 Cr on robust show in hotel booking biz
content: ixigo (Le Travenues Technology Limited) has reported a consolidated net profit of Rs 63.42 crore for the September quarter, aided by the partial sale of stake in Freshbus, an intercity electric bus operator and smart mobility startup, and strong growth in the hotel bookings segment. The travel and ticket booking platform had posted a net loss of Rs 3.46 crore in the corresponding July-September period of the last financial year, as per a regulatory filing. Hotels emerged as ixigo's fastest-growing business line by gross transaction value (GTV), reaching Rs 111.34 crore, up 159 per cent YoY, ixigo stated. This is the first time ixigo has reported hotels as a separate line of business. During the second quarter of 2026-27, ixigo's revenue from operations increased to Rs 320.96 crore from Rs 284.23 crore a year ago. Total expenses were higher at Rs 309.51 crore as against Rs 291.89 crore. "In Q2 FY27, we delivered resilient growth with quarterly gross transaction value (GTV) of Rs 5,304 crore, up 22 per cent YoY, and revenue from operations of Rs 321 crore, up 13 per cent YoY. Our PAT (profit after tax) was an all-time high aided by our partial sale of stake in Freshbus," ixigo Group CEO Aloke Bajpai, Group Co-CEO Rajnish Kumar, and Group CFO Saurabh Devendra Singh said in a joint statement. "We continue to invest in Hotels and AI as key drivers of our long-term growth," they further stated.

title: Magicbricks appoints Mayank Jain as CEO
content: Real estate classifieds Magicbricks has appointed Mayank Jain as chief executive officer (CEO), effective October 1. In a statement on Friday, Magicbricks, one of the leading property platforms, said Jain has joined from CarDekho, where he served for over five years as CEO of Auto Classifieds. Jain has more than two decades of experience across digital, media, technology and consumer businesses. "At Magicbricks, Mayank will focus on accelerating the company’s next phase of growth by leveraging its digital capabilities, advancing technology-led innovation and strengthening its consumer-centric approach," the company said. His priorities would include driving business transformation, improving operational and financial performance, and further reinforcing Magicbricks’ position in India’s evolving real estate ecosystem, it added. Jain holds an MBA from INSEAD, a PGDM from Management Development Institute (MDI), Gurgaon, and a degree in Computer Engineering. He will be based at Magicbricks’ Noida office and will report to N Subramanian, Executive Director and Group CEO of The Times Group. Magicbricks said it has monthly traffic exceeding 2 crores and an active base of over 15 lakh property listings. The company has become a full-stack service provider for all real estate needs, with services including home loans, interiors, and expert advice.

title: India’s AI opportunity could run into trillions of dollars, creating new possibilities for startups
content: India’s artificial intelligence (AI) opportunity could extend well beyond the $100 billion discussed by industry leaders, with the technology potentially adding $1 trillion to the country’s GDP by 2035. For startups, the opportunity lies in using AI to address large, underserved markets and building businesses that can scale across India and beyond. At a fireside chat with Shradha Sharma, founder & CEO, YourStory and The Bharat Project at Techsparks 2026 on the topic - India’s $100 Billion AI Opportunity, Ashutosh Sharma, Head of Investments and M&A, India, Prosus, and Keshav Reddy, Founder and CEO of Equal AI, highlighted how the technology could transform businesses, improve productivity and create new categories of consumer and enterprise companies. Ashutosh Sharma said previous technology waves, particularly the internet and smartphones, created large businesses by democratising access to products and services. AI could take this transformation further by democratising access to intelligence. “We are taking one more step. We are democratising something else, something new, and something much more powerful, and that’s intelligence. Everyone, after the proliferation of AI, will be more intelligent, more productive than before,” he said. He added that the internet and smartphone revolutions had already generated businesses worth billions of dollars by helping consumers meet previously unmet needs. “There is no doubt in my mind. With something that is more powerful, the outcomes will only be larger. $100 billion, trillion? I don’t know,” he said, pointing to the potentially enormous scale of the AI opportunity. For Indian startups, Ashutosh Sharma believes the opportunity exists across virtually every sector. India has a large consumer market, a substantial talent pool and access to venture capital and private equity funding. More importantly, the country has numerous problems that could be addressed using AI. He identified the shortage of quality education as one example of an area where AI-powered products could bridge the gap between demand and supply. Healthcare and other essential services offer similar opportunities for entrepreneurs to develop scalable solutions. Reddy said India’s large-scale adoption of AI presents an opportunity for domestic companies to capture more of the value generated by the technology. “We are the largest consuming AI country in the world, and it is only going to get more and more and more, and we need to make sure that that value is captured by Indian companies, by Indian consumers,” he said. Reddy cited Equal AI’s experience as an example of how addressing a specific consumer problem can create opportunities for rapid growth. The company developed an AI-native call assistant in response to the prevalence of spam calls in India, where phone calls and messages remain important modes of communication. According to figures shared during the discussion, Equal AI grew from around 70,000 monthly active users in January to 3.5 million in the preceding month. It was forecasting 15 million monthly active users by March. The company had also crossed one million daily active users and was targeting 10 million daily active users over the following 12 months. “You have to go deep, find a problem, solve it well, and then just expand from there,” Reddy said, explaining the approach that startups could adopt to build successful AI businesses. He also stressed the need for Indian companies to build consumer technology platforms capable of competing with global players. However, he identified computing costs as a major constraint on AI businesses seeking to serve millions of users. Ashutosh Sharma said local understanding would be a key differentiator for Indian startups competing with international companies. Businesses that understand the nuances of Indian consumers and their everyday challenges could develop products better suited to the domestic market. The panellists also urged entrepreneurs to focus on building sustainable competitive advantages. Sharma said falling product development costs and faster innovation cycles made it essential for founders to identify what would protect their businesses over the long term. “The market is not a moat anymore,” he said, urging founders to think from the outset about the competitive advantage they were building. Reddy emphasised the need for patient capital and a long-term commitment to entrepreneurship, noting that building large technology businesses often involves years of experimentation and failure. For India's startup ecosystem, the opportunity is therefore not limited to the size of the AI market itself. The larger prize lies in converting the country's consumer scale, technology talent and unmet demand into globally competitive AI products and platforms. Whether the opportunity ultimately reaches $100 billion or extends into trillions of dollars will depend on how effectively Indian businesses deploy AI to solve real-world problems and capture the resulting economic value.

title: Snabbit FY26 loss widens multifold to Rs 167.75 Cr; revenue rises to Rs 12.25 Cr
content: Maestroedge Solutions, which runs home services platform Snabbit, has posted a net loss of Rs 167.75 crore for 2025-26, nearly 30 times lower than the previous year, as spending on service providers, marketing and staff rose with the expansion of its business, according to financial statements filed with the Registrar of Companies. The Mumbai-based company reported a loss of Rs 5.70 crore in FY25. Its revenue from operations rose to Rs 12.25 crore in FY26 from Rs 26.35 lakh a year earlier. Platform services brought in Rs 10.82 crore, and the sale of uniforms to its service providers, whom it calls experts, stood at Rs 1.42 crore. Other income was Rs 14.77 crore, while total income was recorded at Rs 27 crore. Total expenses rose to Rs 194.76 crore from Rs 6.81 crore in FY25. Expert service cost was the largest expense at Rs 63.07 crore, up from Rs 27 lakh. Marketing spending rose nearly 60-fold to Rs 48.69 crore. Employee benefit expenses grew to Rs 46.02 crore from Rs 3.27 crore, and service fulfilment expenses to Rs 23.83 crore from Rs 48 lakh. "FY26 was our first full year of operations, and we made a deliberate choice to invest ahead of scale to build a category, not just a company," Snabbit founder and CEO Aayush Agarwal said. Agarwal said the company began the year with about 500 jobs a day across eight micro-markets and ended it at a run rate of 35,000 daily jobs across more than 100 micro-markets. During the year, it acquired nearly a million customers and onboarded over 20,000 experts, according to Agarwal. Losses were mainly due to investments in geographic expansion, customer and expert acquisition, and long-term operating capabilities, Agarwal added. The company was incorporated in January 2024. Its platform lets customers book house help, with an initial focus on maids for cleaning and cooking. The company had 309 employees as of March 31, 2026. Agarwal, who holds 98.98% of its equity shares, drew a salary of Rs 60 lakh in FY26, up from Rs 15.47 lakh. "Given the pace of growth and the investments required to build this category from the ground up, FY26 financials do not fully reflect the underlying economics or the maturity of the business today. "As we continue to scale, the benefits of operating leverage, improving unit economics and increasing network density are becoming increasingly evident," Agarwal said.

title: AI execution company RapidCanvas raises $29M in Series B
content: AI execution company RapidCanvas has raised $29 million in Series B funding led by Vertex Ventures SEA & India. The round also saw participation from Hitachi Ventures and existing investors, including Accel, Peak XV Partners, Valley Capital Partners and Titanium Ventures. The startup has raised a total funding to $52.5 million. RapidCanvas will use the Series B funding to grow its go-to-market teams and expand its network of private equity and advisory partners, who bring managed AI execution to their portfolio companies and clients. It will also grow its field AI engineering team across India, the US and Brazil. Further, the company plans to invest in its three products: deepening the Enterprise Context Engine, expanding the skills library behind the Visual Development Canvas, and strengthening governance in the Operational Harness. RapidCanvas pairs its AI platform with field AI engineers to deliver custom AI solutions. AI engineers learn each customer's business processes, design and build custom AI applications, and stay accountable for the applications' outcomes after delivery. The RapidCanvas AI platform brings together three products: The Enterprise Context Engine lets an enterprise capture how a business process runs, from requirements and tribal knowledge to data schemas and decision history, and the enterprise owns that context. The Visual Development Canvas lets AI engineers rapidly build custom AI solutions that meet industry benchmarks, drawing on a skills library that gives each new solution a 60% head start from proven, benchmarked code. The Operational Harness manages and governs AI solutions once they're deployed in production. RapidCanvas offers its Hybrid Approach at subscription pricing, changing the economics of enterprise AI. So far in 2026, more than 75 enterprises in manufacturing, financial services, retail, business services and infrastructure have made 1.4 million AI-led decisions with applications built on RapidCanvas. More than 40% of RapidCanvas' customers now run multiple AI use cases in production, said the company in a press statement. "AI can be the great equaliser, but so far its biggest wins have gone to the Fortune 100. We want to give every enterprise the same opportunity," said Rahul Pangam, co-founder and CEO of RapidCanvas. "Vibe coding has made it easy to start building with AI. Getting AI into production reliably and safely still remains the biggest gap. Our growth over the past six quarters is evidence that AI in enterprises is moving beyond pilots into production and real operations." RapidCanvas serves an underserved market: enterprises with $100 million to $10 billion in revenue that have AI budgets and C-suite mandates but no proven path to outcomes. In conversations with more than 400 business leaders, RapidCanvas found that most C-level executives expect a return on AI within six to 12 months, yet very few have moved beyond pilots and proofs of concept.
