title: Welcome competition but Indian laws apply to all: Reliance breaks silence on Musk's satcom row
content: Reliance Industries Ltd on Friday broke its silence on Elon Musk's public criticism of India's satellite communications landscape, saying it sees a competitive market as the true test of who serves customers best, and welcomes competition, including from Starlink, but asserted that every player must obey Indian laws. In its first direct response to Musk's recent barbs, the company said it was placing "the facts on record." Musk had criticised Reliance and argued that more competition would benefit consumers in satcom. "At Reliance, we have never feared competition. We see it as the truest test of who serves the customer best," the Mukesh Ambani--led company said in a statement. The company backed its stance citing Jio's own record. Jio entered India's crowded telecom market in 2016 as the newest player, with not a single customer, and in a matter of just ten years, earned the trust of over 530 million customers, offering Indians some of the best digital infrastructure and most affordable data in the world, it said. "We welcome competition in satellite communications, including Starlink. Every player, Jio included, must serve the people of India and abide by the laws and policies of the land," the statement said. Reliance said India's openness to investment and innovation, homegrown or international, rests on the rule of law. "Like every Indian enterprise, Reliance has grown in an India that welcomes investment and innovation, homegrown or international, that improve the lives of the people. That openness rests on the rule of law," it said. As the government has maintained, it applies the same process to every applicant, Indian or foreign, Reliance said, adding "Jio's own satellite services await clearances". Earlier this week, addressing the Bloomberg New Economy Forum 2026, Bharti Airtel Chairman Sunil Mittal said his satellite communications venture Eutelsat OneWeb was significantly ahead of Elon Musk's Starlink in the queue to launch services in India. His remarks added a fresh twist to a public dispute over regulatory approvals and competition in the country's satellite internet market. Government sources, responding to the controversy surrounding Starlink and Musk's recent claims, have made it clear that any company operating in India must comply with the law of the land. The Centre's position has been clear and consistent throughout, they added. "Government's position has been very clear, and was so even at the time they had applied, that if you don't follow Indian laws, you cannot do business here...So to do business here, you have to follow Indian laws," sources had said.. "I think I am significantly ahead in the queue from him. I applied five years back," Mittal said, and added "We don't have the permission, so we'll be very happy to get it at least a few days before him". Mittal said OneWeb's ground network has been ready for three years, and its satellites have been hovering over India for five years, but the company is still awaiting permission to begin commercial operations. The pushback from Mittal, and now Reliance, comes after Musk, the world's richest man, accused powerful business interests of blocking Starlink's entry into India. In a series of posts on social media platform X recently, Musk took aim at Reliance Industries chairman Mukesh Ambani, sarcastically addressing him as "Prime Minister Ambani" and questioning whether he wielded greater influence over India's decisions than Prime Minister Narendra Modi. Musk has alleged that some business groups are seeking to preserve a "monopolistic chokehold" on Indian consumers. However, the Ministry of Communications rejected the charge, describing suggestions that the regulatory framework or its application was unfair or discriminatory as "baseless and misconceived". The government said satellite operators must meet the same regulatory requirements, including security conditions and spectrum allocation rules, before they can begin commercial services. Communications Minister Jyotiraditya Scindia has said three ventures -- Musk's Starlink, Reliance's Jio Satcom and Bharti-backed Eutelsat OneWeb -- had secured satellite communications licences. Amazon's Project Kuiper has expressed interest but must follow the established procedure, he said. Scindia made it clear that spectrum would be assigned once the government finalised a revenue-based charging framework and individual operators fulfilled security requirements. The Telecom Regulatory Authority of India (TRAI) and the Department of Telecommunications (DoT) were close to a decision on satellite spectrum pricing, he added. The distinction between a licence and operational approval is central to the dispute: securing a licence does not automatically allow a company to begin commercial services. Spectrum assignment and the fulfilment of security conditions remain key steps. The dispute comes at a consequential time for Reliance, which is preparing for the initial public offering of Jio Platforms, its digital services business. Jio has set a price band of Rs 1,065 to 1,119 a share for its offer of up to 27 crore new shares, about 3 per cent of the existing capital, with no offer-for-sale component. At the top of the band, the sale would raise about Rs 30,213 crore, ahead of Hyundai Motor India's Rs 27,870 crore share sale in October 2024, the country's biggest. The price implies a market value of about Rs 10.3 lakh crore, short of the roughly Rs 11 lakh crore the company had earlier been said to seek. Bidding runs from October 21 to 23, with anchor investors bidding on October 19. The shares are expected to begin trading on October 28. Reliance is also developing its satellite ambitions, including a proposed constellation of about 1,600 low-earth-orbit satellites aimed at extending internet connectivity to 600,000 villages. That would put Jio in more direct competition with Starlink, which is seeking access to a vast market where satellite broadband could serve remote communities and locations poorly covered by terrestrial networks. Ironically, Reliance and SpaceX last year signed an agreement to explore ways of bringing Starlink services to Indian customers through Jio's retail network.

title: Shubhra Saxena’s It Matters A Lot: 5 Lessons on conscious living
content: I attended the launch of It Matters A Lot by author and bureaucrat Shubhra Saxena on October 16, 2026, at the India Habitat Centre in New Delhi. Published by Rupa Publications, the book features a foreword by the Dalai Lama and explores self-awareness, conscious choices and what makes life meaningful. The event brought together personalities from literature, diplomacy, academia, healthcare and public service, including Gurcharan Das, Pavan K. Verma, Prof. Kusum Lata Kedia, Abha Sharma and Dr Shweta Mathur Lall. The discussions reflected the book’s call to pause and reconsider our beliefs, relationships and ambitions. At a time when success is often measured through professional achievements and social recognition, It Matters A Lot asks whether we are living by our own values or following others’ expectations. Spanning life stages from childhood to old age, the book examines how upbringing, relationships, social conditioning and life experiences shape our perspectives. Rather than offering a formula for happiness, Saxena encourages readers to question their assumptions and discover what gives their lives meaning. Here are five important lessons from It Matters A Lot that encourage readers to reflect on their lives and embrace conscious living. 5 Lessons from It Matters A Lot by Shubhra Saxena 1. Question what success means to you Success is often defined by society through career progression, financial security, recognition and status. While these achievements can be meaningful, they do not necessarily guarantee contentment. It Matters A Lot encourages readers to examine whether their ambitions reflect their genuine desires or the expectations of family, peers and society. The pursuit of conventional milestones can become automatic when we rarely question why we want them in the first place. The lesson is to develop a personal understanding of success. Instead of measuring your life entirely against someone else's achievements, consider what gives you a sense of purpose, fulfilment and peace. 2. Understand how your past shapes you Our understanding of ourselves begins forming long before we can consciously evaluate our beliefs. Childhood experiences, family relationships, parental expectations and social norms influence how we approach relationships, handle challenges and perceive our own worth. These influences can remain with us well into adulthood, sometimes shaping our decisions without our awareness. Saxena's exploration of life's different stages invites readers to look back at these formative experiences and consider their continuing influence. Recognising the origins of our beliefs does not mean blaming our past. It means understanding which patterns serve us and which may need to change. Self-awareness begins when we learn to distinguish between what we have inherited and what we consciously choose to believe. 3. Make choices instead of following expectations From education and careers to relationships and family responsibilities, life presents countless decisions shaped by social expectations. It can be difficult to distinguish our own preferences from the pressure to meet other people's standards. The book encourages readers to question whether their choices reflect their values or a desire for acceptance and approval. Living consciously does not mean rejecting every expectation or disregarding the people around us. It means understanding why we make particular decisions and taking responsibility for their consequences. Before committing to a goal or making an important decision, ask yourself whether it aligns with the life you want to build. Even small moments of reflection can help you approach life with greater independence and intention. 4. Treat relationships with greater empathy Self-understanding is not limited to personal growth. It can also transform the way we relate to other people. When we become more aware of our own insecurities, emotional responses and assumptions, we may find it easier to recognise that other people have their own struggles, experiences and perspectives. This awareness can reduce unnecessary conflict and encourage more thoughtful communication. It Matters A Lot connects conscious living with empathy, compassion and responsibility towards others. Its broader message is that a meaningful life is not measured solely by individual accomplishments but also by the quality of our relationships and the care we extend to the people around us. Understanding ourselves can become a starting point for understanding others. 5. Accept change and rethink what matters Life rarely unfolds exactly as planned. Ambitions change, relationships evolve, opportunities disappear, and loss becomes part of the human experience. As people move through adulthood, midlife and old age, their priorities may change alongside their circumstances. The book encourages readers to reflect on these transitions rather than remain attached to outdated definitions of success or happiness. Acceptance does not mean giving up on personal growth. It means recognising that some circumstances cannot be controlled and learning to respond to them with greater clarity. As life changes, the things that once seemed essential may become less important, while relationships, inner peace, compassion and a sense of meaning may take on greater significance. Conscious living requires us to keep asking what matters to us now, rather than assuming that yesterday's priorities must define tomorrow. Why it matters a lot is relevant today Modern life leaves little room for reflection, with work, digital distractions and the pressure to achieve more often taking priority over questions of meaning and fulfilment. Saxena’s book encourages readers to examine their habits, assumptions and priorities. Rather than offering quick fixes, it uses questions at the end of each chapter to help readers find insights that reflect their own experiences and values. The book also connects self-awareness with empathy and responsibility towards others, showing how personal reflection can shape our relationships, communities and the way we live. Final thoughts In It Matters A Lot , Shubhra Saxena explores questions of identity, ambition, beliefs and what makes life meaningful. Featuring a foreword by His Holiness the Dalai Lama and published by Rupa Publications, the book encourages readers to reflect on their choices, cultivate self-awareness and practise compassion through different stages of life. At its heart, the book reminds us that living well means looking beyond milestones to understand our purpose, value our relationships and focus on what truly matters.

title: 7 Books that explain why we're connected but still lonely
content: You can have hundreds of followers, dozens of unread messages and conversations happening across multiple apps, yet still feel as though you have no one to talk to when life gets difficult. You can spend hours scrolling through other people's lives and still feel disconnected from your own. In a world where reaching someone takes seconds, loneliness has become a surprisingly familiar experience. Technology has changed how we maintain friendships, meet new people and share our experiences. Yet constant communication does not always translate into emotional closeness. A like cannot always replace a meaningful conversation, and a video call cannot always provide the comfort of being physically present with someone. Understanding this contradiction requires looking beyond screen time and social media habits. Loneliness is also connected to how we build relationships, experience belonging and find meaning in our communities. These seven books explore why modern life can leave us feeling disconnected, even when we are more digitally connected than ever. 1. Alone Together by Sherry Turkle In Alone Together , sociologist Sherry Turkle explores how technology changes our relationships and our expectations of companionship. We can communicate constantly through messages and social media while avoiding the deeper conversations that help us understand one another. The book asks an important question: are our digital connections making our relationships more meaningful, or simply making us feel less alone for a moment? 2. The Lonely Century by Noreena Hertz Noreena Hertz examines how technology, changing workplaces and weakening community ties contribute to isolation. The Lonely Century argues that loneliness is not simply an individual problem; it is also shaped by the way modern societies are organised. The book encourages readers to consider how stronger communities, meaningful interactions and shared experiences can help rebuild a sense of belonging. 3. Digital Minimalism by Cal Newport Checking notifications can make us feel socially active without necessarily helping us build closer relationships. In Digital Minimalism , Cal Newport explores how constant digital engagement can distract us from activities that bring genuine satisfaction. He encourages readers to use technology more intentionally and prioritise valuable experiences, including hobbies, focused conversations and spending time with people in person. 4. The Anxious Generation by Jonathan Haidt Jonathan Haidt examines the relationship between smartphone-based childhoods, social media and young people's mental well-being. The Anxious Generation explores how increased online engagement and reduced opportunities for independent play and face-to-face interaction may affect young people's development. It offers a starting point for understanding why digital connection does not always provide the emotional benefits of real-world friendships. Also Read 7 Books that explore the complexity of human relationships 5. Bowling Alone by Robert D. Putnam In Bowling Alone , political scientist Robert D. Putnam examines the decline of community participation and social connections in American life. He explores how people have become less involved in certain shared activities and organisations, weakening the relationships that help communities function. Although the book focuses primarily on the United States, its ideas offer a useful perspective on why belonging requires more than having a large online network. 6. Together by Vivek H. Murthy In Together , physician Vivek H. Murthy explores loneliness as a social and public health concern. He explains why human connection matters and how relationships, community involvement and everyday acts of care can help people feel less isolated. The book reminds readers that meaningful connection does not always require a large social circle; even a few supportive relationships can make a difference. 7. Reclaiming Conversation by Sherry Turkle Sherry Turkle returns to the relationship between technology and human connection in Reclaiming Conversation . She explores how the convenience of texting and online communication can sometimes come at the expense of meaningful conversation . By examining relationships at home, work and school, Turkle makes the case for giving people our full attention and creating space for conversations that build empathy and trust. Final thoughts Being connected is not the same as feeling connected. Social media helps us stay in touch, but meaningful relationships need trust, understanding and emotional closeness. These seven books explore modern loneliness, the role of technology and the importance of community. They encourage us to use digital spaces more mindfully and invest in real connections. Sometimes, feeling less lonely means spending less time seeking connections and more time nurturing the ones that matter.

title: Tech can improve governance, says Krishna Byre Gowda; Why Indian startups should build for the world from day one

He also said technology can help bridge the trust gap between people and the government. Highlighting Bengaluru’s economic weight in GCC investments and IT service exports, he urged entrepreneurs and builders to apply their innovation beyond commercial software to real socio-economic challenges. “ Bengaluru continues to be the centre for dynamism that nurtures talent and is able to be the home for a lot of people who contribute productively to their own lives, the economy, and the services of the country as well as the larger global space,” said Gowda. In a panel discussion on deeptech capital , venture capitalists said the deeptech ecosystem is giving rise to new kinds of founders and bold ideas. In a fireside chat with Shradha Sharma, Founder & CEO, YourStory and The Bharat Project, Tally’s Managing Director Tejas Goenka and Executive Director Nupur Goenka spoke about how the company has stayed relevant for 40 years. title: MumbaiSemi aims to become a global supplier of high-quality RF chips
content: India has developed its own satellite navigation system, NavIC, but much of the hardware required to receive its signals is still imported. ﻿ MumbaiSemi ﻿ , an IIT Bombay (IIT-B) spinout, aims to address this gap with an indigenous radio-frequency (RF) chip that can process signals from NavIC and other satellite navigation systems. Founded in late 2024, the Mumbai-based deeptech startup is commercialising DhruvaPro, a programmable RF chip designed for the front end of navigation receivers. Unlike conventional chips that typically operate on specific frequency bands, DhruvaPro can be programmed to work across different bands, offering greater flexibility. “We had almost six years of research at IIT-B, initially because there was a government project to develop an RF chip for NavIC . We went through two silicon iterations, both of which were successful, and started getting good feedback from the industry. That’s when we decided to take this technology forward as a company,” says Vijay Kanchetla, Co-founder of MumbaiSemi. The startup has an 11-member team, including Co-founder Rajesh Zele, who is also a professor at IIT Bombay. From NavIC research to commercial pilots The founder says DhruvaPro is one of India’s first reconfigurable RF navigation receiver chip. An antenna picks up weak, high-frequency satellite signals, while the RF chip filters out unwanted signals, amplifies, down-converts, and digitizes the navigation signals before this binary data reaches the receiver's processor for decoding the receiver's position, velocity, and time. Kanchetla says the original motivation was to design an RF chip capable of receiving India’s NavIC signals. However, the team decided to make the technology compatible with all global navigation systems. “We designed a chip such that it is not just for the Indian market, but to be able to supply to the entire world,” he says. “So what we did is make this chip work for NavIC, GPS, Galileo, GLONASS, and BeiDou—all navigation satellite systems of the world.” According to the company, DhruvaPro can also be reprogrammed to operate on new frequency bands, allowing navigation systems to adapt without replacing the RF chip. “Most existing chips are locked to one particular navigation frequency band, whereas DhruvaPro can be programmed to any frequency band. You can change it on the fly. That's something no one has, and that's what we are bringing in. It would add a lot of flexibility to the receiver system,” Kanchetla explains. He adds that DhruvaPro integrates with any processor and can receive navigation signal across any frequency band, allowing receiver systems to use multiple navigation satellite systems without replacing hardware. MumbaiSemi has completed multiple pilots and is currently pre-revenue. However, the deeptech startup expects to generate revenue soon. One challenge, Kanchetla says, is that customers operating in large-scale sectors like vehicle tracking, freight management, and logistics require full receiver modules consisting of RF and digital baseband chips with certain interfaces. MumbaiSemi is focused on making its technology easy to integrate. By simplifying the system architecture, the company is enabling receiver module manufacturers to seamlessly upgrade their hardware and reduce their reliance on imported modules. “The deployment cycles are very long,” he says. “Customers ask us to give them a compatible receiver module that they can plug in and replace their existing one.” The founder believes that by delivering a highly adaptable, indigenous alternative to legacy chips, the company is well positioned to serve both domestic and global daily navigation needs. Building an RF chip company MumbaiSemi operates from IIT Bombay's SINE incubator. DhruvaPro was developed by the same team at IIT Bombay and subsequently licensed to the startup. The company’s newer development work is being carried out internally. Kanchetla sees MumbaiSemi as part of India’s efforts to develop a domestic semiconductor ecosystem. While government initiatives have helped accelerate chip design, he believes the country still needs to build capabilities in packaging, system integration, and fabrication. “The technology is not new to us. It's just that the entire business and the ecosystem building around it are new,” he says. Kanchetla expects the company to pursue a formal funding round within six months, after achieving additional milestones. While DhruvaPro remains its immediate focus, MumbaiSemi is also developing a next-generation navigation chip aimed more directly at end-user applications, including vehicle tracking and high-value asset tracking. The startup is exploring opportunities beyond satellite navigation as well. “We have a few ideas that could greatly help upcoming technologies, such as high-frequency lidar communications, and high-speed data-centre communications,” Kanchetla says. Over the next five years, the company aims to establish itself as a specialist supplier of highly engineered RF chips for global markets. “We believe MumbaiSemi is one place where we can build such chips. In the next five years, we see ourselves producing very high-quality chips for the world,” Kanchetla says. MumbaiSemi is part of YourStory's Tech30 cohort—a showcase of India's most promising startups of 2026, unveiled at TechSparks Bengaluru. Edited by Teja Lele

title: TechSparks 2026 Day 3: Here’s all that’s happening
