title: 5 Lessons from Grief burns like fever by Minakshi Thakur
content: What happens when life changes overnight, leaving people to deal with loss, fear and uncertainty? In difficult times, some people struggle to find their way, while others discover a strength they never knew they possessed. Grief Burns Like Fever by Minakshi Thakur explores these experiences against the backdrop of a harsh lockdown. The novel brings together the lives of an ambulance driver transporting bodies, an adolescent coping with his mother's death, a woman questioning her marriage and another trying to escape decades of captivity. Through these interconnected stories, Thakur explores love, longing, grief and the different ways people respond to suffering. 5 Key lessons on resilience and human connection 1. Grief affects everyone differently Losing someone or something important can change the way we see the world. While some people express their pain openly, others withdraw into themselves or struggle to understand what they are feeling. The novel explores grief through characters facing different forms of suffering, reminding readers that there is no single way to experience loss. What helps one person cope may not work for another. The lesson: Give yourself and others the time and space needed to process grief. Healing does not follow a fixed timeline, and nobody should have to prove how deeply they are hurting. 2. Difficult times reveal human nature When a crisis disrupts everyday life, people often reveal sides of themselves that remain hidden during more comfortable times. Some respond with kindness and courage , while others become overwhelmed by fear or uncertainty. Set during a lockdown, Grief Burns Like Fever examines how extraordinary circumstances affect ordinary people and their choices. The lesson: Difficult situations can test our values, but they can also reveal our capacity for compassion. Even small acts of kindness can make a difference when the world feels uncertain. 3. Human connection matters more than we realise During periods of isolation and loss, the presence of another person can offer comfort that words alone cannot provide. Feeling understood, supported or simply remembered can make overwhelming circumstances easier to face. The interconnected lives in Thakur's novel highlight how people can become linked through circumstances beyond their control, even when their personal struggles seem entirely different. The lesson: Never underestimate the importance of being there for someone. A listening ear, a thoughtful gesture or a little patience can help another person feel less alone. Also Read 5 Quotes on human connection from the Anxious Generation 4. Sometimes, survival requires finding your own strength The adolescent in the novel must confront life after his mother's death, while another woman struggles to break free from a situation that has confined her for decades. Their circumstances differ, but both face difficult questions about survival and the possibility of change. Their experiences invite readers to reflect on the courage it takes to continue when life offers no easy answers. The lesson: Strength does not always mean being fearless. Sometimes, it means taking the next small step even when you feel uncertain, exhausted or afraid. 5. Hope can exist even in the darkest moments Grief, fear and uncertainty can make the future appear impossible to imagine. Yet difficult periods do not erase every possibility of change, healing or a new beginning. Through its exploration of love, longing and human suffering, Grief Burns Like Fever reflects the complicated nature of life during a crisis. People may experience heartbreak and disappointment while still searching for something worth holding on to. The lesson: Hope does not require you to ignore your pain. It simply allows you to believe that your present circumstances do not have to define every part of your future. Final thoughts Grief Burns Like Fever by Minakshi Thakur explores loss, confinement, relationships and survival during a collective crisis, showing how people respond to difficult circumstances. Thakur is also known for her Hindi poetry collection Neend Ka Akhiri Pul , shortlisted for the Sahitya Akademi Yuva Puraskar in 2012, and her debut novel Lovers Like You and I , shortlisted for the Tibor Jones South Asia Prize in 2013. The novel's central themes invite readers to look beyond their own experiences and recognise the struggles others may be carrying. Its most meaningful reminder is that even when suffering connects people in unexpected ways, compassion and human connection can help them navigate uncertainty.

title: The math behind why young startup employees are underinsured by over Rs 1 Cr
content: Many young professionals assume their existing cover is sufficient. However, the question they need to ask is ‘ how much term insurance do I need’, to adequately protect their family from outstanding liabilities and future financial goals. A life cover of Rs 50 lakh can sound substantial at 28. You may have just received an appraisal, begun an SIP, and perhaps taken a home loan with the confidence that your career is still on an upward curve. But life cover is not meant to reflect where your income stands today alone. It needs to account for the financial responsibilities your family would have to manage if your income stopped unexpectedly. Consider a 28-year-old startup employee earning Rs 15 lakh a year. He has Rs 50 lakh of existing cover: Rs 20 lakh through his employer and a Rs 30 lakh individual policy. On paper, he is insured. In reality, he could still have a protection gap of Rs 1.2 crore. Why existing cover can create false comfort Employer-provided insurance is useful, but it is usually linked to your job. If you switch companies, take a career break, or lose your job, that cover may not continue. An individual term Insurance policy is portable because it stays with you as long as you pay the premiums and meet the policy conditions. The bigger issue is that many people choose a round figure without calculating their actual financial responsibilities. A Rs 50 lakh cover may have been enough when you were single and had no loans. It may be inadequate once you have a home loan, parents who depend on you, a spouse, or plans for children. At 28, you also have a long earning runway ahead. Your family is not only losing your current salary if you are no longer around; they may lose the future financial support your career could have provided. The math behind the Rs 1.2 crore gap Here is a simple illustration for a startup employee with a monthly take-home income of about Rs 1 lakh. Assume that he contributes Rs 75,000 each month towards household expenses, savings, and family commitments. Financial need Income replacement for 12 years at ₹9 lakh a year - Estimated amount: ₹1.08 crore Outstanding home loan - Estimated amount: ₹50 lakh Support for dependent parents and medical needs - Estimated amount: ₹20 lakh Future family goal or child’s education - Estimated amount: ₹30 lakh Emergency reserve for the family - Estimated amount: ₹12 lakh Total financial requirement: ₹2.20 crore Less liquid savings and investments: ₹30 lakh Required life cover - Estimated amount: ₹1.90 crore Existing cover - ₹70 lakh Protection gap - Estimated amount: ₹1.20 crore This is only an illustration, not a universal recommendation. Your required cover will differ based on your income, debts, savings, dependants, and financial goals. Still, it shows why choosing cover based only on a familiar number can leave a major shortfall. How much term insurance do I need? A practical calculation The question is not simply whether you have a policy. It is how much term insurance do I need for the people and obligations that depend on me? Start with the amount your family would need to maintain their lifestyle. Include regular expenses, loan repayments, education costs, medical support for parents, and major goals you have committed to. Then subtract assets that your family can access immediately, such as liquid savings, fixed deposits, and existing investments. Do not count every investment at its current market value without thought. Long-term investments may be earmarked for retirement, and selling them at the wrong time can disrupt your family’s future. Similarly, do not assume your employer’s cover will always remain available. A term insurance calculator can help you estimate the cover required by bringing these numbers together. Use realistic inputs, especially for liabilities and income replacement, rather than selecting the lowest premium shown. Why young startup employees need to look beyond salary Startup careers can grow quickly, but they can also change quickly. Your compensation may include variable pay, stock options, or performance-linked incentives. These elements can make you feel financially secure while leaving your family dependent on a salary that may not be easily replaced. You may also have responsibilities that do not show up in your monthly budget. For instance, you may contribute towards a parent’s treatment, help a sibling with education, or be planning a house purchase with your partner. These commitments should be reflected in your term insurance cover. Buying earlier can help because premiums are generally lower when you are younger and in good health. It also gives you the opportunity to secure a longer policy term before health concerns or lifestyle changes affect your eligibility or premium. Do not use a simple salary multiple blindly A common approach is to choose cover worth 10 or 15 times your annual income. This can be a useful starting point, but it is not the final answer. A person earning Rs 15 lakh with no debt and substantial savings may need a different cover amount from someone with the same income and a Rs 50 lakh home loan. Instead, use salary as one input within a wider calculation. If your family needs Rs 75,000 each month, estimate how long they would need this support. Then add liabilities and future goals. Finally, reduce the total by assets that can genuinely be used by your family. When you ask how much term insurance do I need , focus on the financial gap rather than a headline number. The goal is to ensure that your family does not have to compromise on essential needs, education, or loan repayments after an unexpected event. What should you review before buying? Choose a policy term that covers your highest-responsibility years. This may be until your home loan is repaid, your children become independent, or you build enough retirement savings. Also check whether your nominee would benefit more from a lump-sum payout, monthly income or a combination of both. Disclose your health history, lifestyle habits, and occupation accurately. Incorrect or incomplete information can affect claim assessment later. Keep your nominee details current and tell your family where the policy documents are stored. A term insurance calculator is helpful when comparing different cover amounts and policy terms. But it should support your decision, not replace a clear review of your financial responsibilities. The real cost of waiting The Rs 1.2 crore gap in this example is not caused by a lack of intent. It comes from delaying the calculation while responsibilities quietly increase. At 28, you may feel that a larger cover can wait until you are married, buy a home, or become a parent. By then, the premium may be higher, and the financial consequences of remaining underinsured may be greater. The right term insurance cover should reflect the life you are building, not just the salary you receive today. Review it whenever your income, debt or family responsibilities change. That simple review can turn a policy into meaningful financial protection for the people who count on you. (Disclaimer: The views and opinions expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the views of YourStory.)

title: TechSparks 2026: meet the innovators exhibiting at India’s premier startup tech summit
content: Launched in 2014, PhotoSparks is a weekly feature from YourStory, with photographs that celebrate the spirit of creativity and innovation. In the earlier 1,020 posts, we featured an art festival, cartoon gallery. world music festival , telecom expo , millets fair, climate change expo, wildlife conference, startup festival, Diwali rangoli, and jazz festival. TechSparks is India’s most beloved startup conference and exhibition, organised for the past 17 years by YourStory . In this photo showcase, we feature teams from many startups and ecosystem enablers exhibiting at TechSparks in Bengaluru. See our earlier exhibitor showcases from TechSparks in 2025, 2024, 2023, 2019, 2018, 2017, and 2016. Also check out our quotes compilations from the conference editions in 2022, 2021, 2020, 2019, 2018, 2017, 2016, 2015, and 2014. Also Read Tech in governance can minimise corruption, bridge trust gap between people & govt: Krishna Byre Gowda The theme of TechSparks this year is The New Tech Order. AI, deep tech and new digital infrastructure are changing how technology is built, who can build it, and how quickly ideas can reach billions. TechSparks 2026 is about the people, technologies and businesses shaping what comes next, and putting ideas into action. A galaxy of industry leaders, founders and investors are addressing a wide range of questions. What happens when every business can build its own software? What will India’s next technology advantage be? What does Indian deeptech need to become globally iconic? Does every founder need to build an audience? Also Read TechSparks 2026: Here’s all that’s happening on Day 2 In this photo essay, we feature some of the dozens of exhibitors at TechSparks – Startup Park, Sushi Tech Tokyo, PayU, Incred Wealth, Bhasha Bharat, Niti Bodh, Mitra for Life, Feltiv, XSpecies, SearchJob.AI, Pro1 Analytics, Dolphin AI, RentenPe, Aria, Makers Hive, and Rapyder. Startup Park is an entrepreneurial ecosystem platform designed to help founders turn early-stage ideas into scalable businesses. Its offerings include coworking spaces, innovation labs, incubation programmes, mentorship, networking opportunities, business education, and startup support services. An abbreviation for the Sustainable High City Tech Tokyo, its focus is on using advanced technology to address urban and societal challenges. Also Read New tech order will be built from Karnataka: Priyank Kharge PayU is a financial technology company that provides digital payment infrastructure to businesses, enabling them to accept and process online payments through multiple payment methods. Its services support merchants with payment processing, transaction management, and related financial technology capabilities for digital commerce. Its offerings include personalised investment strategies, wealth creation, family office services, estate planning, wealth protection, and support for business owners managing complex financial needs. Its approach emphasises community-based support, working with families and schools, parent education, specialised therapies, and care delivered closer to where children live. Also Read Srinath Ravichandran and Suyash Singh on overcoming failure in spacetech Feltiv is a technology company focused on AI-powered localization to help businesses adapt content for different languages and markets. Its focus on localisation is relevant to businesses expanding internationally, as well as digital platforms that need multilingual content at scale. xSpecies is a Bengaluru-based deep-tech robotics company developing physical AI systems that combine artificial intelligence, robotic hardware, perception, and dexterous manipulation. By connecting rental history with financial identity, RentenPe aims to address a gap in which regular rent payments do not traditionally contribute directly to a tenant's credit profile. Its products include KalArm, a mobile-app-enabled bionic hand intended to help people with upper-limb amputations regain practical hand functionality. title: Bengaluru plans to expand metro network to 400 km by 2037, says Krishna Byre Gowda
content: The Karnataka government has ambitious plans for Bengaluru as it seeks to maintain the city’s dynamism while addressing key infrastructure challenges. During a fireside chat with Shradha Sharma, Founder and CEO, YourStory and The Bharat Project, Karnataka Minister for Greater Bengaluru Development, Krishna Byre Gowda, said, “Bengaluru continues to be the centre for dynamism that nurtures talent and is able to be the home for a lot of people who contribute productively to their own lives, economy and to the services of the country as well as the larger global space.” The State government plans to create technology spaces, mixed usage locations that will attract knowledge professionals and also investments. According to the minister, the Greater Bengaluru Authority covers a geographical area of about 750 square kilometers, while Bengaluru's existing urban space already occupies about 1,200 square kilometers. “We are already planning the 2,000 square kilometer space around Bengaluru,” the minister remarked. Bengaluru’s economic significance is reflected in several indicators. The city accounts for 36% of the new office space created in the country, hosts 40% of India’s global capability centres (GCCs), and contributes around 40-45% of the country’s $300 billion in exports. Despite the city’s breakneck pace of growth, Gowda highlighted the role of its social ecosystem in sustaining its dynamism. The minister said the state government plans to expand Bengaluru’s metro rail network from the current 96 kilometres to 170 kilometres over the next 18 months. “By 2037, Bengaluru will be 500 years old and hopefully by then we can have at least 400 kilometres of metro,” he said. Besides the metro rail, the State government is also planning to expand the suburban railway network and expand the city's bus fleet. “We do have at least a 10-15 year plan. We are working to crystallize it and put it in place so that it just doesn't remain as a plan on the paper,” the minister said. The minister acknowledged that Bengaluru faces significant challenges across transport, roads, and civic cleanliness. He noted that these issues should have been addressed at least 25 years ago. “Hopefully, in the next six months, we can show demonstrable results in making Bengaluru relatively a cleaner city,” the minister said. Gowda acknowledged the government’s shortcomings and said it was keen to address them. However, he also stressed the need for citizens to change their behaviour, particularly when it comes to waste disposal, to bring about meaningful improvements in the city. “We understand the sentiment of the people. We acknowledge it. We have a job to do and are taking our job seriously,” the minister said.

title: TechSparks 2026 Day 2: From Krishna Byre Gowda’s Bengaluru blueprint to Stripe’s global playbook, and more
content: On the second day, the 17th edition of TechSparks 2026 in Bengaluru moved between policy and product, with conversations on governance, the city’s infrastructure future, global-first startups, and India’s deeptech opportunity. YourStory ’s flagship startup-tech summit brought together founders, investors, policymakers, and technologists to explore how India can build for itself and for the world. The day’s headline conversation featured Krishna Byre Gowda, Minister for Greater Bengaluru Development, Government of Karnataka, in a fireside chat with Shradha Sharma, Founder and CEO, YourStory and The Bharat Project. Drawing on his time in the state’s Land Revenue Department, Gowda said technology in governance can minimise corruption and help bridge the trust gap between citizens and the government. “The more technology we adopt in governance, the better will be our delivery of services to people, and lower will be the levels of corruption,” he said. He also cautioned that technology alone cannot fix systemic problems without a shift in civic behaviour. Out of an estimated 35 lakh to 50 lakh properties in Bengaluru, he noted, only 23 lakh have registered khatas and just 18 lakh pay property taxes. The minister also laid out an ambitious plan for the city’s growth. The state government aims to expand Bengaluru’s metro network from 96 km to 170 km over the next 18 months, and hopes to reach 400 km by 2037 , the year the city turns 500. Planning is already underway for a 2,000 sq km area around Bengaluru, well beyond the 750 sq km covered by the Greater Bengaluru Authority. “Hopefully, in the next six months, we can show demonstrable results in making Bengaluru relatively a cleaner city,” Gowda said. Moving to global ambitions, Manish Maheshwari, Managing Director, Stripe India, said AI is making it faster and cheaper to build world-facing companies from India, giving rise to what he called the “minimum viable company.” According to him, Indian founders can now go global from day one. He pointed to Emergent hitting $100 million in ARR in eight months, and Stripe data showing 76% of customers prefer paying in their own currency. Maheshwari also confirmed Stripe’s agreement to acquire OpenRouter, which routes AI queries to the most suitable model, a bet on helping companies control fast-rising AI costs. “In some of the new-age companies, the amount of money people are spending on tokens is more than what they are spending on salaries,” he said. Deeptech took centre stage in a panel featuring Vishesh Rajaram of Speciale Invest, Mayuresh Raut of Seafund, Anirudh Singh of Avatar Venture Partners, and Abhishek Srivastava of Kae Capital. The investors said deeptech is giving rise to new kinds of founders, driven by India’s talent advantage and the geopolitical push for self-reliance in critical technologies. Raut said there is still an eight-to-10-year window of opportunity, while Rajaram noted that “nerve and patience” set apart the founders who endure. Day 3 of TechSparks 2026 will continue to unpack how India can build, own, and scale the technologies of the new tech order. The agenda features conversations on rethinking engineering education with Prof Ashok Jhunjhunwala, building global companies from day one with Omio’s Naren Shaam, AI sovereignty and the next 500 million users, climate innovation in energy, water, and clean air, and India’s $100 billion AI opportunity, before the summit closes with a fireside chat with Zakir Khan.

title: Deeptech is giving rise to new kinds of founders and bold ideas: VCs
content: Deeptech has become a key investing theme in India, and the country's differentiated capabilities has led to the emergence of new kinds of founders, believe venture capitalists focused on this segment. At a panel discussion at TechSparks 2026, moderated by Shradha Sharma, Founder and CEO, YourStory and The Bharat Project, the panellists were of the view that bold new ideas are coming from founders and entrepreneurs. Vishesh Rajaram, Managing Partner, Speciale Invest, said, “Everybody's so bold about coming out and doing it. I don't think early capital is going to hold anyone back anymore. I think we will see a lot more innovation coming out of the country.” In the current context, artificial intelligence (AI) is dominating the headlines, attracting investor interest. The deeptech segment, in particular, offers different kind of opportunities. In addition, the geopolitical environment has created the need for self-reliance in critical technologies. On the reason for the increased number of deeptech entrepreneurs, Mayuresh Raut, Co-founder & Managing Partner, Seafund, said, “There is still a window of opportunity of eight to 10 years.” He noted that there were numerous gaps in multiple areas of the deeptech ecosystem, and entrepreneurs need to identify them and come out with the right products. Anirudh Singh, General Partner, Avatar Venture Partners, cited an example of an India-based radiator company, which is supplying its products across the globe. He further expounded that in segments like AI and data centres, it will be very challenging for India to match the capabilities of countries like the US and China. But the one advantage that the country has is the availability of talent, he added. Abhishek Srivastava, General Partner, Kae Capital, noted that given the current geo-political situation it is important to be self-reliant in critical technologies, and this opens up new opportunities. “It is going to be a bigger opportunity both for investors and founders as the country kind of shapes up for the next few decades,” he said. The panellists were of the view that deeptech founders must identify niches where they have expertise in and build their solutions around them. The traditional manner of creating products will no longer work, they said. The VC panellists also highlighted the challenges that deeptech founders will face in their entrepreneurial journey. Raut remarked that being a startup founder is probably the most arduous undertaking any human can undertake. “These guys (founders) just have an inhuman, almost extraterrestrial ability to just show up the next day, no matter how many knocks they get,” he said. Rajaram said, “Nerve and patience are two qualities we've seen in the ones (founders) who have outlasted themselves and their businesses.”

title: Tech in governance can minimise corruption, bridge trust gap between people & govt: Krishna Byre Gowda
content: Krishna Byre Gowda, Minister for Greater Bengaluru Development, Government of Karnataka, highlighted technology’s role in improving governance, enhancing transparency, and reducing corruption. Speaking at a fireside chat with Shradha Sharma, Founder & CEO, YourStory and The Bharat Project at TechSparks 2026, YourStory’s annual summit, the minister drew on his previous experience in the state’s Land Revenue Department to illustrate how technology can improve public service delivery. Gowda said technology-driven solutions could automate government processes, make administration more transparent, and improve public service delivery. “We implemented a lot of technology-based solutions to completely or partly automate government functioning, make the process a lot more transparent and visible to people, and introduce technology at whatever level possible,” he said, recalling his tenure at the Land Revenue Department. He said these interventions had significantly improved the government’s ability to deliver results, made processes more transparent, and reduced opportunities for corruption. “Technology has the ability, if we are willing, to deliver better governance, at least minimise corruption, and be able to meet people's expectations,” said Gowda. He emphasised that technology can help bridge the trust gap between governments and citizens today. He added that it could do so by enabling governments to respond more effectively and deliver better services. “I believe—and since I have done it and I could see the results—so now with a lot more confidence, not just as an idea, I can say that the more technology we adopt in governance, the better will be our delivery of services to people, and lower will be the levels of corruption,” he said. However, Gowda cautioned that technology alone cannot eradicate systemic corruption without a parallel shift in civic behaviour. Stressing that corruption is “not a one-way street,” he noted that “unless two hands meet, the clap doesn’t happen”. Illustrating the gap in public compliance, he revealed that, out of an estimated 35 lakh to 50 lakh properties in Bengaluru, only 23 lakh possess registered titles ( khatas ) and a mere 18 lakh pay property taxes. Similarly, on civic issues like waste management, he emphasised that government accountability—such as ensuring daily doorstep garbage collection—must be matched by citizen cooperation, rather than dumping garbage by the roadside. Addressing the ethical challenges of modern governance, Gowda offered a candid look into political reality. “In today’s political system, you keep a conscience and try to do the best you can, and don’t sell your soul,” he said, acknowledging that while compromises cannot be entirely avoided, leaders must navigate the system without abandoning their core duty. Facing steep public scrutiny and administrative friction, he described his daily ethos as simply getting up every morning to “either break your head or break the damn wall” to deliver results. This administrative push comes against the backdrop of decades of unplanned expansion and infrastructure deficits. Pointing to severe bottlenecks, Gowda noted that planned localities like Jayanagar allocate 23% of their land area to roads, whereas problem-ridden unplanned areas have as little as 8%. To halt further degradation, the government has stopped new illegal layouts and initiated proactive planning across 2,000 square kilometres—far beyond the current 750-square-kilometre Greater Bengaluru Authority geography—to avoid repeating the mistakes of the past 25 years. Speaking about the city’s tech ecosystem, Gowda highlighted Bengaluru’s economic weight—the city hosts 40% of India’s GCC investments and generates over 40% of the $300 billion IT service exports. He urged entrepreneurs and builders to apply their innovation beyond commercial software to real socio-economic challenges, insisting that Indian tech leaders must position themselves at the “head" of the pack—and not follow the pack—to shape the nation’s future.

title: The/Nudge secures $15M from Google.org to develop AI tools for small businesses
content: The/Nudge, an Indian action institute focused on livelihoods and economic inclusion, is receiving a $15 million funding commitment from Google.org, Google’s philanthropic arm, to develop artificial intelligence (AI) tools for India’s micro, small and medium enterprises (MSMEs). The funding aims to improve access to formal credit, market opportunities, and regulatory compliance for small businesses. The programme will include an open call for proposals to identify practical solutions to business challenges. It will also develop a multilingual, voice-led platform to train people in Tier III and IV towns in job-ready skills and connect them with small businesses. Google’s announcement estimates that more than 90 million small businesses in India employ over 345 million people, although many continue to face difficulties securing finance and reaching digital markets. Preeti Lobana, Google India’s Vice President and Country Manager, said the AI technology must address everyday business needs. “For AI to be truly successful in India, it must become a practical multiplier for the millions of small businesses that drive our economic growth,” she said. The funding comes amid growing investment in technology-led lending to small businesses. In February, Chennai-based Prayaan Capital raised Rs 110 crore in a Series A round led by venture capital firm Peak XV Partners to build a technology-enabled lending platform. In October 2025, Bengaluru-based Optimo Capital raised Rs 150 crore from founder Prashant Pitti and existing investors Blume Ventures and Omnivore, alongside separate debt funding of Rs 110 crore from IDFC and Axis Bank. Subhashree Dutta, Chief Executive of the^delta, an organisation supporting social entrepreneurs, said the initiative would use “stage-gated grand challenges”, meaning competitive rounds with defined milestones, to support solutions across compliance, market access, quality and credit. She argued that these barriers reinforce one another. Dutta also said the initiative’s open standards could make MSMEs more competitive, creditworthy and globally visible. Government initiatives are also targeting the sector’s financing and technology constraints. The IndiaAI Mission, approved in 2024 with an outlay of Rs 10,371.92 crore over five years, supports computing capacity, skills, startup financing, and AI applications. In October, the Union Cabinet approved a separate Rs 10,000 crore SME Growth Fund for direct equity investment in growth-oriented businesses. Public-sector banks are also using digital credit assessments based on verifiable business data. Official figures show that 98,995 MSME loan applications were sanctioned under this model between April 1 and July 15, 2025.

title: Stripe India MD on why Indian startups should build for the world from day one
content: Ask Manish Maheshwari what has changed for Indian startups with global ambitions, and his answer is speed. Speaking at the 17th edition of TechSparks, the Managing Director of Stripe India said AI is changing how quickly, and how cheaply, a company can start selling to the world. "We are seeing the creation of a new way of operating, the minimum viable company," Maheshwari told Shradha Sharma, Founder and CEO of YourStory and The Bharat Project, in a fireside chat on taking startups from early traction to global scale. "The entrepreneurs in India can think global and go global on day one now." The financial infrastructure platform helps companies of all sizes manage their payments. Maheshwari had examples ready. Emergent, he said, reached $100 million in annual recurring revenue (ARR) in eight months, and Pocket FM has recently crossed half a billion in ARR. "If you had asked me two years ago which companies were hitting that level of revenue that fast, I could not have told you," he said. Stripe's own numbers point the same way. Over the past five years, Maheshwari said, the number of companies using Stripe Atlas, its incorporation and compliance service, to collect money from more than 100 countries has quadrupled. And for most businesses, over a quarter of revenue now comes from outside their top 10 markets. Stripe , valued at $160 billion and still pre-IPO, pitches itself as the layer that takes the pain out of all this. Maheshwari said founders should not be burning engineering hours on payments plumbing. "As a founder, you want to focus on your core product," he said. "If you are spending your engineering time customising your financial infrastructure, maybe you are not using your engineering in the best way." Stripe's idea, he said, is to make money programmable "through a single API". Founders need not even travel. "You can sit in India and sell to the world, and earn foreign exchange for your country." Localisation, he argued, is where the money is. Stripe's data shows 76% of customers prefer to pay in their own currency, and that offering local payment methods beyond cards lifts revenue by roughly 12%. "You are leaving 12% of the money on the table by not offering them," he said. It matters for physical goods too, he added, pointing to Purely Copper, which makes copper bottles in India, has built a following in the US, and takes payments through Stripe before shipping. The OpenRouter bet Maheshwari confirmed that Stripe has agreed to acquire OpenRouter, a platform that routes AI queries to the most suitable model. The logic, he said, is that AI bills are climbing fast. "In some of the new-age companies, the amount of money people are spending on tokens is more than what they are spending on salaries." Stripe already helps companies earn money through subscriptions, usage-based billing and invoicing. OpenRouter would help them keep a lid on what they spend. "If you want to build a solid P&L, you need great revenues, but you also have to keep your costs in control," he said. "That is when you make a profit." Agents and checkout An audience member asked whether AI agents will finally be able to complete payments on their own. Maheshwari said agentic commerce is "becoming more and more mainstream", at least in the US. He said Stripe's one-click payment product, Link, lets users authorise an agent to spend within a set limit, and that Stripe is helping shape payment protocols for agent-led shopping. "Stripe has a ringside view of this because we are integrated into all the major AI companies," he said. Retailers, he added, are already redesigning their websites so they are "machine readable as well" as human friendly.

title: 'Govern yourself like HDFC or SBI, build like Google or Amazon': PhonePe's Sameer Nigam
content: PhonePe Founder and CEO Sameer Nigam said the fintech company hopes to revive its initial public offering (IPO) plans once global markets stabilise, even as it prepares to expand beyond India with a full-stack payments business in the UAE. Speaking at the 17th edition of YourStory's TechSparks in Bengaluru on Tuesday, Nigam said PhonePe had completed much of the groundwork for its public listing before geopolitical tensions and market volatility forced it to pause the process earlier this year. "I think hopefully not too far away," Nigam said when asked about the IPO by Shradha Sharma, Founder and CEO of YourStory and The Bharat Project. "We got our board approvals. We were almost over the line. We'd done our roadshows," he said, recalling how escalating conflicts disrupted the company's plans. "The first moment of stability, we would like to get back out there," he added, without committing to a listing date. PhonePe had announced a pause in its IPO plans in March 2026, citing geopolitical uncertainty and volatile market conditions. Nigam declined to discuss the company's potential valuation, saying its draft prospectus reflected the past rather than the future. Govern like a bank, innovate like big tech Nigam said payments carry a responsibility other consumer tech does not. "Yes, it's fintech. Yes, it's a consumer tech business. But really, it's a business of trust," he said. PhonePe operates under the oversight of the Reserve Bank of India (RBI), Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) and Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India (IRDAI) through its various businesses. Nigam said the company undergoes around 130 to 140 external audits annually, roughly once every two working days. "You can't wing it. It has to become a way of life," he said. His guiding principle is to balance the pace of technology innovation with the governance standards expected of a large financial institution: "Govern yourself like an HDFC or an SBI, build like a Google or an Amazon. Also, in this sector, never switch the two. You'll be dead." He credited the company's compliance culture to a leadership team that has largely stayed together for a decade and mandatory orientation for every hire, including its roughly 50,000-strong sales network across the country. The message, he said, never changes: "You can't do jugaad at this scale, and ethics are non-negotiable." UPI for feature phones PhonePe has taken UPI to feature phones through encrypted SMS-based payments, reviving a technology approach that had initially struggled to gain traction about five years ago, when the industry expected feature phones to disappear. The company subsequently renewed its efforts as smartphone affordability became a growing concern. PhonePe publicly announced its UPI 123Pay offering in August 2026, following its acquisition of Gupshup’s GSPay technology stack in June 2025. Nigam said job and income losses after COVID, and rising component costs partly linked to demand for AI infrastructure, have made entry-level smartphones increasingly unaffordable for many Indians. "Sales numbers are in decline in India for the first time in 15 years," he said. The offering, which PhonePe is working to make available across devices from HMD, Nokia, Itel and Lava, is adding around 15,000 to 20,000 users a day, according to Nigam. It has reached about three lakh transactions a month, up from one lakh the month before. "It is growing like a hockey stick on a small base," Nigam said. Users can send money, check balances after direct benefit transfers and receive payments through a UPI QR code. The company is also expanding the range of services, including bill payments and mobile recharges, available on feature phones. His rationale was simple: "If we are a payments company, our job is to leave no one behind." He added that AI could tackle another barrier, language: "It's not just Bhashini, but conversation will change the game." Taking PhonePe's payments business overseas PhonePe has so far enabled Indian travellers to make UPI payments at participating merchants abroad. That falls short in markets such as the UAE and Singapore, where merchants may accept UPI but do not always prominently advertise it, prompting Indian travellers to continue using cards. PhonePe's international CEO, Ritesh Pai, therefore pushed for a broader strategy in the UAE that includes the app, merchant acquiring and remittances. In September 2026, PhonePe received in-principle approval from the Central Bank of the UAE for two licences covering retail payment services and card schemes, and stored value facilities. Commercial operations remain subject to final regulatory approval. Singapore is the other market the company has applied in, Nigam said. Nigam hopes others follow. "I would be disappointed if others didn't. We have all the resources. We have all the VCs. We have all the talent. We have all the agency. Now we should go abroad," he said. Purpose over pay On AI anxiety, Nigam was sceptical of predictions that technology would fundamentally replace human relationships: "We are not going to get an AI agent as a lifetime buddy and sequester ourselves from mankind." He acknowledged that technological change was disrupting careers and employment, but argued that companies must offer employees a sense of belonging and purpose rather than purely transactional relationships. To founders, he said money matters less than purpose. "Once you have roots, everything else is a waste," said Nigam, who still lives in the house he moved into 14 years ago. What excites him, he said, is seeing PhonePe QR codes in Leh-Ladakh, Tawang and the Andamans, and the prospect of expanding access to loans from three million people to 30 million. For Nigam, expanding financial access and building sustainable jobs are more meaningful measures of entrepreneurial success than personal wealth. "That is fun."

title: Tejas Goenka and Nupur Goenka on how Tally stayed relevant for 40 years
content: Tally Solutions' journey began much before the SaaS, UPI, GST, and startup boom. Founded in 1986, the accounting software company has outlasted several technology cycles and built a customer network of close to three million. In a fireside chat with Shradha Sharma, Founder & CEO, YourStory and The Bharat Project, Tally's Managing Director Tejas Goenka and Executive Director Nupur Goenka explained how Tally, a homegrown product company, has stayed relevant over four decades. Nupur Goenka attributed Tally's success to its focus on ownership. Tally handcrafted its stack from the start, she said, with its own database, its own memory manager, and a programming language invented in-house. The company has rewritten its entire stack five times without carrying over a single line of code. “The willingness to do that, because you remain uncompromising about your objectives, has been the culture of the company since day one,” she said. Tejas Goenka stressed on the company' founding principle. "The cost post-purchase should be near zero,” he said, recalling the days when releases were shipped with a support team of one. Drawing a distinction between being boring and being comfortable, Nupur spoke about the culture of change in the company. “There’s a tendency sometimes to confuse the boring and successful with the comfortable,” she said. “When you find yourself in any form of comfort zone, it signals unwillingness to change and inertia.” She shared her father’s suggestion to usher in a change every few months to keep the company alive. On the advent of AI, the Goenkas concurred that the fundamentals will not change: cost, reliability in a business of trust, and privacy. The company uses AI to make Tally useful for founders without compromising customer data. Tejas talked about a textile manufacturer with revenues of around Rs 1,500 crore where only four people know the customer names. “Imagine giving that data to AI,” he said. Nupur recalled being told on her first day at Tally that a customer’s data is only the customer’s data. Nobody inside the company has access to it, she said. The challenge is to deliver insights and access to credit without breaking that promise. The Goenkas also acknowledged the criticism that Tally serves accountants rather than owners. An attempt in 2020 to make changes in its software did not go well. “People threw shoes at me almost,” said Tejas. “We are now not shackled by what was, and we can now make what should be,” he said. Tejas was candid about the missed opportunities: payroll, which Tally ventured into in Dubai around 2004-05 without finding users, and a retail product it later retired. He still sees payroll as a white space. Looking ahead, Tejas struck an optimistic note. Tally has made about seven releases in the last three to four years that many customers are yet to discover, and UI changes are due in the coming weeks and months, he said. Tally is also betting on new geographies, particularly the Middle East and Africa. “We have an incredible two, three decades in front of us... It would be a shame if we let that opportunity slip to create an impactful technology company out of this country.” Edited by Swetha Kannan

title: TechSparks 2026 is here; Zetwerk targets Rs 5,012 Cr IPO
content: Namaskara, Bengaluru! India’s tech capital is buzzing. TechSparks 2026 kicks off today, where the rules of technology are being rewritten, live from Taj Yeshwantpur. Under this year’s rallying cry, ‘The New Tech Order,’ YourStory’s 17th edition is bringing together 10,000+ visionaries, 500 speakers, 1,000 startups, and 300 investors. We aren't just discussing the future of AI, deep tech, and digital infrastructure—we're asking: who gets to build it, and how fast can it scale to billions? From Zoho’s Sridhar Vembu setting the tone on why prosperity cannot be imported and why sovereign tech is India's ultimate shield to CTOs from ShareChat, Angel One, Amagi, and Innovaccer discussing India’s next technological moat beyond cheap talent and massive scale, the event covers a wide range of topics. In a conversation with Shradha Sharma, Founder and CEO, YourStory, Priyank Kharge, Minister for Home, IT, BT & E-Governance, Government of Karnataka, will discuss Karnataka’s new tech-state playbook and how India’s startup capital can learn to govern and secure new technology, not just build it. And don’t miss the official launch of this year's batch of India’s top 30 early-stage innovators setting the agenda for the next decade. In other news, The Wealth Company Alternates said that its Bharat Value Fund, a Category II AIF, has invested about Rs 400 crore in homegrown sports brand Boldfit as part of its Series B funding round. Lastly, Tonbo Imaging India plans to open its Rs 852 crore initial public offering (IPO) on October 15, with a price band of Rs 665-700 per share. The issue comprises 1.22 crore existing shares offered for sale by promoters and investors, with no fresh issue. Incorporated in 2003, the Bengaluru-based company develops thermal imaging equipment, tactical sights and integrated defence sensor platforms. In today’s newsletter, we will talk about Meet IndianRaga founder Sriram Emani Zetwerk sets price band of Rs 143–151 a share Here’s your trivia for today: Which noble gas, named after the Greek word for "hidden," is used to produce blue-white lasers in semiconductor manufacturing? (Scroll down for the answer) Music Meet IndianRaga founder Sriram Emani Having established IndianRaga as a premier global platform for Indian performing arts—fostering thousands of artistic collaborations across the world—Sriram Emani is broadening his creative focus into cinematic storytelling. title: Mesa School of Business raises Rs 110 Cr co-led by Dharana Capital and Elevation Capital
content: Mesa School of Business has raised Rs 110 crore in funding co-led Dharana Capital and existing investor Elevation Capital. This funding round is a combination of equity and debt. The equity component comprised Rs 85 crore and the venture debt of Rs 25 crore was from InnoVen Capital and Alteria Capital. Founded in 2023 by Ankit Agarwal and Varun Limaye, Mesa School of Business will use this funding to build on AI-first curriculum for existing programmes, launch & grow new programmes and build strategic partnerships with the startup ecosystem. According to Mesa, it runs residential programmes built around learning by doing real things. Every student builds and runs a small business, and learns to use AI to build and launch a tech product and claims that more than 100 founders have taught on campus, and students have worked on over 200 projects with startups. Mesa is also backed by founders including Kunal Shah (CRED), Vidit Aatrey (Meesho), Abhiraj Bhal (Urban Company) and Vijay Shekhar Sharma (Paytm). “Mesa is growing quickly, but our tenets haven’t changed: every student builds something real, every student learns new age skills & AI, and founders are always in the room to give them feedback. Those tenets are why startups hire our students, and why so many of them go on to build their own startups. We believe this is the future of education for the top students.” said Ankit Agarwal, co-founder, Mesa School of Business. Mesa has grown from a single postgraduate cohort to over 550 students across three programmes in the last 3 years: a one-year Post Graduate Programme in Startup Leadership, a four-year undergraduate programme on business & entrepreneurship, and Forge, a one-year programme for fresh graduates. “The rapid evolution of modern tech has exposed a glaring disconnect in higher education: students feel unprepared for new-age roles, and companies can’t find job-ready talent. Mesa is bridging that gap by rethinking business education for an AI-first world, ensuring students develop proven, high-impact operational capabilities.” said Vamsi Duvvuri, Founder and Managing Partner, Dharana Capital.

title: Welcome to TechSparks 2026! Here’s all that’s happening on Day 1
content: Namaskara Bengaluru! India’s startup capital is officially ready for TechSparks 2026. The rules of technology are changing, and so is who gets to write them. As YourStory hosts the 17th edition of TechSparks , over the next three days at Taj Yeshwantpur, more than 10,000 attendees, 500 speakers, 1,000 startups and 300 investors will come together under this year’s theme, ‘The New Tech Order’. It is about the people, technologies and businesses shaping what comes next as AI, deep tech and new digital infrastructure change how technology is built, who can build it, and how quickly ideas can reach billions. On the inaugural day, October 13, the stage opens with Sridhar Vembu, Chief Scientist and Co-founder, Zoho, who will make the case that prosperity cannot be imported, and why genuine economic resilience requires India to build more of its underlying technology at home. Following this, YourStory will launch Tech30 2026, unveiling India’s top 30 early-stage tech innovators shaping the next decade of technology. Next, in a panel discussion, Nitin Jain (CTO, ShareChat & Moj), Ajit Narayanan (CTO, Angel One), Srividhya Srinivasan (CTO, Amagi) and Ankit Maheshwari (Founder and CTO, Innovaccer) will decode where India’s next technology advantage will come from now that talent, cost and scale are no longer enough. As the day progresses, hear Srinath Ravichandran, Co-founder and CEO, AgniKul, and Suyash Singh, Co-founder and CEO, GalaxEye, discuss what it takes to build India’s full-stack space economy after the first launch. In a fireside chat, Ambarish Kenghe, Group CEO, Angel One, will explore where the next wave of wealth will come from in India’s AI decade, and how more Indians can participate in it. In the evening, Priyank Kharge, Minister for Home, IT, BT & E-Governance, Government of Karnataka, will be in conversation with Shradha Sharma, Founder and CEO, YourStory. They will discuss Karnataka’s new tech-state playbook and how India’s startup capital can learn to govern and secure new technology, not just build it. Ravi Garg, Managing Director, Enterprise Sales – APAC, Meta, will share how Meta has rebuilt its stack around AI, from Meta AI models to agents on WhatsApp and Instagram, and what that means for businesses building in India. Don’t miss Sameer Nigam, Founder and CEO, PhonePe, as he shares lessons from India’s payments decade and the blueprint for a trillion-transaction economy. The main stage wraps up with Varun Mayya, Founder and CEO, AEOS, on whether every founder needs to build an audience. Other speakers for the day include Nicolas Sauvage, Founder and President, TDK Ventures; Auksė Žirgulė, VP of Product, Hostinger; Manu Saale, MD and CEO, Mercedes-Benz Research and Development India; Anjali Bansal, Partner, Avaana Capital; Anand Jain, Co-founder and CMO, CleverTap; and Rajeev Rastogi, VP – Machine Learning, Amazon, among others. Beyond the main stage, attendees can join masterclasses, hands-on Action Labs and a roundtable on the agent economy. So are you ready to dive in? Because The New Tech Order starts now!

title: Priyank Kharge on Karnataka’s plans to drive tech growth beyond Bengaluru
content: Karnataka’s strategy to ease pressure on Bengaluru is to bring investment to where talent already exists, rather than making talent come to where the investment is, Priyank Kharge, Minister for Home Affairs, Information Technology, Biotechnology, and E-Governance, Govt. of Karnataka, said. The minister was speaking on the sidelines of TechSparks, YourStory’s flagship startup and technology event. In a fireside chat with Shradha Sharma, Founder & CEO, YourStory and Bharat Project, Kharge spoke about the government’s plans to create opportunities for startups and talent beyond Bengaluru through targeted policies, infrastructure and region-specific centres of excellence. “Because of the government’s constant push on its Beyond Bengaluru Mission and local economic acceleration programmes, Mysuru is today delivering close to Rs 4,000 crore in IT exports, Mangaluru close to Rs 3,500 crore, and Hubballi-Belagavi-Dharwad close to Rs 3,000 crore,” the minister highlighted. He said manufacturing units and global capability centres (GCCs) have come up across the state, and that one of Apple’s supply chain partners operates out of Belagavi, doing precision manufacturing. The state has also announced a Bioeconomy Mission covering biotech and agritech, along with related schemes. Kharge said the state runs dedicated entrepreneurship programmes for startups outside Bengaluru and cited recent deals to emphasise the state’s Beyond Bengaluru policy. He said NTT acquired two Udupi-based startups for an undisclosed sum. There have also been acquisitions involving semiconductor design companies in Belagavi and Mangaluru. He added that the founders involved are only 23 or 24 years old. The government is setting up centres of excellence matched to each region’s strengths, Kharge said. “Wherever there is innovation possible, wherever we are able to ensure that the demography or the talent is good, we are tailor-making policies for that region, and we are ensuring that we accelerate growth,” he said. “The government is extremely serious about this, which is why we are building centres of excellence based on each region’s geography and demography. We have an AI centre of excellence at IIIT Dharwad and another at IIIT Raichur. We have an agritech centre in Kalaburagi, and we are setting up a horticulture centre in Bagalkot. Wherever innovation is possible and talent is strong, we tailor policies for that region to accelerate growth,” he added.

title: Apollyon Dynamics quits building drones to make defencetech for the military
content: When Jayant Khatri and Sourya Choudhury started ﻿ Apollyon Dynamics ﻿ in May 2025, the focus of the Hyderabad-based defencetech startup was building drones. Its early portfolio included trainer, endurance, multirole, and FPV systems, with the company selling drones worth more than Rs 1.5 crore last year. But foresight prevails over immediate success. Anticipating saturation in the market, Apollyon has now pivoted. “We have stopped building regular drones. Instead, we have completely shifted towards making higher value products,” says Khatri, Co-founder and CEO of Apollyon Dynamics. The founder says the conventional drone market had become too crowded, with limited room for differentiation. “It’s basically a race to the bottom now. People are just assembling stuff. That included us as well. There’s not a lot of value addition,” he says. The startup’s current portfolio has been rebuilt around three core products: Nightshade, Ahuti Mk II, and Project Piranha. Apollyon now has around 20 full-time employees, two manufacturing labs, and an office in Hyderabad. The new defencetech portfolio Khatri says Nightshade is a jet-powered platform that can be configured as a target drone , decoy, or loitering munition. The company has already conducted multiple tests. “We were the first company in India to launch it from top of a car, a jet-powered system,” he says. The startup plans to begin supplying pilot batches of the target-drone variant to the Indian Army by December, while trials of the loitering-munition version are expected to begin next year. Nightshade's three configurations are designed for different battlefield roles. The target-drone variant is intended to simulate threats during air-defence training, while its decoys can help identify enemy radar positions. The loitering-munition variant combines a jet-powered platform with components typically associated with more expensive missile systems. Khatri says that Apollyon has also repurposed Ahuti, its earlier flagship drone, into an interceptor. “After several iterations, it has reached a top speed of 498 kmph, making it the fastest multirotor drone in India. The India Book of Records has certified this,” shares the CEO, adding that the platform is part of a Make II programme (a special system used by the Indian army to build military hardware) and is being developed with defence partners. Project Piranha expands Apollyon's ambitions beyond aerial systems. The company hasn’t revealed much about it, only that it is a marine-based unmanned system. “We wanted to make a family of products, a family of unmanned systems, and we don’t want to be just known as a UAV-making company,” Khatri says. “We want to be a proper defencetech company with multiple products in our portfolio.” The evolving industry of military tech Apollyon has also stopped selling its mobile drone lab and is instead integrating its systems into command-centre products with companies like the Noida-based Raphe mPhibr and Hyderabad-based Dhruva Space in a collaborative effort. Raphe and Dhruva Space are also customers of Apollyon; they buy Ahuti interceptors. In June 2026, the startup had conducted a pre-seed round raising $480,000 led by Naandi Ventures. The startup is now looking to raise $5 million through a seed round within the next six months. Started as a drone-making student startup, Apollyon’s ambition is now considerably larger: developing cruise-missile-class systems capable of carrying thousands of kilograms and travelling at least Mach 1 by 2030. M R M Babu, who led DRDO’s Agni-V missile programme, has joined as an advisor to help with hiring, programme planning and fund allocation. For 21-year-old Khatri, collaboration will be important as Indian defence companies become larger. “If we want to survive, we can’t do it alone,” he says. “Others have realised that too and have become a lot more collaborative. It’s a good thing for the long term.” Apollyon Dynamics is part of YourStory’s Tech30 cohort—a showcase of India’s most promising startups of 2026, unveiled at TechSparks Bengaluru. Edited by Teja Lele

title: Kubo Care uses radar technology to keep elders safe at home
content: As families increasingly live in different cities and countries, keeping ageing parents safe at home can be a challenge. Full-time attendants require trust and may not always be reliable, while video cameras can feel intrusive, particularly in bathrooms, where more than half of serious falls occur. Wearable devices such as smartwatches and panic pendants offer another option, but seniors may forget to wear or charge them. Bengaluru-based Kubo Care is addressing this problem with a system that monitors movement continuously without recording video or audio, while keeping families informed. The healthtech startup was founded in 2024 by CEO Ayush Agrawal and COO Anurag Ram Chandran. Agrawal, who previously co-founded senior care ecommerce platform Seniority and worked as an AVP at CARS24, experienced the problem firsthand when his father suffered a stroke and fell while alone at home. He remained undiscovered for hours. Chandran, a Schwarzman Scholar who previously ran an Indian NGO, became the primary caregiver for his grandmother after she was diagnosed with Alzheimer’s disease. His experience exposed him to gaps in elderly care. The two met in early 2024 at Antler’s Bengaluru residency and combined their experience in age-tech to develop a system for monitoring seniors at home. Monitoring movement through radio waves Kubo Care’s main device is mounted on a wall or ceiling and uses 60 GHz millimetre-wave (mmWave) radar technology. Similar to how bats use echolocation, the sensor transmits radio signals to map a room in three dimensions, tracking human presence and movement without capturing video or audio. The system uses proprietary AI to analyse this spatial data and identify patterns of movement. It can detect sudden falls in less than a second while distinguishing them from deliberate movements, such as someone slowly lowering themselves onto the floor. Beyond emergencies, the software establishes a baseline of daily habits, tracking sleep restlessness, night-time awakenings, and washroom visits. Changes in these routines can help care teams identify possible health issues, including urinary tract infections or gradual vision decline. Kubo Care holds patents in India and the US for software that converts raw point-cloud data into real-time skeletal models to assess posture and gait. It also has a patented method that reduces false alarms by more than 99%. The startup develops its technology in-house, including hardware, custom firmware, cloud applications and AI analytics. In larger spaces, its software transfers tracking data between multiple wall-mounted devices, allowing continuous monitoring as a resident moves between rooms, including areas with blind spots. For institutional operators, the system provides customisable alerts for bed exits, prolonged washroom stays, and wandering. The hardware can also be connected to ambient sensors that measure room temperature, humidity, lighting and air quality. The information is available through an enterprise management portal for care facility staff and a mobile application for family members. Global B2B plans Kubo Care operates on a Software-as-a-Service (SaaS) model and plans to charge senior care operators between $50 and $70 per device per month. The startup is currently pre-revenue and conducting pilots in India, Japan, and the US. In India, retirement community developers are integrating its hardware into model homes as part of the standard infrastructure. Over the next year, Kubo Care plans to expand its B2B presence in senior care facilities across Japan, the US and India, while preparing for a broader direct-to-consumer launch. “We are able to reduce false alerts by over 99% through our patented method,” Agrawal says. “The roadmap over the course of the next year is to establish ourselves in B2B, especially in the US and Japan, the two largest senior living markets in the world, while preparing for a direct-to-consumer launch by late next year.” Kubo Care is part of YourStory's Tech30 cohort—a showcase of India's most promising startups of 2026, unveiled at TechSparks Bengaluru. Edited by Teja Lele

title: Tech30 2026: Meet the 30 startups building India’s next generation of technology
content: India’s startups are no longer just finding new ways to use existing technology. A growing number are building the technology itself, from satellites and autonomous robots to advanced materials, medical diagnostics and cleaner construction methods. Their work is taking them into sectors that demand years of research, specialised expertise, and significant investment, with the potential to change how industries operate. This shift is at the heart of TechSparks 2026 , YourStory's flagship startup-tech summit, themed ‘The New Tech Order’. One of its key highlights is Tech30, YourStory's annual selection of 30 promising startups working on technologies that could shape India’s future. Sridhar Vembu, Chief Scientist and Co-founder of Zoho Corp, unveiled and presented this year's Tech30 at TechSparks 2026. Speaking on ‘Prosperity cannot be imported: The road to tech independence’, he emphasised the need for India to develop technologies that address its own challenges. "The new tech order is to learn to solve our own problems — foundational problems from agritech to material science to lasers, and also AI. But AI is not to be the be all and end all of it,” Vembu said. Yoonmin Cho, APJ Lead, Snowflake for Startups, and Amar Dixit, CEO, WOI India, also joined Vembu in celebrating this year's Tech30 cohort on stage. Chosen from a pool of applicants, the startups are evaluated by a jury of experienced members of the startup ecosystem, along with YourStory's senior editorial and research teams. The Tech30 report was unveiled at TechSparks 2026, bringing attention to companies working across a range of sectors and technologies. This year’s selection reflects the growing ambition of Indian startups to develop their own technologies and apply them to practical problems. From improving industrial processes and strengthening critical infrastructure to developing new products and markets, these companies are working on challenges in India and overseas. Here are the 30 startups selected for Tech30 2026. Apollyon Dynamics Apollyon Dynamics develops autonomous drones and counter-unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) systems for defence applications. Its portfolio includes high-speed interceptor drones such as Ahuti Mk II, designed to neutralise hostile drones, and Nightshade ADX-1, an autonomous strike platform. Arctus Aerospace Arctus Aerospace is developing high-altitude, long-endurance unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) that operate at around 50,000 feet and can remain airborne for up to 24 hours. Equipped with onboard AI for autonomous navigation, obstacle avoidance, and flight planning, its platforms are designed to provide persistent aerial surveillance and high-resolution imaging for defence, agriculture, infrastructure monitoring, and disaster response. Attox Research Laboratories Attox Research Laboratories develops diagnostic technology to accelerate antibiotic sensitivity testing and help address antibiotic resistance. Its flagship device, Bactolizer, analyses electrical signals from patient samples using specialised algorithms to identify effective antibiotics and appropriate dosages in around two hours, compared with the 24–48 hours typically required by conventional methods. The system uses a reusable testing unit and disposable cartridges designed for hospital settings. Balisto Agritech Balisto Agritech has developed the Balisto 130 Pro, an electric farm machine that combines multiple agricultural operations, including weeding, sowing, spraying, rotavating, and harvesting, on a single platform. Powered by detachable batteries, the machine can be controlled through an onboard dashboard or remotely, while an internet-connected system enables cloud-based monitoring and remote diagnostics. CaliperAI CaliperAI builds AI infrastructure for robots and autonomous machines, using sensor fusion, localisation, and perception to help them navigate the physical world. Its platform captures, analyses, and annotates data from cameras, LiDAR, and navigation sensors, supporting the development of autonomous systems. CraftifAI CraftifAI builds AI software that automates development for embedded systems, edge AI, and IoT devices. Its Orbit platform generates, compiles, and validates code directly on target hardware, helping companies develop software for robotics, drones, industrial equipment, and automotive systems. Curium Life Curium Life is developing AI models that interpret surgical videos, anatomy, and operating-room workflows to support surgeons during procedures. Its technology aims to provide real-time guidance, identify anatomical structures, and flag potential risks, alongside tools that analyse CT scans to assess preoperative risks and abdominal-wall conditions. Dognosis Dognosis is developing BreathEasy, a non-invasive cancer screening test that analyses a person's breath to identify potential cancer risk across multiple cancer types. The system combines trained dogs' ability to detect cancer-related chemical patterns with brain-computer interfaces and machine learning to interpret their responses, flagging higher-risk individuals for confirmatory tests such as imaging and biopsies. Ecopath Ecopath turns industrial waste into construction materials, replacing conventional cement with alternatives designed to cut emissions and water use. Its EcoConcrete supports applications ranging from road construction to masonry products, while its soil-stabilisation and waterproofing solutions address other infrastructure needs. Enerzolve Smart Technologies From battery storage to grid infrastructure, Enerzolve works on the power electronics and instrumentation needed to manage electricity reliably. Its technology portfolio spans bidirectional power converters, software-driven solid-state transformers, and ultrasonic water, gas, and energy meters, serving utility developers, data centres, and defence organisations. EON Space Labs EON Space Labs’ MIRA imaging payload is now in orbit following a launch aboard SpaceX's Falcon 9, marking a milestone for its space-imaging technology. The startup develops electro-optical and infrared systems for space, aerial, and ground surveillance, including imaging payloads, gimbals, and fixed surveillance equipment, with more than 90% of its components built domestically. Evoxia Agricultural residues could offer an alternative route to producing polysilicon, a critical material for solar panels and semiconductors. Evoxia is developing a plasma-based process to turn this feedstock into high-purity silicon, reporting 6N purity in laboratory validation and targeting lower energy consumption and emissions than conventional production methods. Folium Sensing Folium Sensing turns standard optical fibre cables into sensors that detect vibrations, temperature changes, and mechanical strain over distances exceeding 100 km. Its AI-powered monitoring system helps identify pipeline leaks, railway-track cracks, and security threats across critical infrastructure. Harvested Robotics Harvested Robotics' RAKSHAK uses computer vision to identify weeds and high-powered lasers to remove them without damaging crops. Mounted on a tractor, the device can eliminate 80–100 weeds per minute, offering farmers an alternative to chemical herbicides and manual weeding. Hyperonic Engineering Hyperonic Engineering develops hydrogen technologies for mobility and industrial applications, including its H35 dispenser for safe, precision-controlled refuelling. It is also developing microgrids that combine electrolysers, hydrogen storage, and fuel cells for decentralised power generation. Hypersonic Technologies Hydrogen production need not come with direct CO₂ emissions or a single output. Hypersonic Technologies is developing plasma-based reactors that split methane and other gas feedstocks into hydrogen and solid carbon black, which can be used in tyres, plastics, paints, and coatings. ImmunitoAI Designing antibodies from scratch is the focus of immunitoAI , whose AbInitio platform uses AI to create proteins that bind to specific disease-linked targets. Trained on 3D protein structures, the system generates candidate antibodies for laboratory testing, with potential applications in cancer, autoimmune disorders, blood diseases, and neurological conditions. Integra Robotics Integra Robotics equips factories and defence teams with modular robots built for hazardous and hard-to-reach environments. The hardware ranges from robotic arms and underwater manipulators to mobile platforms capable of carrying 500 kg, while software uses field-operation data to train and improve machine capabilities. Kubo Care Kubo Care uses 60 GHz radar and AI to monitor older adults at home or in care facilities, detecting falls without cameras or wearable devices. Its system also tracks movement patterns, sleep interruptions, and vital signs to flag potential health changes, while alerting caregivers to events such as bed exits and wandering. Metastable Materials Discarded lithium-ion batteries contain valuable metals that Metastable Materials recovers for industrial reuse. Its proprietary recycling process separates lithium, nickel, cobalt, and copper without adding chemicals, supplying recovered materials to industries such as glass, ceramics, stainless steel, and automotive manufacturing. MiCoB From army bunkers to residential structures, MiCoB uses robotic 3D concrete printing to automate construction. Its integrated technology combines specialised concrete mixes, printers, and digital design software, enabling the company to produce structures with less labour and material waste; it has delivered more than 650 3D-printed structures across 13 states. MumbaiSemi MumbaiSemi's DhruvaPro chip enables satellite navigation receivers to work across India's NavIC system and global constellations including GPS, Galileo, and BeiDou. The fabless semiconductor startup is also developing integrated circuits for wireless communications, AI hardware, autonomous vehicles, and low-power IoT devices. Neo San Instead of transporting non-recyclable dry waste to disposal sites, Neo San's machines process it where it is generated, using induction heating to reach temperatures of 1,200 degrees Celsius. Its range handles between 25 kg and 500 kg or more of waste daily, serving buildings, hospitals, and industrial facilities, with the resulting ash tested for use in construction. Pramatra Space Pramatra Space is working on encryption systems designed to withstand future quantum-computing threats. Its integrated photonics chip generates entangled photons to create secure encryption keys, which the startup aims to distribute through fibre networks and satellites to protect enterprise communications and critical infrastructure. Red Balloon Aerospace Red Balloon Aerospace is building platforms to operate in near-space, the region between conventional airspace and outer space. Its portfolio includes high-altitude balloons, tethered aerostats, and autonomous stratospheric airships designed for long-duration communications, remote connectivity, disaster response, and surveillance missions. Sanyark Space Sanyark Space is developing low Earth orbit satellites to improve navigation accuracy from metres to centimetres. Its constellation will transmit correction data and stronger signals to support precise positioning, timing, and more resilient communications for defence and infrastructure applications. Segritech Segritech uses computer vision and deep learning to grade fruit by size, colour, and surface defects, processing up to two to three tonnes an hour with 95% reported accuracy. Its machines currently sort produce such as pomegranates and apples, while the startup is developing an autonomous robot to harvest fruit directly in the field. SpaceFields SpaceFields develops solid-propulsion systems for rockets, unmanned aerial vehicles, and defence applications, with capabilities spanning composite propellants, rocket motors, and energetic materials. Its portfolio also includes an aerospike rocket engine, while its in-house technologies are backed by 32 patent filings, 11 of which have been granted. TeraLumen Solutions Terahertz waves are at the core of TeraLumen Solutions’ imaging and testing systems. Its TeraXPLOR platform supports research and spectroscopy, while TeraNIM detects defects and measures coating thickness in industries such as aerospace, automotive, and oil and gas. The company is also developing a system for detecting cancer margins during surgery. Yaanendriya Yaanendriya develops motion sensors, navigation systems, and control software for autonomous machines, from drones to surgical robots. Its positioning technology is also being adapted for GPS-denied environments, including underwater and indoor settings. To access the full report on Tech30 startups, click here . Edited by Teja Lele

title: 'I look to China as gurus': Zoho's Sridhar Vembu
content: India should look to China for lessons on building technological capabilities rather than continue relying on a model centred on providing software services to global companies, Zoho Co-founder and Chief Scientist Sridhar Vembu said on Tuesday. Speaking at YourStory's TechSparks 2026 in Bengaluru, Vembu argued that China had successfully built and retained ownership of critical technologies, allowing it to capture economic value and develop globally competitive businesses. "As much as we think of China as adversaries, I actually look to them as gurus," Vembu said. "Chinese technology landscape has many more lessons to offer us than America does today," he added. Vembu said Zoho's own journey had drawn inspiration from East Asian economies, including Japan, Taiwan, South Korea and China, which developed sophisticated technology industries despite constraints involving resources, population density and economic development. He recalled how Chinese engineers visiting Zoho's Chennai operations around 25 years ago were perceived by their Indian counterparts as coming from a poorer country. "Nobody would say this today," he said, pointing to China's subsequent transformation into a major technology power. Why ownership matters At the heart of Vembu's argument was a distinction between developing technology for others and owning the intellectual property that generates long-term economic value. India, he said, performs a significant share of the engineering work for some of the world's largest technology companies but does not capture a proportionate share of the resulting profits. Vembu claimed that approximately 40–50% of NVIDIA's chip design work, including substantial verification work, happens in India. He also pointed to the significant software development undertaken in the country for Microsoft, Oracle and Cisco. These estimates were not independently verified. "If you are doing 50% of the work and 50% of the value accrued here in a hypothetical world," Vembu said, Karnataka's GDP could be at least two or three times its current size. Vembu contrasted India's experience with that of China, which invested in domestic technology platforms even when they initially lagged their international competitors. He cited Baidu, which emerged as a Chinese alternative to Google, and WeChat, which became central to China's digital ecosystem.
