These platforms, he argued, helped create the technological capabilities, user bases and data ecosystems that supported subsequent innovation, including the emergence of globally competitive companies such as TikTok and advances in AI. "That foundation layer was necessary for them to build the next stage," he said. For India, the lesson was to invest in the underlying technologies rather than focus exclusively on developing the latest AI models. Preparing for a new software economy The push for indigenous technology capabilities also comes as Vembu anticipates significant disruption to India's traditional software industry. During his keynote, he estimated that AI already writes better code than 60–70% of software engineers and could outperform as many as 90% within three to six months. These were his projections, not independently established benchmarks. He compared software development to the handloom industry before mechanisation, warning that AI could dramatically reduce the number of engineers required to build software. However, Vembu said Zoho was not responding to the prospect of automation by laying off employees. Instead, the company was redeploying engineers to work on other technology capabilities. "We know we can redeploy them to build all this stuff," he said. As AI threatens to change the economics of software development, Vembu believes India must use its engineering capabilities to build more of the underlying technology itself. China's experience, he argued, demonstrates the long-term value of that approach, even if the path requires years of investment and the willingness to develop products that may initially lag established global alternatives. "The new tech order is: you have to learn to solve our own problems," he said.

title: Hypersonic Technologies is turning methane into hydrogen and carbon black
content: Hydrogen is expected to play a larger role in helping industries cut emissions, but conventional production methods can leave a significant carbon footprint. Chennai-based Hypersonic Technologies is working on an alternative that produces hydrogen alongside carbon black, a commercially useful material used in tyres, rubber and pigments. Founded in 2023 by Jayaraman Kandasamy and Jayakumar Venkatesan, the climate-tech startup uses staged-plasma pyrolysis to convert methane and biomethane into hydrogen and solid carbon. By producing two materials through one process, it aims to help industrial customers offset production costs while reducing emissions. Kandasamy has more than a decade of experience in Europe, where he worked on plasma technology for aerospace propulsion and explored converting biomass into fuel and hydrogen-rich gases. After returning to India, he founded Hypersonic Technologies to apply this experience to industrial decarbonisation. “Our main mission is converting methane and biomethane into hydrogen and carbon black using staged-plasma pyrolysis technology,” he says. “The aim is to decarbonise industries, particularly oil refineries, steel, cement, and fertiliser, while also producing carbon black through the same process.” One process, two outputs Plasma pyrolysis uses high temperatures to break down hydrocarbons into hydrogen and solid carbon. Hypersonic Technologies combines dielectric plasma with microwave plasma in two stages, which Kandasamy says can improve efficiency and make the process more stable than a single-stage system. The technology aims to address emissions associated with conventional hydrogen production. Kandasamy says steam methane reforming, a widely used method, can emit around 10 kg of carbon dioxide for every kilogram of hydrogen produced. Carbon black production also generates emissions. “Both methods have to move towards cleaner, climate-oriented options. That is why this technology is important,” he says. “Methane is available in several places, where it may simply be flared. Instead, we can use it as feedstock to produce hydrogen and solid carbon.” The company's prototype is at Technology Readiness Level (TRL) 5, meaning it has been validated in a relevant environment. Its lab-scale system at IIT Madras produces around 500 grams of hydrogen per hour, according to Kandasamy. The technology has received a patent grant, and the startup says it has also been validated through the government-backed NRDC-NETRA programme. The carbon black produced is intended for industrial applications, including pigments, and the company is exploring higher-value grades. Kandasamy says Hypersonic has held discussions with established carbon black manufacturers about possible collaborations, although the technology is still at an early stage. “We are looking at producing carbon black that can be used for pigments and other applications,” he says. “The advantage is that hydrogen and carbon black can both be monetised, rather than relying on hydrogen revenue alone.” Moving from the lab to industry Hypersonic Technologies is targeting refineries, steelmakers, cement companies, and fertiliser manufacturers. It is also exploring commercial models that could include equipment sales, operating partnerships, and payments linked to output. Its immediate challenge is scaling the prototype. Kandasamy says the company needs around Rs 5 crore to advance from TRL 5 to TRL 7, with plans for a larger pilot plant once funding is secured. The startup is also seeking government support and has received a Carbon Zero Challenge grant. “We are a deeptech hardware startup, so we need funding to take the technology to the next level,” he says. “Once we establish a plant producing five kilograms of hydrogen per hour and reach the required validation stage, we can pursue orders from refineries and steel companies.” Kandasamy says industrial adoption will depend largely on cost, particularly because major manufacturers cannot easily replace existing infrastructure. He sees new facilities as a more immediate opportunity than retrofitting existing plants. “Industries are very sensitive to cost. They cannot replace existing technology overnight because they have already invested in it,” he says. “But when they set up new facilities, they can evaluate alternatives such as plasma pyrolysis.” For Hypersonic Technologies, the next step is to demonstrate that its process can produce hydrogen and carbon black reliably and economically at a larger scale. Hypersonic Technologies is part of YourStory's Tech30 cohort—a showcase of India's most promising startups of 2026, unveiled at TechSparks Bengaluru. Edited by Teja Lele

title: Pramatra Space is building chip-based quantum security for space and ground networks
content: Bengaluru-based Pramatra Space is building on the quantum-security technology it has been developing since 2023. The startup has completed a third tape-out of its quantum key distribution (QKD) chip, filed its final patent, and is seeing growing interest in using the technology for terrestrial applications. Founder and CEO Richa Hukumchand says that the 11-member startup plans to raise a funding round soon. She also says Pramatra's QKD chip has progressed from two tape-outs at the time of the previous update to three. "Our QKD chip has progressed from two tape-outs to three now, and our latest chips are being tested. We expect the results within the next 15–20 days," she says. The company has also made progress on its intellectual property. Pramatra, which previously held a provisional patent, has now filed the final patent. The specification is complete and examination is under way. Taking quantum security beyond satellites Pramatra's core technology combines QKD with post-quantum cryptography (PQC). While QKD uses quantum physics to distribute encryption keys, PQC uses mathematical algorithms designed to withstand attacks from quantum computers. Hukumchand says feedback from the defence sector prompted the company to take a hybrid approach. "For holistic security, including authentication, we got feedback from defence that they want hybrid PQC and QKD," she says. "For encryption, you can use QKD, but for authentication we need an additional layer of PQC." The spacetech startup is also developing a software layer to orchestrate the different security hardware it deploys. Its data-centre product remains in development, while the company is also seeing demand for terrestrial free-space applications. Hukumchand says the compact nature of its chip-based technology has led to discussions around applications such as secure communication between telecom towers, and between drones and ground stations. "Pilot discussions are going on to see if it can be used for terrestrial operations," she says. Pramatra is also working with Japanese ground-station company Infostellar Inc to explore additional optical ground stations and define requirements for last-mile security. Hukumchand says the startup has made progress on its "hybrid agile methodology" and on integrating PQC into its broader quantum-security offering. Building a space-to-ground security stack Pramatra's original roadmap centred on satellite-based QKD, with its technology designed to sit inside space payloads and connect secure communications infrastructure on the ground. The startup is currently working with about three satellite companies and plans its first in-space demonstration of the product in 2027. It is targeting its first mission with the product in 2028. Hukumchand says Pramatra sees its ability to work across both satellite and terrestrial infrastructure as an advantage. Its competition in space remains global, with Hukumchand naming qtlabs and IonQ among its competitors. Pramatra was also selected for Bharat Innovates, a government-backed programme involving 120 deeptech companies. IISc has validated the company's results and its hypothesis around using chip-based technology for space-based QKD. Pramatra Space is part of YourStory's Tech30 cohort—a showcase of India's most promising startups of 2026, unveiled at TechSparks Bengaluru. Edited by Teja Lele

title: Karnataka govt cautious on use of AI in governance: Priyank Kharge
content: The Karnataka government is being very cautious about using artificial intelligence (AI) in governance as it first needs to understand how this technology can be used responsibly, said Priyank Kharge, Minister for Home, IT, BT & E-Governance, Government of Karnataka. During a fireside chat with Shradha Sharma, Founder & CEO, YourStory and The Bharat Project, at Techsparks 2026, Kharge remarked that the state government's cautiousness stems from the fact it owns an enormous amount of data across multiple sectors. “While I keep data privacy as part of the core and use models to develop agents or solutions, governance is very important,” the minister said. However, this does not mean that the state government will not use AI in governance. The minister said the technology is being leveraged for basic issues such as citizen grievances, health, and mobility. He also said the government has set up a committee to study how to use AI responsibly in governance. The minister highlighted that the Karnataka government is focused on building the much-needed skill base for AI and is engaged with several companies on this. “One knows how these models (AI) are going rogue; so we are cautious, but at the same time we are investing heavily in skilling,” he said. “In the next couple of months, one will see a lot of startups and companies working with the government to solve problems,” the minister said. Also Read Priyank Kharge on Karnataka’s plans to drive tech growth beyond Bengaluru The Karnataka government recently came out with a policy to engage with startups to solve certain governance challenges. The minister said it will adopt a sandbox environment wherein startups can build their solutions. “If they (startups) succeed, I will ensure that it (solution) is taken across the state. But it should be a proven model and, more importantly, it should be solving real-life problems,” said Kharge. The minister highlighted that startups possess the agility and out-of-the-box thinking to come out with innovative solutions. “I think startups deserve a chance to be with the government,” he remarked.

title: Srinath Ravichandran and Suyash Singh on overcoming failure in spacetech
content: The rise of private spacetech in India is frequently celebrated through triumphant headlines, but behind every successful rocket launch or satellite deployment lies a gritty reality defined by hundreds of investor rejections, acute supply chain bottlenecks, and the constant threat of orbital failure. Speaking with Shradha Sharma, Founder and CEO, YourStory and The Bharat Project, at the 17th edition of YourStory’s flagship tech-startup event, TechSparks, Srinath Ravichandran, Co-founder and CEO of AgniKul Cosmos, and Suyash Singh, Co-founder and CEO of GalaxEye, shared practical insights into the complex task of building aerospace ventures in an emerging market. When AgniKul started in 2017, the Indian regulatory framework for private space technology was still evolving, and local venture capital for deeptech was nearly non-existent. Ravichandran faced 275 investor rejections before securing initial backing. Singh encountered similar headwinds at GalaxEye, facing roughly 100 rejections. Their early survival required breaking down ambitious goals into manageable steps rather than relying on rigid long-term master plans. “The first thing to do is to get started, one way or the other... break it down into smaller milestones and start doing something... patience building was the big thing for me at least,” Ravichandran said. This pragmatic mindset also reshaped how both founders approached business models. In Western nations, legacy aerospace programmes often require half a billion dollars in capital before generating revenue. In contrast, AgniKul focused on a pay-per-kilogram transportation model for small satellites, effectively operating as a cargo carrier to orbit, aiming for commercial viability at the $50 to $60 million mark. Explaining this frugal approach, Ravichandran noted, “It is more like you give me $500 million and then I will start giving you money back. That is not how India works. That is not how I am also built.” Following a successful test launch in May 2024 using 3D-printed engines and a mobile launchpad, AgniKul is now preparing for orbital customer flights while testing rocket stage reusability, bringing hardware safely back to Earth to lower launch costs. While launch providers handle transportation, satellite makers face distinct operational challenges. GalaxEye developed OptoSAR, a patented, world-first technology combining optical cameras with synthetic aperture radar to view the Earth through clouds and darkness. However, hardware in space remains unforgiving. Just 30 days after launching India’s largest private liquid satellite to global praise, GalaxEye lost communication with the spacecraft. Reflecting on the setback, Singh emphasised, “Whatever journey we are going through is dealing with those kinds of failures is also going to be very very important for the space industry.” Despite such risks, market demand is expanding rapidly. Surging geopolitical conflicts across the globe have made space-based Earth observation indispensable. “Geopolitics is hotter, and space based surveillance is not an option. It is mandatory. So I think defence is one of the largest markets,” Singh explained. Yet, scaling space ventures in India reveals persistent structural friction. Growth-stage capital and funding checks of $100 million or more remains scarce as institutional investors slowly adapt to deeptech return profiles, where heavy upfront research and development precedes long-term gains. Supply chains also present difficulties. Startups frequently encounter high minimum order quantities, the smallest number of custom components a manufacturer agrees to supply, forcing founders to rely on European vendors for specialised light sensors when domestic equivalents remain too heavy. Despite these hurdles, both founders remain optimistic about human capital. Strict foreign visa regulations in Western aerospace sectors are encouraging top Indian engineers to stay or return home. Combined with employee stock option schemes that offer real wealth creation, deeptech in India is gaining prestige, pushing the nation’s private spacetech ecosystem to mature. “I left technical engineering to go into finance... realised my heart is in engineering, so I came back... Equity is the only way to really get rich... with ESOPs people are starting careers,” Ravichandran noted.

title: Sridhar Vembu says India must prioritise tech sovereignty over spending billions on GPUs
content: Zoho Chief Scientist and co-founder Sridhar Vembu believes investments should be directed towards building infrastructure in India rather than purchasing graphics processing units (GPUs), amid the current euphoria around artificial intelligence (AI). “If I earn $10 billion right now, as a government, I will spend the money on Bangalore infrastructure, Chennai infrastructure, all that. There's no point spending $10 billion on GPUs right now,” Vembu said in the inaugural keynote address at the 17th edition of TechSparks 2026, YourStory’s flagship event. Vembu made the argument against the backdrop of growing excitement and anxiety around AI advancements, particularly concerns about job losses among technology professionals. “Our world is all revolving around software tech. Approximately 97% of the population doesn't care, and they are only on the consuming side of it,” he said. According to Vembu, technology investments should extend beyond software to other sectors, including agriculture and manufacturing. He cited China, South Korea, and Taiwan as examples of countries that have leveraged technology to boost food production and drive economic prosperity. “We need a lot more know-how to inject into agriculture to grow more food,” Vembu said, and added, “Israel is able to grow food in the desert.” To achieve this, Vembu called for India to build sovereignty in foundational technologies and reduce its dependence on foreign countries. He warned that the current geopolitical tensions could leave the country vulnerable to disruptions in access to critical technologies. “The priorities should go towards foundational and upwards. Then only can we build durable prosperity. Prosperity that stays with us.”

title: AI could outperform 90% of coders in six months: Zoho's Sridhar Vembu
content: Rapid advances in AI software creation are driving an existential shift in the industry. With this, traditional coding is entering its “handloom” era, according to Sridhar Vembu, Co-founder and Chief Scientist of enterprise software firm Zoho. Comparing software to a “handloom business,” Vembu said “powerful machine looms” are emerging, referring to automated systems generating complex computer scripts at high speed. Automated systems can already write functional code faster and more efficiently than many human developers, he added. “AI already can write better code than at least 60-70% of software engineers out there. And in maybe three to six months, when things accelerate, AI can do better software than maybe 90% of software engineers,” Vembu said, speaking at the 17th edition of YourStory’s flagship tech-startup event, TechSparks. Venture capitalists like Chamath Palihapitiya have suggested that intellectual property, the underlying proprietary ownership of written software code, is effectively dead, he added. Despite the impending disruption to tech professionals, a huge part of India's population will remain largely unaffected, said Vembu, presenting a counter-intuitive macro perspective. He pointed out that roughly 97% of the broader population does not write software and operates as consumers of technology. Outside major tech hubs such as Bengaluru, districts like Tenkasi in Tamil Nadu or Patna in Bihar will experience minimal direct economic upheaval if coding jobs disappear, said Vembu. Furthermore, as software creation costs fall, automated efficiency could exert deflationary pressure across the broader economy. Lower production expenses mean non-technology workers, including teachers, nurses, and barbers, effectively gain increased real purchasing power as consumer goods become more affordable. The technology ownership gap The true obstacle to national prosperity is not the loss of outsourcing jobs, but a fundamental lack of technology ownership, according to Vembu. Although Indian engineers write a vast portion of software for Microsoft and Cisco, and design up 40-50% of Nvidia's chip design work, the primary financial returns flow to foreign intellectual property holders, the entrepreneur pointed out. To highlight this disparity, Vembu compared a Swiss school teacher, who can earn an iPhone in 3-4 days of work, with an Indian teacher who needs to put in months of work for the same item, despite neither being directly involved in technology. “Ultimately, who has ownership of the technology determines what is the income level of the non-tech people in that economy. Not the income of tech people alone,” Vembu emphasised. Reflecting on the 1990s, he argued that India was misled by Western commentary, such as Thomas Friedman’s writing celebrating IT services outsourcing, which rewarded labour over true technology ownership. To achieve lasting economic independence, India must adopt the strategy of East Asian nations such as Japan, South Korea, Taiwan, and China. Instead of rushing into top-level AI applications, China established durable national sovereignty by developing foundational domestic layers first, including search engines like Baidu and messaging ecosystems like WeChat. Vembu cautioned against prioritising AI over essential industrial hardware and infrastructure, warning that a nation relying entirely on foreign hardware and foreign operating systems risks extreme geopolitical vulnerability. “One reason I came to AI last is, we obsess about AI. We should not be obsessing about AI first. We should be obsessing about the more foundational layers,” he said. True national resilience requires mastering core technologies such as lasers, x-rays, robotics, operating systems, and agricultural technology, according to him. This philosophy guides Zoho's operational strategy amid rising infrastructure demands. The surge in AI adoption has caused server and graphics processing unit costs to explode, with server prices climbing from $8,000 to $45,000. Instead of executing corporate layoffs, Vembu said Zoho is redeploying its engineering talent towards deeptech hardware, including building server infrastructure in-house. Highlighting this approach, Vembu noted, “As much as our jobs are challenged by the present generation of AI. You know why we don’t lay off anybody? We know we can redeploy them to build all this stuff.” The emerging tech order, according to the entrepreneur, demands a shift from exporting software services to securing genuine national technological ownership. Edited by Swetha Kannan

title: Amansa Investments, SBI Mutual Fund, others invest Rs 413 Cr in Tonbo Imaging ahead of IPO
content: Amansa Investments, SBI Mutual Fund and HDFC Life Insurance Company, among others, have invested over Rs 413 crore in defence electronics maker Tonbo Imaging India Ltd through secondary share transactions, valuing the company at around Rs 4,000 crore. This comes ahead of the company's Rs 852 crore Initial Public Offering (IPO). The transactions, executed on September 29-30, involved existing investors CEAQ Singapore and CEAQ India transferring shares to a group of domestic and international institutional investors, according to the Red Herring Prospectus (RHP). The buyers included Amansa Investments, Malabar India Fund, SBI Emergent India Fund, SBI Optimal Equity Fund, HDFC Life Insurance Company, Susquehanna Asia Technology, Valuequest Founders Conviction and 360 ONE Multi-Stage Defence and Space Fund, it showed. Amansa Investments was the largest buyer, acquiring 24.32 lakh shares at Rs 700 apiece, the upper end of the IPO price band, for around Rs 170.24 crore. Susquehanna Asia Technology Pty Ltd, Valuequest Founders Conviction LVF and 360 ONE Multi-Stage Defence and Space Fund each purchased 5.73 lakh shares for Rs 40.10 crore. Akash Manek Bhanshali bought 5.66 lakh shares for Rs 39.59 crore, while SBI Emergent India Fund acquired 5 lakh shares worth Rs 35 crore. SBI Optimal Equity Fund and HDFC Life Insurance Company purchased shares valued Rs 20.09 crore and Rs 16.03 crore, respectively. The company's IPO will open for public subscription on October 15 and close on October 19, with the price band of Rs 665-700 per share. The issue comprises an Offer For Sale (OFS) of 1.22 crore equity shares by promoters and existing investors, with no fresh issue component. Since the IPO is entirely an OFS, Tonbo Imaging will not receive any proceeds from the issue. Founded in 2003 by technologists who had earlier worked with the US Department of Defense and Sarnoff Corporation, the company shifted its focus to defence product manufacturing in 2012 following a buyout by its current promoters. Tonbo Imaging designs and manufactures sensing, processing, communication and guidance systems for surveillance, reconnaissance, targeting and control applications. Its product portfolio includes thermal imaging cores, weapon sights, handheld thermal imaging binoculars, targeting systems, missile seekers, fire control systems and missile guidance systems. The company supplies its products to global defence forces, law enforcement agencies, homeland security organisations and defence original equipment manufacturers (OEMs).

title: New tech order will be built from Karnataka: Priyank Kharge
content: The new tech order will be built from Karnataka, said Priyank Kharge, Minister for Home, IT, BT & E-Governance, Government of Karnataka, at the ongoing Techsparks 2026 summit in Bengaluru. In a fireside chat with Shradha Sharma, Founder & CEO, YourStory and The Bharat Project, the minister said the state government is focused on building the skill sets required to cater to the needs of the global market. The minister elaborated the various measures taken by the Karnataka government to expand the skills base in the state. “We have to come up with a programme of ensuring that we build skill sets by the industry, for the industry, of the industry to ensure that people unlearn and relearn technologies that are going to be relevant for the next decade or so.” The plan will not be limited to the technology sector and also focus also on blue-collar jobs in sectors such as manufacturing, he said. The minister said that, in the last nine months, the state has attracted close to $4.9 billion investments just from the technology sector. Karnataka’s capital Bengaluru is already the fourth largest technology cluster in the world. “Forty-three per cent of all tech investments in India come to Karnataka, and this speaks volumes about the availability of talent here,” the minister remarked. Kharge also highlighted how the talent in the state is engaged in the various centres of excellence (CoE) that the government has created. These CoEs span multiple sectors including agriculture, aerospace, IoT, and AI. The minister said these CoEs have created more than Rs 10,000 crore in market valuation and added that these are run professionally by the industry, with minimum interference from the government. The Karnataka government's ELEVATE programme provides equity-free grants to startups, and this has now been extended to deeptech startups under ELEVATE Nxt. As part of Elevate Nxt, the state government provides Rs 1 crore of equity-free grant to deeptech startups focused on solutions for problems faced by citizens. It also provides market access programmes with 40 countries. “We will be ensuring that we do everything in our capacity to ensure that you succeed as an entrepreneur,” the minister said. The overall goal is to ensure IP creation, CoEs, state government grants, and local accelerator programmes drive the economic growth of Karnataka. Edited by Swetha Kannan

title: Agentic video startup Clueso raises $10M in Series A funding round
content: Clueso, the agentic video platform for business founded by IIT Madras alumni, has raised $10 million in a Series A round of funding led by Dharana Capital, with Founders Future and Neotribe Ventures joining as new investors. The round also saw participation from Y Combinator and f7 Ventures. This round brings the total fund raised to $12 million. Founded in 2023 by Akash Anand, Prajwal Prakash, and Neel Balar, Clueso is based out of California and Bengaluru. It plans to use the funding to scale its enterprise go-to-market reach, deepen its agentic layer, and expand editing capabilities. The startup says more than 1,000 companies use its platform to create videos for functions such as marketing, customer success and education, onboarding and training. Customers include Atlassian, Zendesk, Gainsight, GlobalPartners, Seismic, and Ironclad. Clueso claims that users have reported productivity gains of over 5x and an 80% reduction in video production costs. Clueso's co-founder & CEO Akash Anand noted that the company started out by helping customer-facing teams create product tutorials faster. “We quickly saw the same problem across marketing, sales, training and internal documentation. That made us realise the opportunity was much bigger. Today, Clueso acts as an AI video production team that anyone or any team in the organisation can rely on, handling the work of creating, editing and maintaining videos as the business moves.” Clueso is building AI agents that understand a company’s products, processes, brand and context, and then use that knowledge to create and maintain video across the organisation. Vamsi Duvvuri, Founder and Managing Partner at Dharana Capital said, “With AI, video is evolving from static media files into living, context-aware assets that continuously adapt as business processes and products change. Clueso is building the infrastructure powering this shift.” Edited by Swetha Kannan

title: TechSparks 2026 Day 1: Sridhar Vembu, Priyank Kharge, spacetech founders chart India's 'New Tech Order'
content: The 17th edition of TechSparks opened in Bengaluru with a clear message for India's tech ecosystem: prosperity cannot be imported, and the country must learn to build and own the technologies that solve its own problems. YourStory's flagship startup-tech summit, themed 'The New Tech Order', brought together founders, investors, policymakers and technologists to examine how India can move from providing technology services to owning foundational technology. Vembu: Own the foundation before chasing AI Setting the tone in his inaugural keynote, Zoho Co-founder and Chief Scientist Sridhar Vembu argued that India should prioritise infrastructure and foundational technologies over heavy spending on graphics processing units (GPUs). "If I earn $10 billion right now, as a government, I will spend the money on Bangalore infrastructure, Chennai infrastructure, all that. There's no point spending $10 billion on GPUs right now," he said. Vembu said the real obstacle to national prosperity is not the loss of outsourcing jobs but a lack of technology ownership. He claimed that India does 40–50% of Nvidia's chip design work and a large share of software development for Microsoft, Oracle and Cisco, but the financial returns flow to foreign IP holders. "Ultimately, who has ownership of the technology determines what is the income level of the non-tech people in that economy," he said. He also predicted major disruption to traditional coding, likening software to a handloom industry about to meet machine looms. By his estimate, AI already writes better code than 60–70% of software engineers and could outperform 90% within three to six months. Rather than lay off staff, he said, Zoho is redeploying engineers to deeptech hardware, including building server infrastructure in-house. Vembu urged India to follow the path of East Asian economies, building foundational layers first, as China did with Baidu and WeChat. "As much as we think of China as adversaries, I actually look to them as gurus," he said. Tech30 2026 unveiled Day 1 also saw Vembu unveil Tech30 2026 , YourStory's annual selection of 30 promising startups building India's next generation of technology. He was joined on stage by Yoonmin Cho, APJ Lead, Snowflake for Startups, and Amar Dixit, CEO, WOI India. Chosen by a jury of ecosystem leaders along with YourStory's senior editorial and research teams, this year's cohort spans spacetech, defence, clean energy, advanced materials, agritech and healthcare. It includes counter-drone maker Apollyon Dynamics, NavIC chip developer MumbaiSemi, quantum-safe encryption startup Pramatra Space, laser-weeding robot maker Harvested Robotics, and Dognosis, which is developing a breath-based cancer screening test. Kharge: Taking investment to where talent lives Priyank Kharge , Minister for Home Affairs, IT, Biotechnology and E-Governance, Government of Karnataka, outlined the state's strategy to ease pressure on Bengaluru by bringing investment to where talent already exists. In a fireside chat with YourStory Founder and CEO Shradha Sharma, Kharge said the Beyond Bengaluru Mission is showing results, with Mysuru delivering close to Rs 4,000 crore in IT exports, Mangaluru close to Rs 3,500 crore, and the Hubballi-Belagavi-Dharwad cluster close to Rs 3,000 crore. He pointed to recent deals as proof of the policy's reach, including NTT's acquisition of two Udupi-based startups and acquisitions of semiconductor design companies in Belagavi and Mangaluru, some led by founders aged just 23 or 24. The state is also setting up region-specific centres of excellence, including AI centres at IIIT Dharwad and IIIT Raichur, an agritech centre in Kalaburagi and a horticulture centre in Bagalkot. Spacetech: Building through rejection and failure The day also turned the spotlight on the gritty reality of building India's private space sector. In conversation with Shradha Sharma, AgniKul Cosmos Co-founder and CEO Srinath Ravichandran and GalaxEye Co-founder and CEO Suyash Singh spoke about surviving hundreds of investor rejections—275 for AgniKul and around 100 for GalaxEye. Ravichandran explained AgniKul's frugal pay-per-kilogram model, aiming for commercial viability at the $50–60 million mark. "It is more like you give me $500 million and then I will start giving you money back. That is not how India works," he said. Singh recounted losing communication with GalaxEye's satellite just 30 days after launch, but said such setbacks are part of building the industry. He added that defence is one of the largest markets for space-based Earth observation. "Geopolitics is hotter, and space based surveillance is not an option. It is mandatory," he said. Both founders flagged the scarcity of growth-stage capital and supply chain hurdles, but remained optimistic that ESOPs and stricter Western visa rules are drawing top engineering talent back to India's deeptech ecosystem.

title: AI will create new kinds of jobs: Angel One Group CEO
content: Artificial intelligence (AI) will usher in huge transformation and create new kinds of jobs that one cannot imagine now, said Ambarish Kenghe, Group CEO, Angel One. During a fireside chat at Techsparks 2026 with Shradha Sharma, Founder & CEO, YourStory and The Bharat Project, Kenghe did not discount the impact of AI on jobs. However, he was optimistic that demand for knowledge work will go up, and this would require every individual to transform themselves. He said as AI brings in more efficiency, resulting in higher usage, it could in turn lead to more number of jobs. That is because demand will go beyond what anybody can imagine today, he said. “More jobs will get created but we cannot imagine the kinds of demands that will be placed on human knowledge work,” Kenghe remarked. On the use of AI in creating wealth, the group CEO of Angel One said the technology has solved for access to various channels that create wealth, but it is yet to solve for information and intelligence. He believes AI can bridge the wealth divide by providing insights to investors on how they can deploy their capital by taking into account all risks. “If it (AI) is able to provide you with that information, I think it bridges that divide,” he remarked. Kenghe said institutional investors have the advantages of capital, strategies, and human resources to generate wealth, and AI now has the potential to deliver similar capabilities to retail investors. On leveraging technology to build products that are simple to use by consumers, he said building a simple product is a complicated process. “The biggest challenge is finding the right pain point and solving it really well,” he remarked, adding that the more one fails the higher are the chances of success. Edited by Swetha Kannan

title: Hostinger’s Auksė Žirgulė on winning customer experience in the AI era
content: As AI lowers technical barriers in website building by making coding cheap and accessible, where does this leave businesses building for an online audience? During a fireside chat on the inaugural day of TechSparks 2026 on October 13, Shradha Sharma, Founder and CEO of YourStory and The Bharat Project spoke with Auksė Žirgulė, VP of Product at Hostinger about the changing customer expectations as AI takes over the bulk of software building. Žirgulė highlighted on that experimentation is now the key to building customer experience. "I’ve noticed that their [customer] questions have become more complex. Earlier, the focus was on building a product. Now, customers are asking questions such as: “The market is saturated, and there are already so many products. What should I do next? How do I attract customers? How do I drive traffic?” "They’re asking more fundamental business questions rather than simply asking how to build something," she added. As AI makes building now easier, Žirgulė noted that innovation still remains the key. "You can build anything, but if you don’t know what problem you’re solving, what’s the point? Founders need to understand the problem they’re addressing and test their products as early as possible. The second factor is innovation. There are so many products in the market that you need to find ways to stand out." Žirgulė drove the point home using Apple as an example. "Apple didn’t invent the mobile phone or the touchscreen. What it did was deliver an exceptional customer experience. We sometimes become so focused on building products and watching our competitors that we forget to look for new ways to solve problems. That’s where innovation comes in." However, she noted that even with AI, founders form the core of the company. "Founders are still the final decision-makers. I don’t know what will happen over the next two years; perhaps AI will eventually make many of these decisions. But, for now, a founder’s job is to understand customers and exercise product judgement. AI can do a lot, but the founder still has the final say," added Žirgulė. Adding to this, she said that although there is a rush to build and test a product, without thinking how to take it to the market, founders need to think about the business model and the route to market, not just the product. With AI tools making website in minutes, Sharma asked if the tools can churn out mediocre designs and how founders can navigate this issue Commenting on this, Žirgulė said,"If you have a website that generates sales and supports your business, it may already be doing its job well. It doesn’t necessarily need to win a design award. The same applies to software. You need to test it, speak to customers and iterate. Ultimately, you need to evaluate whether it delivers the intended results." With the increasing number of products now easily available in the market, Žirgulė said that this will eventually change customer expectations. "As more people gain the ability to build products, expectations will rise. Products that deliver better user experiences and higher quality will stand out." As AI agents are now taking independent decisions in business workflows, Žirgulė advises caution. "We need to test how it works, put the right safeguards and capabilities in place, and observe its actions. Experimentation, testing and quality assurance are essential." Founded in 2004 in Lithuania, Hostinger is a global web hosting and domain provider. It claims to serve 4.6 million businesses and creators across 150+ countries.

title: Why Psychological Safety Is a High-Performance Strategy
content: Some of the most significant organisational challenges in a high-growth workplace rarely stem from a lack of technical capability. It begins with a silent choice: an engineer noticing a structural flaw during design review but choosing not to push back; a manager realising a commissioning timeline is no longer viable yet absorbing the pressure rather than escalating the risk; a junior team member withholding a critical operational insight because the perceived cost of speaking up outweighs the comfort of remaining quiet. On the surface, everything appears on track. The project milestone stays green on the executive dashboard, the meeting ends on schedule, and the targets remain unchanged. Yet, somewhere within the organisation, valuable information may not be flowing as effectively as it could. This is the hard operational reality of psychological safety. It is neither an employee perk nor a shift toward softer management. In large-scale energy and infrastructure workplaces, psychological safety is core risk management. It is the organisational capacity to surface uncomfortable truths early, before they compound into systemic failures. The Unseen Cost of Institutional Silence High-performance organisations rely on decentralised decision-making under conditions of ambiguity. In multi-gigawatt energy developments, complex engineering interfaces, tight capital allocations, and strict grid-interconnection timelines leave very little margin for error. Execution quality depends not just on individual technical mastery, but on whether that mastery can move frictionlessly across institutional hierarchies. When employees do not feel fully comfortable expressing candid perspectives, organisational efficiency and decision quality can be affected. Operational risks are flagged late in the build cycle, driving up rectification costs exponentially. Teams spend disproportionate resources correcting flawed baseline assumptions that could have been challenged at inception. According to Gallup’s State of the Global Workplace, employee engagement in India stands at just 23%, alongside elevated daily stress levels (28%) and workplace anxiety. AN organisation derives the greatest value from its talent only when people feel confident sharing insights, concerns, and ideas openly. Trust Is Tested in Moments of Disagreement Psychological safety cannot be engineered through corporate town halls or policy handbooks. Employees evaluate organisational trust through small, unscripted operational moments. A project review where a site engineer challenges leadership assumptions. A functional head telling the executive committee that a deadline requires recalibration. A team member owning an operational oversight before it propagates downstream. What happens in those immediate seconds dictates organisational behavior. A defensive leadership reaction may discourage future contributions. A measured, problem-solving response demonstrates that candor is a professional requirement. Managers do not merely execute strategy; they serve as the cultural filter through which organisational intent becomes daily reality. High Performance Demands High Psychological Safety There is a persistent myth that psychological safety and uncompromising operational standards exist at opposite ends of a spectrum, that driving accountability requires an environment of quiet compliance. The empirical evidence points in the opposite direction. Recent organisational research published in Frontiers in Psychiatry demonstrates a direct correlation between psychological safety, leadership trust, and workplace flourishing, even within high-stress, highly hierarchical operating environments. The research highlights that organisations are most effective when high standards are supported by high psychological safety, enabling both sustained performance and organisational agility. The objective of leadership is not to eliminate pressure, erase aggressive targets, or avoid uncomfortable conversations. Enterprises exist to deliver complex, ambitious goals. Teams will inevitably face tight timelines, market volatility, and resource constraints. The goal is to create an environment where people feel comfortable raising operational risks, seeking support when needed, and contributing their best work. A workplace capable of hearing difficult information early holds a decisive competitive advantage. It corrects courses faster, protects its capital, and retains its top talent. On the other hand, organisations that encourage open dialogue are often better positioned to identify challenges early and respond effectively. The strategic question for executive leadership extends beyond whether support programs exist on paper. The real test is whether our operating environment gives people the psychological room to voice critical truths when it matters most.

title: Tonbo Imaging’s Rs 852 Cr IPO offers investor exit
content: Tonbo Imaging India will open its Rs 852 crore initial public offering (IPO) on October 15, with a price band of Rs 665-700 per share. The issue comprises 1.22 crore existing shares offered for sale by promoters and investors, with no fresh issue. At the upper end, the company is valued at approximately Rs 4,010 crore, or about 79 times FY26 profit after tax. The offer closes on October 19, with listing expected on October 23. The IPO is primarily an exit opportunity for existing shareholders. The largest sellers are CEAQ Technologies Private Limited, offering 49.98 lakh shares, and CEAQ Technologies Pte. Ltd., offering 41.55 lakh shares. Together, they account for about 75.2% of the shares on offer. Promoters Arvind Kondangi Lakshmikumar, Ankit Kumar and Cecilia D’Souza will sell 11.50 lakh, 5.80 lakh and 2.30 lakh shares, respectively. Other sellers include Vinimaya Advisory LLP, Timothy Guy Mitchell, Artiman Partners and other individual and institutional investors. The selling reflects an already investor-heavy ownership structure. Before the offer, CEAQ Singapore held 25.47%, CEAQ India 8.73% and HBL Engineering 14.25%. The three promoters collectively held 17.43%. Other notable shareholders included Florintree Flowtech LLP with 5.17%, Amansa Investments with 4.25% and Yali Deeptech Fund I with 4.19%. If all offered shares are sold, the promoters’ combined stake would fall to approximately 14.01%, CEAQ India would exit its disclosed holding and CEAQ Singapore would retain about 18.22%. These are calculations based on the disclosed holdings and proposed sale quantities, rather than final post-offer figures. The Bengaluru-based company, incorporated in 2003, develops thermal imaging equipment, tactical sights and integrated defence sensor platforms. Its prospects are supported by demand for indigenous defence technology, but its financial performance remains sensitive to large contracts and delivery schedules. Revenue from operations increased 9.55% to Rs 469.08 crore in FY25 before falling 22.69% to Rs 362.65 crore in FY26. The RHP attributes the fall to “delays in the execution of certain international orders due to disruptions arising from the West Asia conflict, as well as the deferment of certain anticipated orders from Fiscal 2026 to Fiscal 2027.” The firm’s export sales fell 93.42% to Rs 20.21 crore, accounting for 5.57% of operating revenue, against Rs 307.34 crore and 65.52% in FY25. Domestic sales rose 114.89% to Rs 337.47 crore, or 93.06% of operating revenue, but could not offset the export decline. Profit after tax fell 30.07% to Rs 50.88 crore in FY26, while EBITDA, or earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation, declined 24.77% to Rs 104.62 crore. The EBITDA margin eased to 28.85% from 29.65%. The company’s operating cash flow was negative at Rs 63.22 crore in FY26, following an outflow of Rs 136.12 crore in FY25. The earlier outflow partly reflected payments for intellectual property acquired from CEAQ Singapore, while rising inventory and order timing have affected working capital. The five largest customers accounted for 53.03% of FY26 revenue, leaving the company exposed to delays or changes in a relatively small number of contracts. India’s defence exports reached Rs 38,424 crore in FY26, up 62.66% year-on-year, according to the Ministry of Defence. Paras Defence expected its exports to roughly double in FY27 amid heightened geopolitical tensions. These trends may support demand for specialised defence electronics. Tonbo’s confirmed order book stood at Rs 314.24 crore at June 2026, with another Rs 118.15 crore of orders received between July and September.

title: IndianRaga founder Sriram Emani explores identity and belonging in Jam Boy
content: Sriram Emani, the founder of IndianRaga, a global platform for Indian performing arts, has an album on Facebook showcasing all the cups he’s collected from different Starbucks outlets in New York. Each of the 74 images shows his name being misspelt. “It’s one of the most common names on the planet. But it was still spelt as ‘Syrian’, ‘Shadam’; not a single person got it right. If you can say Schwarzenegger, Saoirse Ronan, you can say Sriram,” says Emani. This frustrating experience, commonly faced by immigrants, planted the seeds for Jam Boy , Emani’s first film as a writer, director, co-producer and lead actor. Sriram Emani Jam Boy is about a model immigrant who has done everything to be chosen but has not noticed what it costs him to choose himself. Spanning 22 minutes 22 seconds, the film has already won Best Film and Best Web Series at DC Independent Film Festival, received Special Recognition at the Boston International Film Festival, and is now travelling through a growing international festival run. It will premiere on October 13 at the International Film Festival of South Asia, Toronto, North America's largest South Asian film festival. In 2012, Emani started IndianRaga while at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology. Fourteen years later, IndiaRaga has grown into a global performing arts organisation. Its online education programme, Raga Labs Academy, teaches Carnatic vocal music, Hindustani vocal music, Bharatanatyam, and Kathak through a structured syllabus with certification at every level. IndianRaga, headquartered in Boston, Massachusetts, also offers a Raga Fellowship that selects artists through a competitive international panel to create professionally produced collaborative performances. Its artists have performed at the United Nations General Assembly, Lincoln Centre, Jacob’s Pillow, and TEDx. When Emani first spoke about IndianRaga, the platform was just beginning its journey of taking Indian classical arts to new audiences. Since then, several moments have marked its rise. When Shape of You - New Age Carnatic Mix crossed a million views in less than a day, critics who had questioned the blending of classical music with pop began to reconsider. “Maybe this actually works, and maybe this is what's required,” Emani recalls. Another defining moment was Shiva Shambho , which went on to become the world’s most-watched Bharatanatyam video online. The pandemic pushed IndianRaga to move its fellowships, collaborations, and education programmes online. Its artists have since performed at iconic venues, including Lincoln Centre, and at the World Government Summit in Dubai, where three young dancers earned an opportunity after someone in the organising team discovered their work on YouTube. South Asian stories on the global stage Emani is now embracing his own identity as an actor and filmmaker, with a desire to bring South Asian stories to the global stage. He explains, “I wanted IndianRaga to stand on its own, without my name overshadowing the brand. Over time, I realised people also wanted to know the person behind it, so I’m embracing that through acting and filmmaking, telling global stories with South Asian heritage at their centre.” Emani's foray into acting got off to a great start. “I played the first-ever South Asian Bob Cratchit in A Christmas Carol, with 20 shows for 20,000 people. We staged Tiny Tim's funeral in the Hindu tradition, and I did some Sanskrit chanting on stage,” he says. With Jam Boy , Emani is beginning to explore his next chapter, combining his experience of building a platform for South Asian arts with a larger ambition to bring South Asian stories into mainstream global entertainment. The origin of Jam Boy A still from Jam Boy Jam Boy has its roots in Emani’s experiences navigating the South Asian diaspora in the United States. He often noticed that many Indian families stayed within their communities. Children hesitated to take familiar food, such as idli-sambar, to school for fear of being told it smelled. Even accomplished professionals were reluctant to assert their cultural identity. This hesitation percolated into the performing arts space as well, he observed. After graduating from MIT, Emani spent a year hosted by 50 families across 50 cities. It shaped his understanding of how people engage with Indian performing arts beyond the stage. “For IndianRaga, I wanted to see what people think of Indian performing arts when they’re at their least guarded: at dinner table conversations, during a hectic morning, when college applications are coming up, and they have to submit an art supplement,” he says. While working as a summer intern at Lincoln Centre, he found that the Indian diaspora had no idea what they needed to present about South Asian culture on stage. “Indians are building most of the tech in North America that powers the world’s technology and leading these companies, but they are just a simple face. Nobody knows anything behind it,” he says. Hollywood was no different, Emani realised. Actors of South Asian heritage were often restricted to comic roles rather than romantic leads, detectives, or action heroes. He understood that this stemmed from the lack of stories that captured the complexity of South Asian lives. “The diversity, richness and texture I want to portray can only come if I write the story,” he says. That conviction gave rise to Jam Boy . Set in a near future where immigrant workers promised freedom are secretly indentured, Jam Boy follows an Indian coder who smuggles his mother’s forbidden tamarind rice into work and discovers why the company needs him to forget home. Emani says Jam Boy is speculative fiction that plays on the theme that the model immigrant is rewarded for being impressive. “But being impressive is not the same as being fully seen. It’s a character who’s done everything possible to be chosen, but doesn’t realise the cost of choosing himself. He’s led to believe that if he just reaches the next milestone, he can go home or get certain things. But the goalpost keeps changing, because they know model immigrants just keep working, working, working,” he elaborates. The sci-fi element in the film also lets audiences see something that might be happening in the present but isn’t being seen, by imposing boundaries through exaggerated worlds. Emani points out that the film is based on the real-life stories of many of his friends, some of whom have had to refuse promotions to protect their positions because of their H-1B visas, which keep them in technical roles. There’s also a segment about food racism that Indians experience in the US, and also internal gaslighting. “There’s a scene that resonated most with kids growing up here: the protagonist opens his pressure cooker and wants to smell the food, but he’s worried the smell will get on his shirt. So he puts on a rain poncho and comes in to work like that. Every kid from age four to 18 who has watched it says, ‘Whoa, that’s so true.’ That’s what the next generation is taking from it.” A personal connection The film also brings a deeply personal connection—Emani's mother plays his mother in Jam Boy . She has already featured in two IndianRaga videos that garnered over 2 million views across platforms. “On a spiritual level, it feels like an ancestral blessing to have my actual mom in my first film about my culture,” he says. The international premiere in Toronto is a meaningful milestone for Emani as the city has a large South Asian community. “We are waiting to get into one of the festivals in India so we can come to the country through that route first. Then I have a plan to release it online next year,” he says. Meanwhile, the short film is opening doors to larger possibilities: a feature-length version of Jam Boy . He is now working with the Rickshaw Film Foundation’s writers’ room to revise the script while exploring a web series adaptation. Beyond Jam Boy , Emani is developing thrillers that place South Asian protagonists in global settings. As a Trust and Storytelling Fellow at Boston University, his mission is to use storytelling devices to build trust in institutions and people. “I’m calling my umbrella Ancestors and Algorithms . It examines what we inherit and what happens to it as the world around us changes: inheritance through migration, technology, and cultural change,” he says. Edited by Swetha Kannan

title: Ecomm festive sales hit Rs 24,000 Cr in two days; VC funding drops as large deals dry up
content: Dear Reader, India’s ecommerce platforms clocked around Rs 24,000 crore in sales during the first two days of festive shopping, with mobile phones accounting for the largest share by value, according to Redseer Strategy Consultants. Around 6-6.5 crore shoppers placed 8-9 crore orders, with demand extending to electronics, appliances and fashion, particularly among consumers in Tier II cities and smaller towns. India’s digital infrastructure is also drawing attention, with Elon Musk vowing to make Starlink affordable in the country. The move could set up a contest with Mukesh Ambani’s Reliance Jio, as both companies await government clearance for their satellite internet services, days before Jio Platforms’ planned $106 billion IPO. As AI adoption accelerates, questions around safety and accountability are coming to the fore. Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella has called for an “emergency brake” for advanced AI models , urging companies to assume these systems could be compromised and build safeguards from the outset. He wants human-controlled shutdown mechanisms, independent audits and tamper-proof records of AI actions to ensure transparency and accountability as AI agents become more autonomous. The push for stronger safeguards is also bringing independent AI safety evaluators into focus. As OpenAI and Anthropic face growing pressure to subject their models to third-party audits, concerns persist over evaluators’ funding, access to sensitive systems and ability to operate independently, fuelling calls for greater government oversight. In today’s newsletter, we will talk about Zakir Khan, Varun Mayya, and more at TechSparks 2026 VC funding drops as large deals dry up Here’s your trivia for today: Microsoft entered the video game market with which console? (Scroll down for the answer) Events Zakir Khan, Varun Mayya, and more at TechSparks 2026 Zakir Khan, Varun Mayya, and Keshav Reddy are among the latest names on the speaker lineup for YourStory’s TechSparks 2026. The three-day summit will bring together founders, investors and industry leaders to discuss AI, emerging technologies and India’s evolving startup ecosystem. TechSparks 2026 will be held in Bengaluru from October 13 to 15 under the theme ‘The New Tech Order’. Key takeaways: Comedian Zakir Khan, entrepreneur Varun Mayya, and Keshav Reddy are among the latest additions to the speaker roster. Discussions at TechSparks 2026 will explore AI, deeptech, innovation and the changing dynamics of India’s startup ecosystem. TechSparks 2026 will take place in Bengaluru from October 13 to 15, bringing together founders, investors, technology leaders and policymakers. Funding VC funding drops as large deals dry up VC funding into Indian startups fell sharply to $168 million in the week of October 3-9, down from $418 million the previous week. The decline came amid an absence of large deals, with the biggest transaction being myTVS’ $44 million fundraise. Consumer tech brands attracted investor interest, while AI-focused investments remained a key area of attention. Key takeaways: Indian startups raised $168 million across 28 deals, compared with $418 million across 22 deals in the previous week. myTVS raised $44 million, DailyObjects secured $34.3 million, and Lumio raised $12 million. Beyond Appliances raised $11.3 million, deeptech startup Quanfluence secured $10 million, and edtech firm byteXL raised $9 million. News & updates Acquisition: Nvidia is in early talks to invest further in or acquire AI startup Reflection AI. The move could strengthen its push into open-weight AI models as US firms compete with lower-cost Chinese alternatives. Global Economy: The Middle East war, soaring energy prices, and record-high debt are set to dominate this week’s IMF-World Bank meetings in Bangkok, as policymakers grapple with inflation and mounting economic risks, particularly for developing nations. What you should watch out for YourStory’s flagship startup and technology summit, TechSparks 2026 , is bringing together founders, investors and industry leaders, with discussions on AI, emerging technology, and entrepreneurship. Apple’s October 13 “Welcome Home” launch is expected to focus on its smart home ecosystem, with a new smart home hub featuring a display and AI-powered Siri among the anticipated announcements. title: Zetwerk sets IPO price band at Rs 143-151, aims to raise Rs 5,012 Cr
content: Zetwerk, the Bengaluru-headquartered manufacturing marketplace, has set a price band of Rs 143–151 per share for its initial public offering (IPO), targeting a valuation of Rs 25,583 crore. The IPO comprises a fresh issue of shares and an offer for sale (OFS). The company has expanded the size of the public issue to Rs 5,012 crore. The fresh issue has been increased from Rs 2,600 crore to Rs 2,830 crore, while the OFS component has been expanded from 9.68 crore shares to 14.45 crore shares. Early investors, including Peak XV Partners, Lightspeed Venture Partners, Accel India, and Kae Capital, have increased the number of shares they plan to sell. The proposed share sale by the founders remains unchanged. Lightspeed Venture Partners plans to sell 2.51 crore shares, followed by Peak XV Partners with 2.34 crore shares and Accel India with 1.2 crore shares. Zetwerk’s promoters, Amrit Acharya and Srinath Ramakkrushnan, will sell 1.42 crore shares, while promoter group entity Creovate Innovation will offload 2.30 crore shares. The IPO will open for subscription on October 15 and close on October 19. The anchor investor book will open on October 14, and the shares are expected to list on the stock exchanges on October 23. Zetwerk plans to use around Rs 2,160 crore from the fresh issue to repay debt. The remaining proceeds will be allocated towards acquisitions, strategic investments and general corporate purposes. The company reported revenue of Rs 15,913 crore in FY26, a 40.4% increase from Rs 11,332 crore in FY25. However, its losses widened to Rs 1,606.2 crore in FY26 from Rs 370.7 crore in the previous fiscal year, largely due to a one-time charge. Established in 2017, Zetwerk is a digital manufacturing marketplace that connects businesses, manufacturers and suppliers on one platform. In Q1 FY27, its revenue from operations grew 55% year-on-year to Rs 4,118 crore, while losses from continuing operations narrowed to Rs 64 crore from Rs 881 crore in the year-ago quarter.

title: Startup news and updates: daily roundup (October 12, 2026)
content: From ShuruKar, billed as the first nationwide district-level movement of its kind that aims to help young Indians identify a problem worth solving in their district, to India’s ecommerce platforms recording around Rs 24,000 crore in sales during the first two days of festive shopping, here are the latest developments across sectors . Featured Stories ShuruKar: Your next business could start in your hometown A big idea does not need a big city. That was the message from Patna, where The Bharat Project, an initiative by YourStory, launched ShuruKar at Dr. APJ Abdul Kalam Science City in Rajinder Nagar. Developed in partnership with DPIIT and Startup India, ShuruKar is billed as the first nationwide district-level movement of its kind. It aims to help young Indians identify a problem worth solving in their district, build a business around it, and continue growing it. The launch drew Shri Nitish Mishra, Minister, Urban Development and Housing Department, Government of Bihar, along with founders, students and young entrepreneurs from across the state. The consultancy firm estimated that shoppers placed about 8-9 crore orders across all platforms, including Amazon, Flipkart, Meesho, Ajio and many other marketplaces. Redseer Strategy Consultants, Associate Partner, Nikhil Dalal told PTI that the first two days pointed to India's festive e-commerce basket getting wider. The growth is being led by order volumes, with consumers spreading spend beyond mobiles into fashion, electronics and appliances as well.
